Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. List the methods of training to improve muscle performance in post-traumatic fracture at the wrist joint.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 1a — Interventions for impaired muscle performance

★ Memory hook — Muscle-performance staircase: isometric in cast → active/AROM after cast → isotonic resisted → CKC / isokinetic / PNF → functional grip. Progress when pain-free and the callus is mature.

1Introduction

This answer lists the methods of training used to rebuild muscle performance after a post-traumatic fracture at the wrist (typically a distal-radius / Colles' fracture). Because the wrist is immobilised while the fracture unites, training must respect the healing stage, protect the fracture site and progress from isometric work inside the cast to resisted and functional loading. The methods below are grouped by that healing-driven logic.

2Physiology

Principle first

After a distal-radius/colles' wrist fracture, muscle performance is rebuilt in a healing-driven sequence: immobilisation → post-immobilisation → remodelling. Treatment moves from isometric (no joint motion, protects the fracture site) → active/isotonic → resistant → functional training, governed by callus maturity, pain and effusion.

3Pathophysiology

After a distal-radius (Colles') fracture the wrist is immobilised while the fracture unites. Disuse during this period causes atrophy and weakness of the muscles crossing the immobilised joint (wrist flexors and extensors), accumulation of oedema, and pain and stiffness that limit motion. These are the deficits — loss of strength, endurance and grip — that the training methods below must reverse without stressing the healing fracture site or the immature callus.

4Answer

Isometric (during cast/early healing)

Isometrics of the muscles crossing the immobilised joint — tendon-gliding isometrics for wrist flexors/extensors and the "cast-squeezing" routine: gentle graded holds (6–10 s ×10) within pain limits prevent atrophy and pumping oedema. Include shoulder/elbow/full-hand work outside the cast to preserve the kinetic chain; teach AROM of free fingers hourly.

Isotonic & isoinertial progression

Once radiological union and pain allow: active → active-assisted → dynamic (isotonic) contractions against gravity, then graduated resistance — wrist curls, reverse wrist curls, pronation/supination with a small dumbbell or elastic band; eccentric emphasis later for tendon tolerance. Progressive-resistance principle (DeLorme/Zinovieff or daily adjustable): 2–3 sets of 8–12 at 60–75% of estimated 1RM, progressed ~5–10% when 12 repetitions become easy.

CKC, isokinetic and PNF
  • Closed-kinetic-chain weight-bearing — palm-down table pressing, quadruped rocking, wall push-ups — loads the wrist in functional co-contraction with less shear.
  • Isokinetic dynamometry at 6–12 weeks — constant-speed training for objective, accommodated resistance and documented torque curves.
  • PNF — rhythmic stabilisation around the wrist for endurance of the stabilisers; contract–relax for wrist-flexion ROM restriction.
Functional & grip progression

Grip: putty progression (soft → firm), pinch boards, towel wringing; dexterity — pegboards, coins, writing; then task-specific loading (carrying a bucket, turning a jar). Outcome tracking: dynamometric grip strength (target: within 10–15% of the uninjured side), PRWE score.

Fig 1 — The muscle-performance staircase from in-cast isometrics to function. Sequencing drawn as steps is what earns the phase-logic marks without you writing paragraphs.
The phrase the evaluator circles: "sequence dictated by fracture healing — isometrics in cast, isotonic after union." A list of exercises without phase-logic and without grip-strength outcome target stays a 6/10.

5Recent advances

  • Coughlin et al. (2021) — randomised trial in non-operatively treated distal radius fracture found that a self-managed advice leaflet or video gave patient-reported outcomes equivalent to face-to-face therapy after cast removal.
  • Menek & Dansuk (2025) — randomised trial showed closed-kinetic-chain exercises (wall loading, ball rolling) improved joint position sense, DASH function, wrist range of motion and activity-related pain over conventional therapy in conservatively treated distal radius fractures.
  • Gutiérrez-Espinoza et al. (2022) — systematic review and meta-analysis found that adding mobilisation-with-movement and manual lymphatic drainage significantly improves wrist and upper-limb function and reduces hand oedema after distal radius fracture.
  • Soares et al. (2023) — updated meta-analysis found supervised and non-supervised exercise programmes give similar results, so a structured self-management programme is a reasonable alternative to costly one-to-one therapy.
  • Handoll & Elliott (2015) — Cochrane review of rehabilitation for distal radial fractures confirmed exercise-based rehabilitation is safe and aids early return of function, but the evidence is low quality and progression should follow fracture healing.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 1a.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — resistance exercise chapters.
  3. Hislop H et al. Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing. (reference 7).
  4. Hoppenfeld S, Murthy VL. Treatment and Rehabilitation of Fractures. (reference 16).
  5. Coughlin T, Norrish AR, Scammell BE, Matthews PA, Nightingale J, Ollivere BJ. Comparison of rehabilitation interventions in nonoperatively treated distal radius fractures: a randomized controlled trial of effectiveness. Bone Joint J. 2021;103-B(6):1033–1039.
  6. Keene DJ, Srikesavan C, Achten J, et al. Flexibility and resistance exercises versus usual care for improving pain and function after distal radius fracture in adults aged 50 years or over: protocol for the WISE randomised multicentre feasibility trial. Pilot Feasibility Stud. 2022;8:55.

On the evaluation form — Q1: Femoral shaft fracture — muscle performance training

I. Subjective examination

Mr Ravi, 28 years. History: road-traffic accident 10 weeks ago — right distal femoral shaft fracture treated by open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) with a locking plate; non-weight-bearing for 6 weeks, now partial weight bearing. Chief complaints: thigh pain (NPRS 4/10 on walking), knee stiffness, quadriceps weakness and an axillary-crutch gait. Red-flag caution: fever after immobilisation would suggest DVT or infection — refer. Vitals: BP 122/80 mmHg, PR 84/min.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Well-healed lateral thigh scar; moderate quadriceps atrophy; mild effusion.

On palpation. Scar mobile; no callus tenderness.

1. Motor assessment. Knee ROM (active and passive) 10-90° with a 10° extension lag. MMT (MRC 0-5): quadriceps 3/5, hamstrings 3+/5, hip abductors 4/5. Girth: 3 cm less on the right at 15 cm above the patella. Reflexes: knee jerk diminished (attributed to pain inhibition).

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation intact; straight leg raise negative.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Stairs managed with a rail. Outcome measures: LEFS 0-80 (higher = better); TUG; NPRS 0-10; MRC 0-5; thigh girth.

4. Gait analysis. Axillary-crutch gait at 50% weight bearing.

5. Balance. Single-leg stance 5 seconds; TUG 18 seconds.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this lower-limb case; axillary-crutch handling noted under gait.

7. Coordination. Not formally documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

Serial radiographs of the femur per the orthopaedic surgeon to confirm union (progression to hopping only after radiological union); no current films reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Percussion (heel tap)Tap the heel with the knee extendedPain at the fracture siteCallus irritable; continue protection — result not documented (no callus tenderness on palpation)
Vibration (128 Hz fork)Place the fork over the fracture regionPain reproducedDelayed union; monitor radiographs — result not documented
Homans' signPassive ankle dorsiflexionCalf painPossible DVT — refer; result not documented in this patient
Weight-bearing toleranceGraded axial loading from 25%Pain at the fracture siteNot ready for full weight bearing — positive in this patient (currently 50% partial weight bearing, pain 4/10 on walking)
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Quadriceps 3/5
  • Knee ROM 10-90°
  • Pain 4/10 on walking

Functional limitations

  • Assistive (crutch) gait
  • Stair difficulty

Disabilities

  • Unable to work or ride a two-wheeler
11. Functional diagnosis

Right distal femoral shaft fracture 10 weeks after ORIF, with quadriceps weakness (3/5), knee ROM restriction (10-90°), pain on walking and a partial-weight-bearing axillary-crutch gait, limiting stair climbing and preventing return to work and two-wheeler riding.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): pain ≤2/10; knee ROM 0-110°; quadriceps 4/5; one-crutch gait.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): full ROM; quadriceps and hamstrings 5/5; reciprocal stairs; return to work by 12 weeks.

13. Treatment plan

Phase 1 (weeks 1-2): isometric quadriceps sets — 10 × 10-second holds, 4 times/day; patellar mobilisations; cryotherapy after exercise. Phase 2 (weeks 3-6): progressive resisted exercise — knee extension in the 90-40° arc, hamstring curls and hip abduction, 3 × 10 on alternate days, load increased 5-10% at 10 repetitions (10-RM rule); mini-squats 0-45° and 10-cm step-ups. Phase 3 (weeks 6-10): isokinetics at 60-180°/s; resisted cycling 20 minutes; hopping only after radiological union.

14. Home programme

Daily quadriceps sets; straight-leg raises in three planes, 3 × 10; heel slides; cycling 20 minutes; gait drills.

Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Explain the mechanism of pain relief using electrotherapy modalities.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 2b — Electrotherapy in managing pain

★ Memory hook — TENS pair: conventional 40–80 Hz (DeLisa; 80–100 Hz in Indian texts) vs 2–4 Hz (up to 8 Hz) acupuncture-like (with contraction, naloxone-reversible).

1Introduction

Pain relief by electrotherapy rests on three linked mechanisms — segmental gate control, endogenous-opioid (descending) inhibition, and counter-irritation — each reached with a different current and dose. This answer explains each mechanism and then matches it to the modality and parameters used in practice (TENS, IFT, HVPG, ultrasound).

2Physiology

Segmental gate control — the workhorse

TENS floods large-diameter Aβ afferents, which excite the substantia gelatinosa interneurons of the dorsal horn and close the gate on nociceptive transmission to T cells (Melzack & Wall — cross-reference Paper II Q8). Conventional TENS: high frequency 80–100 Hz, short pulse duration 50–100 μs, amplitude strong but comfortable — rapid onset, short carry-over, best for acute pain.

Endogenous opioid (descending) systems

Low-frequency acupuncture-like TENS (2–4 Hz, 200–300 μs, high intensity enough to produce rhythmic muscle contraction) drives C-afferent/muscle afferent input → hypothalamic-PAG activation → raphe magnus & locus coeruleus descend via dorsolateral funiculus → serotonergic/noradrenergic inhibition of dorsal-horn cells; β-endorphin, met-enkephalin and dynorphin are released — naloxone-reversible, giving slower onset but hours of carry-over, best for chronic pain.

Other mechanisms
  • Counter-irritation / hyperstimulation analgesia — intense input suppresses pain at spinal and supraspinal levels (brief-intense TENS).
  • Vasomotor & anti-oedema effects — muscle pumping and IFT improve circulation, clearing algesic metabolites; HVPG reduces oedema-dependent pain.
  • Placebo/expectation — a genuine neurobiological component via descending pathways; honest explanation of the modality potentiates it.

3Pathophysiology

Nociceptive (pain) signals travel to the dorsal horn on small-diameter Aδ and C fibres and are relayed by transmission (T) cells to higher centres. The gate-control model holds that activity in large-diameter Aβ afferents can inhibit this relay; when nociceptive input is intense or the gate is held open, pain is felt. Central sensitisation of dorsal-horn neurons can amplify and prolong this input — which is why different mechanisms and different current parameters are needed for acute versus chronic pain.

4Answer

Modality-wise application
ModalityKey settingsDominant mechanism
Conventional TENS80–100 Hz, 50–100 μs, 20–30 minGate control
Acupuncture-like TENS2–4 Hz, 200–300 μs, muscle twitchOpioid/descending
IFTBeat 20–80 Hz (DeLisa); 90–130 Hz analgesia common in practice (2–10 Hz also); vector & quadripolarGate + circulation
HVPGHigh voltage, twin-peaked pulsesDeep comfort + oedema
Ultrasound3 MHz superficial, 1 MHz deepThermal + non-thermal tissue repair
Fig 2 — The TENS decision flow: pain type on the left, parameters and mechanism on the right. Reproducing this flow in the exam answers mechanism AND prescription together.
Answer format that scores: mechanism → parameters → clinical situation for each modality. The exam trap is writing only "TENS closes the gate" — the opioid mechanism with 2–4 Hz and naloxone-reversibility is what carries the remaining half.

5Recent advances

  • Johnson et al. (2022) — the meta-TENS systematic review and meta-analysis (381 randomised trials, 24,532 participants) found moderate-certainty evidence that strong non-painful TENS at or close to the painful site reduces pain intensity during or immediately after application, irrespective of diagnosis.
  • Johnson et al. (2022) — the same work found that stimulation frequency did not modify the outcome once a strong non-painful sensation was produced, so the quality (intensity) of the TENS sensation matters more than the exact frequency.
  • Gibson et al. (2017) — Cochrane evidence indicates low-frequency TENS analgesia is mediated mainly via µ-opioid receptors and high-frequency via δ-opioid receptors, which is clinically relevant when a patient is already on opioid medication.
  • Gibson et al. (2017) — the updated Cochrane review of TENS for neuropathic pain reports low-certainty evidence of benefit over sham, with only minor adverse events such as skin erythema and itching.
  • Gibson et al. (2019) — a Cochrane overview of reviews (51 randomised trials) found the evidence that TENS relieves chronic pain remains of very low certainty, so it should be used as an adjunct to active therapy rather than a stand-alone cure.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 2b; Paper II Unit 10.
  2. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. — pain-suppression systems.
  3. Melzack R, Wall PD. Science. 1965 (primary).
  4. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).
  5. Gibson W, Wand BM, Meads C, Catley MJ, O'Connell NE. Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) for chronic pain – an overview of Cochrane Reviews. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2019;4:CD011890.
  6. Johnson MI, Paley CA, Howe TE, Sluka KA. Efficacy and safety of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) for acute and chronic pain in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 381 studies (the meta-TENS study). BMJ Open. 2022;12(2):e051073.
Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Methods used to improve balance after an ankle sprain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 3c — Postural stability and balance in rehabilitation

★ Memory hook — Balance progression ladder: floor → foam → disc → wobble board → BOSU → perturbation.

1Introduction

Balance retraining is central after an ankle sprain because ligament injury damages the mechanoreceptors that drive postural control. This answer explains why balance training is needed and then lays out the static, dynamic, reactive and sport-specific methods, with progression and discharge criteria.

2Physiology

Postural control integrates visual, vestibular and somatosensory input — including the mechanoreceptors of the ankle ligaments and capsule — to keep the centre of mass over the base of support. The ankle contributes heavily in single-leg stance, so its joint-position sense and the speed of the peroneal (evertor) reflex are the key physiological determinants tested by balance tasks.

3Pathophysiology

Why balance training at all

Ligament injury damages mechanoreceptors of the ATFL/CFL → arthrogenic proprioceptive deficit — delayed peroneal reaction time and impaired single-leg stance — the strongest predictor of chronic ankle instability and re-sprain. Balance retraining cuts recurrence roughly by half in trials: the treatment rationale an evaluator wants in line one.

4Answer

Static balance progression
  • Single-leg stance on floor — eyes open → eyes closed → head turns; progress to foam/air-disc surfaces, stork with reach tasks.
  • Bilateral → unilateral stance on tilt board fixed to one plane.
  • Time and sway (reach direction) targets: 30–45 s stable single-leg stance as a milestone before dynamic tools.
Dynamic balance training
  • Wobble/rocker boards and BOSU: two-leg → single-leg → with ball-catch; 3–5 min sets daily.
  • Star Excursion / Y-Balance Test as both training and retest (target: within ~90%+ of the uninjured limb and no pain).
  • Multi-directional stepping/lunges onto discs, resisted band walks in single-leg control.
Reactive & sport-specific
  • Perturbation training: therapist nudges the tilt board while the patient stabilises; sudden ball drops for reaction training.
  • Hopping/jumping progressions — sagittal, frontal, rotational; single-leg hop-and-stick landings.
  • Agility: shuttle runs, ladder drills, cutting and turning on the previously injured ankle; taping/bracing as an adjunct during early return.
Progression & discharge criteria

Progress by surface (stable→unstable), stance (bilateral→unilateral), sensory (eyes open→closed→distracted) and task (static→dynamic→reactive). Discharge: symmetric SEBT reach, ≥95% hop-test limb symmetry, and confident single-leg balance — before return to sport.

Fig 3 — The balance progression ladder — floor to sport. Every rung is one treatment session you can plan; the discharge criterion sits at the top.
The examiner expects the causal chain: torn mechanoreceptors → poor balance → re-sprain — THEN the methods. Quote the ~50% recurrence-reduction figure as "balance training halves recurrence" only if you attribute it correctly to trials (Verhagen et al.) — otherwise write "substantially reduces".

5Recent advances

  • Mollà-Casanova et al. (2021) — a systematic review and meta-analysis (15 randomised trials) found balance training significantly improves function, ankle instability and dynamic balance in people with chronic ankle instability.
  • Kim et al. (2021) — a randomised controlled trial showed that adding stroboscopic (partial visual-deprivation) glasses to balance training further improved perceived instability and Star Excursion Balance Test anterior reach.
  • Taghavi Asl et al. (2022) — a randomised trial confirmed that wobble-board training improves balance, ankle proprioception and jump-landing kinetics in chronic ankle instability.
  • Luan et al. (2021) — a systematic review and meta-analysis found that progressive strength training for chronic ankle instability produces clinically detectable improvements in balance and patient-reported outcomes, supporting loading alongside balance work.
  • Shamseddini Sofla et al. (2021) — whole-body vibration combined with a shoe with an unstable surface improved dynamic balance and hop performance in chronic ankle instability.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 3c.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — balance training chapter.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).
  4. Verhagen E et al. Balance-board training & ankle-sprain recurrence. Am J Sports Med. (primary evidence)
  5. Mollà-Casanova S, Inglés M, Serra-Añó P. Effects of balance training on functionality, ankle instability, and dynamic balance outcomes in people with chronic ankle instability: systematic review and meta-analysis. Clin Rehabil. 2021;35(12):1694–1709.
  6. Taghavi Asl A, Shojaedin SS, Hadadnezhad M. Comparison of effect of wobble board training with and without cognitive intervention on balance, ankle proprioception and jump landing kinetic parameters of men with chronic ankle instability: a randomized control trial. BMC Musculoskelet Disord. 2022;23:888.

On the evaluation form — Q3: Balance retraining after ankle sprain

I. Subjective examination

Ms Anita, 22 years old, badminton player. Chief complaints: left ankle pain with "giving way" on uneven ground, and inability to run or hop. History of present illness: inversion injury of the left ankle 3 weeks ago during badminton — grade II lateral ligament sprain (ATFL ± CFL). This is her first sprain, and the aim is to prevent chronic lateral ankle instability. No past medical, family or socioeconomic history is recorded. Symptom analysis — site: left ankle below the lateral malleolus; onset: traumatic, 3 weeks ago; type: pain with episodes of giving way; severity: NPRS 3/10; aggravating factors: uneven surfaces; relieving factors: rest. Red-flag screen: none reported. Vitals normal.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Mild swelling below the lateral malleolus with resolving ecchymosis; attitude of the foot in slight eversion; slightly everted antalgic gait.

On palpation. Tenderness over the ATFL and CFL insertions.

1. Motor assessment. Active inversion limited by about 30% due to pain; manual muscle testing — peronei 3/5, dorsiflexors and plantar-flexors 4/5; circumferential girth +1.5 cm at the malleolar level.

2. Sensory assessment. Light touch intact (no dermatomal loss documented); ankle joint position sense impaired with the eyes closed — this proprioceptive deficit is driving the instability.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Unable to run or hop; fewer than five single-leg heel raises on the left. Outcome measures: TUG 11 s; Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool 0–30 (lower = worse); FAAM — ADL subscale 0–84, sports subscale 0–32; NPRS 0–10; Star Excursion Balance Test; Balance Error Scoring System.

4. Gait analysis. Slightly everted antalgic gait.

5. Balance. Timed single-leg stance with eyes closed shows clear asymmetry (impaired proprioception); Balance Error Scoring System in use.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this lower-limb presentation.

7. Coordination. Not separately documented; the balance deficit is attributed to impaired ankle joint position sense (see 2 and 5).

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Anterior drawerStabilise the tibia, draw the heel forwardsExcess anterior talar shift, soft end-feelATFL laxity — result not documented for this patient
Talar tiltInvert the calcaneus in neutralExcess talar tiltCFL laxity — result not documented for this patient
Squeeze / external rotationCompress the fibula on the tibia; rotate the foot outwardsDistal syndesmotic painSyndesmosis injury — no syndesmotic findings documented
Single-leg stance, eyes closedTimed one-leg standClear asymmetryImpaired proprioception — positive in this patient
10. Problem list

Impairments.

  • Pain NPRS 3/10 with impaired ankle joint position sense (eyes closed)
  • Peroneal weakness (3/5)
  • Inversion limited by about 30% due to pain
  • Mild residual swelling with resolving ecchymosis

Functional limitations.

  • Unable to run or hop
  • Unable to walk on uneven ground (giving way)
  • Antalgic gait

Disabilities.

  • Away from badminton
11. Functional diagnosis

Grade II left lateral ankle sprain with peroneal weakness, pain-limited inversion and impaired ankle joint position sense, producing dynamic balance deficits and inability to run, hop or walk on uneven ground, keeping the patient away from badminton.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): pain ≤1/10; full pain-free ROM; eyes-closed single-leg stance 30 s; normal gait.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): peronei 5/5; 10 heel raises; hop and Star Excursion within 10% of the right; return to badminton with a brace.

13. Treatment plan

Phase 1 (wk 1–3): resisted eversion with a band 3 × 10; single-leg stance eyes open 30 s × 5/day. Phase 2 (wk 3–5): eyes-closed stance with head turns; wobble board double then single leg 2 × 2 min. Phase 3 (wk 5–8): BOSU squats, lateral step-downs, hops two-leg to single to diagonal 3 × 10. Phase 4 (wk 8–12): cutting drills; semi-rigid brace in sport for 3–6 months.

14. Home programme

Daily balance routine 15 min; heel raises 3 × 15; calf stretch 3 × 30 s.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Functional training in individuals who have undergone TKR.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 3e — Functional training & physical activity promotion

★ Memory hook — TKR timeline skeleton: day 0–2 bed exercises + first ambulation; ≈2 wk ~90° flexion, wounds healed; ≈6 wk normal gait pattern; ≈3 months full function.

1Introduction

Functional training after total knee replacement (TKR) practises the real tasks the patient must return to — transferring, walking, climbing stairs and Indian-context activities of daily living — built on the range-of-motion, strength and endurance foundation established in the early post-operative phase. The programme is criteria-based and follows post-operative days and weeks.

2Physiology

The knee functions through the interplay of range of motion, muscle strength and endurance. After TKR the implant restores the joint surface while soft-tissue healing and muscle re-activation determine function; the early programme therefore works on the ROM–strength–endurance foundation before loading functional tasks.

3Pathophysiology

Knee osteoarthritis destroys articular cartilage and is the usual reason for TKR; after surgery the deficits are post-operative, not osteoarthritic — joint effusion, arthrogenic muscle inhibition (reflex quadriceps weakness), an extension lag, a flexion contracture, and restricted patellar glide that risks arthrofibrosis. These impairments limit stair climbing, floor sitting and Indian-toilet use, and are what functional training must overcome.

4Answer

Principles

Functional training practises the task itself — transferring, walking, climbing — retraining movement patterns in the real environments the patient will return to (home/fields/factory floors), built on the ROM–strength–endurance foundation. After TKR the sequence follows post-op days and is criteria-based, not calendar-based.

Phase-wise programme
  • Day 0–3: ankle pumps, quad sets, SLR (if active extension allows), CPM as per protocol, cryotherapy; sit on the bed edge; standing within the frame — hallux-to-hip activation, not just the knee.
  • Day 1–5: transfer training — log-roll to sit, sit-to-stand from a raised chair pushing armrests; gait in a walker/rollator (frame → crutches → stick, progress as quad control returns); short ward-walk distances building to 100 m; stair training late week 1–2: "up with the good, down with the bad."
  • Week 2–6: functional strengthening — mini-squats (0–45°), step-ups on a 10–15 cm block, sit-to-stand from lowering chair heights, leg press in safe ROM; stationary cycle starting with high seat gradually lowered; outdoor uneven-terrain walking.
  • Week 6–12: advanced function — reciprocal stairs, single-leg balance, tai-chi-style weight-shifts, cycling outdoors, swimming (avoid breast-stroke whip-kick with prosthetic stress), return to light work and driving (usually ≥6 weeks once quad control and reflexes are sound).
ADL integration & criteria

Train the actual tasks: squatting to a low Indian toilet (practise with a commode chair initially), floor-level activities with caution for high-flexion prostheses, carrying weights while walking, temple kneeling/lotus positions graded per implant flexion limits (most standard implants 110–125° flexion — deep squat/sitting cross-legged needs caution and prosthetic design advice). Progress criteria: independent painless gait, stair descent control, TUG <12 s, Knee Society Score improvement.

Fig 4 — The TKR milestone timeline with the stair rhyme and Indian ADL adjustments written under the axis. Timelines like this scream 'clinical protocol knowledge' for one minute's drawing.
Indian-context sentences earn bonus credit: low-toilet transfers, sitting cross-legged, and temple-floor kneeling — always with the flexion-limit caveat. Also remember the gait-training maxims "good leg to heaven, bad leg to... " — examiners smile at correct stair rules quoted with the rhyme.

5Recent advances

  • Xu et al. (2021) — a randomised controlled trial found a self-developed home-based enhanced-knee-flexion programme (low stool plus exercycle) was non-inferior to standard supervised physiotherapy after TKA, with better early range of motion.
  • Bäcker et al. (2021) — an app-based rehabilitation programme randomised trial was as effective as usual physiotherapy after TKA, supporting app-based telerehabilitation for the functional phase.
  • Bade et al. (2017) — an early high-intensity versus low-intensity rehabilitation trial found high-intensity progressive resistance training is safe after TKA, but its early benefit is limited by arthrogenic muscle inhibition.
  • Artz et al. (2015) — a systematic review and meta-analysis (18 randomised trials) found physiotherapy exercise after TKR improves physical function and pain in the short term (3–4 months), although the benefit is not maintained long term.
  • Nguyen et al. (2022) — a randomised trial of multidisciplinary prehabilitation before total knee replacement found no short-term improvement in functional independence, so prehabilitation is not a guaranteed gain.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 3e.
  2. Maxey L, Magnusson J. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. (reference 13) — TKR protocol.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — functional training chapters.
  4. Efficacy and safety of a self-developed home-based enhanced knee flexion exercise program compared with standard supervised physiotherapy to improve mobility and quality of life after total knee arthroplasty: a randomized control study. J Orthop Surg Res. 2021;16:382.

On the evaluation form — Q4: Functional training after TKR

I. Subjective examination

Mrs Kamala, 62 years old, homemaker. Chief complaints: difficulty climbing stairs and rising from the floor; her daily routine includes cross-legged sitting and the use of an Indian toilet. History: total knee replacement 6 weeks ago for knee osteoarthritis. Pain evaluation: NPRS 3/10, worse with kneeling and stairs, relieved by rest and ice. Red-flag screen: none reported. Vitals stable.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Well-healed midline surgical scar, knee effusion, quadriceps atrophy; single-cane gait.

On palpation. Scar mobile; patellar glide restricted; effusion present.

1. Motor assessment. Knee ROM 5–110° (aim 0–125° for floor sitting); extension lag 5°; quadriceps and hamstrings 4/5; circumferential girth +1.5 cm.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation intact except mild numbness lateral to the scar (expected); knee jerk present.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Stairs managed step-to with a rail; floor rising assisted. Outcome measures: TUG 12 s; WOMAC 0–96 (higher = worse); KOOS 0–100 per subscale; Oxford Knee Score 0–48 (higher = better).

4. Gait analysis. Single-cane gait; step-to stair pattern with a rail.

5. Balance. Single-leg stance 15 s.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation.

7. Coordination. Not separately documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

Patellar glidePassive medial-lateral patellar glidingGlide under one quadrantRestricted — positive; mobilise (arthrofibrosis risk)

10. Problem list

Impairments.

  • 5° flexion contracture with 5° extension lag; knee flexion limited to 110°
  • Quadriceps and hamstrings 4/5 with quadriceps atrophy (+1.5 cm girth)

Functional limitations.

11. Functional diagnosis

Post-TKR status (6 weeks) with residual knee flexion contracture, extensor lag, effusion and quadriceps weakness, restricting reciprocal stair climbing, floor sitting and Indian-toilet use, and preventing independent household management.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): ROM 0–120°; extension lag abolished; cane-free indoor gait; TUG under 10 s.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): flexion 125–130° for assisted cross-legged sitting; reciprocal stairs; independent Indian-toilet use; WOMAC improved by 30%.

13. Treatment plan

Phase 1 (0–2 wk post-op): quad sets, SLR, heel slides, cryotherapy. Phase 2 (2–6 wk): cycling with the seat lowered; extension and curl PRE 3 × 10; aqua walking. Phase 3 (6–12 wk, functional training): step-ups 10–20 cm; chair stands 3 × 10; step-over-step stairs; graduated floor sitting — long sitting, side sitting, then assisted cross-legged sitting on a cushion; squat progression with chair support and grab bars at the Indian toilet; no loaded deep kneeling for 3 months. Phase 4 (3–6 months): community walking, cycling.

14. Home programme

Daily quad sets 3 × 10, heel slides, step-ups, cycling 15 min; ice after activity.

Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Describe the neurodynamic management of the peripheral nervous system.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 4b — Neurological concepts & functional methods in MSK dysfunction; syllabus references 26–27

★ Memory hook — Neurodynamics rule: tensioners lengthen both ends (strong); sliders move one end while the other releases (gentle) — slide for irritable, tension for stable.

1Introduction

Neurodynamic management examines and treats the mechanical interface of the peripheral nervous system — the nerve's ability to glide, slide and elongate within its containers. This answer covers the concept, the neurodynamic tests, the slider-versus-tensioner treatment techniques, and progression with precautions.

2Physiology

Concept

Neurodynamics (Butler, Shacklock) examines and treats the mechanical interface of the nervous system: nerves must glide, slide (a few mm) and elongate (~2–15% strain tolerance) within their containers — intervertebral foramina, muscle tunnels (carpal tunnel, pronator), fascial beds. When interfaces narrow (disc bulge, oedema, fibrosis) or the nerve itself becomes mechanically sensitive, movement reproduces symptoms — "adverse neural tension."

3Pathophysiology

When the interfaces that contain a nerve narrow (disc bulge, oedema, fibrosis) or the nerve itself becomes mechanically sensitive, movement of the limb reproduces symptoms — "adverse neural tension" or neurogenic mechanosensitivity. The nerve loses its normal longitudinal and transverse excursion, so even ordinary movements become painful. Neurodynamic management is directed at restoring this gliding and reducing mechanosensitivity.

4Answer

Neurodynamic tests
  • ULNT1 (median nerve): shoulder abduction–external rotation, forearm supination, wrist–finger extension, elbow extension, contralateral/ipsilateral neck side-flexion sensitises.
  • ULNT2 (median, anterior): shoulder girdle depression + elbow extension + wrist supination/extension; ULNT3 radial; ULNT4 ulnar bias.
  • Lower limb: straight-leg-raise + ankle dorsiflexion/eversion, slump long-sit — neural vs hamstring differentiation.
  • Interpret by symptom response across sensitising additions, side-to-side differences, and whether structural differentiation changes the symptoms.
Treatment techniques
  • Sliders (gliding): move the joint proximal to the nerve one way while the distal joint moves the opposite way — maximal nerve glide, minimal tension; painless, used in irritable conditions (e.g., during ULNT1, abduct shoulder while flexing the neck).
  • Tensioners: lengthen both ends of the nervous system simultaneously (e.g., knee extension with cervical flexion) — stronger stretch, used only when irritability is low, always short of symptom reproduction.
Progression & precautions

Dosage: low amplitude, low velocity, frequent (10–15 oscillations, several sets daily), progressed by range and load. Contraindicated/cautioned over acute inflammation, spinal cord signs, unresolved central sensitisation, recent nerve repair. Evidence: neural mobilisation adds small-to-moderate benefits over exercise alone for carpal tunnel syndrome and cervicobrachial pain — combine with interface treatment, never as an isolated ritual.

Fig 5 — Slider vs tensioner side by side: two nerves, two arrow pairs. Once you can draw these two panels, the entire technique section of the answer organises itself.
Define slider vs tensioner in ONE crisp sentence each — "slide one end while releasing the other" vs "lengthen both ends." Then give one named technique with its nerve bias (ULNT1 = median). Vague hand-waving about "nerve stretching" loses the whole c-section.

5Recent advances

  • Basson et al. (2017) — a JOSPT systematic review and meta-analysis (40 trials) found neural mobilisation reduces pain and disability in chronic low back pain and neck–arm pain, with positive neurophysiological effects (such as reduced intraneural oedema) in carpal tunnel syndrome.
  • Núñez de Arenas-Arroyo et al. (2021) — a systematic review and meta-analysis in JOSPT (22 randomised trials, n = 1203) found neurodynamic techniques reduce pain and improve function in carpal tunnel syndrome (very low certainty), with no clear effect on symptom severity or grip strength.
  • Jiménez-Del-Barrio et al. (2021) — a meta-analysis of manual therapy in carpal tunnel syndrome found that neurodynamic mobilisation (sliding and tensioning) improved pain, function and nerve-conduction studies versus sham or control.
  • Nee et al. (2012) — a randomised trial in the Journal of Physiotherapy found that neural tissue management (education, manual therapy and nerve gliding) gave immediate, clinically relevant pain relief and functional gain in nerve-related neck and arm pain, with no evidence of harm.
  • Zaheer & Ahmed (2023) — a meta-analysis reported neurodynamic techniques significantly reduced Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire symptom and functional severity scores and improved nerve conduction in mild-to-moderate carpal tunnel syndrome.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 4b.
  2. Butler DS, Jones MA. Mobilisation of the Nervous System. (reference 26).
  3. Shacklock M. Clinical Neurodynamics. (reference 27).
  4. Short-term effects of neurodynamic techniques for treating carpal tunnel syndrome: a systematic review with meta-analysis. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2021;51(12):566–580.
  5. Neurodynamic techniques in the treatment of mild-to-moderate carpal tunnel syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Clin Med. 2023;12(15):4888.

On the evaluation form — Q5: Carpal tunnel syndrome — median neurodynamics

I. Subjective examination

Mrs Sunitha, 45 years old, tailor. Chief complaints: 8 months of night-time numbness and tingling in the right thumb, index and middle fingers, relieved by shaking the hand ("flick sign"); she drops pins. Aggravating factors: repetitive pinning and a flexed-wrist sleeping posture. Red-flag screen and relevant negatives: no neck pain, no diabetes; no other medical, family or socioeconomic history given. Vitals normal.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Early thenar flattening; protracted shoulders and a flexed wrist posture at the machine.

On palpation. Tender, taut carpal tunnel.

1. Motor assessment. Thumb abduction (APB) 4/5; grip about 70% of the left; pinch reduced; full passive ROM.

2. Sensory assessment. Altered light touch and two-point discrimination in the median digits (thumb, index, middle); the palm is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the tunnel.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Buttoning, threading and scissor use slowed; writing tolerated for 20 minutes. Outcome measures: QuickDASH 0–100; Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire (symptom severity and function scales); Semmes-Weinstein monofilament testing.

4. Gait analysis. Normal.

5. Balance. Not relevant to this upper-limb presentation.

6. Hand function. Reaching, grasping and releasing preserved but fine-motor control slowed — buttoning, threading and scissor use slowed; pins are dropped during tailoring; no assistive device.

7. Coordination. Not separately documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

Nerve conduction study: mild-to-moderate median nerve compression at the wrist.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Phalen's / reverse PhalenFull wrist flexion (or extension) held 60 sMedian-digit paresthesiaCarpal tunnel compression — result not separately documented (NCS confirms the diagnosis)
Tinel's signPercussion over the tunnelTingling into the median digitsMedian nerve irritation — result not separately documented
Carpal compressionSustained pressure over the tunnel for 30 sSymptoms reproducedCarpal tunnel syndrome — result not separately documented
ULNT-1 (median neurodynamic)Shoulder abduction, elbow extension, wrist/finger extension, cervical lateral flexion awaySymptoms reproduced, eased by lateral flexion towardNeurogenic mechanosensitivity — result not separately documented
10. Problem list

Impairments.

  • Median nerve paresthesia (night-time, median digits)
  • APB weakness (4/5) with early thenar flattening
  • Restricted neurodynamic excursion

Functional limitations.

  • Slowed fine-motor tailoring (buttoning, threading, scissor use)
  • Disturbed sleep

  • Reduced work output
11. Functional diagnosis

Mild-to-moderate right carpal tunnel syndrome with median-digit paresthesia, APB weakness and restricted median neurodynamic excursion, slowing fine hand function and disturbing sleep, with reduced tailoring output.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): night symptoms abolished with a neutral wrist splint; sleep uninterrupted; daytime tingling ≤1/10.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): pain-free grip and pinch within 10% of the left; symptom-free tailoring shifts; independent self-management.

13. Treatment plan

Phase 1 (wk 1–2): education, neutral wrist night splint, activity modification (neutral wrist at work, padded handles). Phase 2 (wk 2–4, neurodynamics): median nerve sliders — elbow extension with wrist flexion, then elbow flexion with wrist extension, 10 repetitions, 2–3 sessions/day, pain-free; tendon glides (straight, hook, table-top, full fist) 5 each, 3 times/day; tensioners (cervical lateral flexion away with wrist extension, 30-second holds) once irritability settles. Phase 3 (wk 4–8): putty grip 3 × 10, wrist PRE, scapular re-education.

14. Home programme

Night splint for 6–12 weeks; daily sliders and tendon glides.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. What are the therapeutic effects of orthotics? What are the various orthotics used in the upper limb?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 5b & Paper IV Unit 6c — Prescription of orthotic devices; role of assistive devices

★ Memory hook — Every orthosis answer starts at the three-point pressure system: one corrective force, two counter-forces.

1Introduction

An orthosis is an externally applied device used to support, immobilise, correct or assist a body segment. This answer states the therapeutic effects of orthotics, classifies them, lists the common upper-limb orthoses with their indications, and gives the principles of prescription.

2Physiology

Joints and segments are held in balance by the interplay of bony alignment, capsuloligamentous restraint and muscle forces. An external device can change this balance by applying controlled forces — classically the three-point pressure system, in which one corrective force is balanced by two counter-forces — and by positioning a segment to protect healing tissue.

3Pathophysiology

The conditions orthoses treat share a common pathology of malalignment, imbalance and tissue stress: joint instability, muscle weakness or spasticity, and the soft-tissue contractures that develop when a segment is held in a poor position. Left unchecked, these produce deformity, pain and loss of function — the targets of corrective, supportive and assistive orthoses.

4Answer

Therapeutic effects

An orthosis (external applied device) acts by: support & stabilisation (rest painful joints), immobilisation/ protection (fracture, tendon repair), correction or prevention of deformity (serial casting principles; prevent contracture), assistance/substitution of weak muscles (dynamic splints), controlled motion (hinged joints permitting a safe arc), oedema & scar control, reduction of pain through rest and alignment, and functional enhancement (positioning hand for use).

Classification

Static (no moving parts) vs dynamic (with springs/rubber-band outriggers); prophylactic vs corrective vs functional; serial vs wearable; material: low-temperature thermoplastics, plaster, prefabricated vs custom.

Upper-limb orthoses — name and indicate
  • Hand & wrist-hand: cock-up/ resting wrist splint (median nerve palsy, wrist tendonitis, carpal tunnel), static resting hand splint (spastic hand, burns), thumb spica (de Quervain's, CMC OA, scaphoid), gutter/ MCP-ulnar drift splint (RA), opponents splint, finger gutter & mallet-finger splints, knuckle-bender & dorsal block (after flexor-tendon repair), swan-neck/zig-zag correction rings.
  • Dynamic splints: spring-wire outriggers for radial nerve palsy (wrist drop), low-profile dynamic MCP flexion assist, reverse knuckle benders.
  • Elbow: static posterior splint / hinged-locked brace (ligament injury, post-op limits), turnbuckle splint for elbow flexion contracture.
  • Shoulder: sling/abduction pillow (post-op repair, humeral fracture — 30–45° for rotator cuff repair), airplane splint (burn axilla), clavicle strap, figure-of-eight; hemi-sling for subluxation after neurological injury.
Prescription principles

Match the orthosis to the pathology phase and the goal; check fit (no pressure over bony prominences — ulnar head, radial styloid), skin checked at each removal and daily; 3-point pressure system for correction; review at every visit; combine with therapeutic exercise — the splint positions, the muscle still has to be retrained.

Fig 6 — The orthosis classification tree with examples filling the leaves. An examiner can mark five examples straight off this sketch even if your prose rambles.
Answer one orthosis = one indication = one joint position. Examiners test this as a matching list (e.g., "which splint for wrist drop? radial nerve — spring-wire dynamic cock-up"). Two or three joint-position specifics ("MCPs at 60–70° flexion in the resting splint") lift the whole answer.

5Recent advances

  • Karjalainen et al. (2023) — the Cochrane review of wrist splinting for carpal tunnel syndrome found limited evidence: splinting may give little or no short-term benefit, though night-time splinting may improve the patient's overall sense of improvement.
  • Aranceta-Garza & Ross (2021) — a study of ten commercially available wrist–hand orthoses found that many do not adequately restrict wrist motion or preserve grip strength, so fit and design features matter to the outcome.
  • Synek et al. (2023) — a systematic review found moderate evidence that dynamic orthoses improve grasp, pinch and dexterity after stroke when combined with therapy as usual.
  • Alexander et al. (2022) — a systematic review and meta-analysis found non-robotic dynamic hand orthoses improved upper-limb function and dexterity after stroke, although the included trials were small and at high risk of bias.
  • Oud et al. (2021) — a scoping review found emerging evidence for 3D-printed hand orthoses in forearm fractures and spasticity, but high-quality controlled trials are still lacking.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 5b & Paper IV Unit 6c.
  2. Chui KC et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation. (reference 18).
  3. Saunders R et al. Hand and Upper Extremity Rehabilitation. (reference 20).
  4. Cooper C. Fundamentals of Hand Therapy. (reference 21).
  5. Splinting for carpal tunnel syndrome. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2022.
  6. Effectiveness of 3D-printed orthoses for traumatic and chronic hand conditions: a scoping review. PLoS ONE. 2021;16(11).

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation diminished over the dorsal radial hand and first web space; median and ulnar territories intact.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Unable to grip, write or hold tools; tenodesis grasp possible with the wrist splinted. Outcome measures: QuickDASH 0–100 (higher = worse); grip and pinch dynamometry; MRC 0–5.

No imaging or electrodiagnostic reports reviewed at this assessment; the humeral shaft fracture is clinically healed (non-tender) in a brace.

Radial nerve palsy (wrist drop) secondary to a humeral shaft fracture, with absent wrist and finger extension and diminished dorsal radial sensation, preventing grip and tool use and causing work disability.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): functional position maintained in a cock-up splint; passive ROM preserved; oedema controlled.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): extension returns with regeneration (about 1 mm/day); functional grasp and pinch; return to work by 4–6 months.

13. Treatment plan

Therapeutic effects of the orthosis: protection, substitution of lost movement, contracture prevention, assistance of weak muscles, oedema control. Phase 1 (wk 1–2): static cock-up splint worn by day, removed 3 times daily for passive extension and tendon glides; retrograde massage; elevation. Phase 2 (wk 2–6, reinnervation signs): EMG biofeedback and motor re-education; graded resisted exercise; dynamic splint when voluntary extension appears. Phase 3: grip and pinch tasks, tool handling, web-space sensory re-education.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Describe the evidence-based electrotherapy management in soft tissue injury.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 5 (b–e) — Physical agents, currents for tissue healing, evidence-based electrotherapy

★ Memory hook — Match the modality to the healing phase: inflammation (TENS/IFT + cryotherapy + pulsed US/HVPG) → proliferation (thermal US + laser + graded load) → remodelling (shockwave + eccentric loading); exercise is the driver, modalities buy the window.

1Introduction

Evidence-based electrotherapy in soft-tissue injury means matching the modality and its dose to the phase of tissue healing, with exercise — not machines — as the primary driver of repair. This answer maps the modalities onto the inflammatory, proliferative and remodelling phases and adds the evidence caveats.

2Physiology

Phase-logic first

Soft-tissue healing passes through haemostasis/inflammation (days 0–5), proliferation (day 5–3 wk) and remodelling (3 wk–12+ mo). "Evidence-based" means: the modality and dose must match the phase's cell population, and exercise — not machines — remains the primary driver of repair.

3Pathophysiology

Acute soft-tissue injury disrupts collagen fibres and the microvasculature, triggering haemostasis and an inflammatory cascade (days 0–5) with pain, swelling and loss of function. The proliferative (day 5 – 3 wk) and remodelling (3 wk – 12+ mo) phases then rebuild and reorient the tissue. The modality must match the cell population and events of the current phase — an anti-inflammatory dose in the acute phase, a loading/tensile stimulus later.

4Answer

Acute/inflammatory phase
  • Analgesia without adding swelling: conventional TENS (80–100 Hz) or IFT (beat 20–80 Hz per DeLisa; 90–130 Hz for pain in Indian practice) for pain gate; cryotherapy first 48 h for vasoconstriction and analgesia.
  • Pulsed shortwave (non-thermal, Metres/CMV ~low intensity) and low-dose therapeutic ultrasound (pulsed 1:4, 0.1–0.3 W/cm²) to support membrane repair and oedema resolution — evidence modest; use where pain/effusion blocks active movement.
  • HVPG for oedema control (muscle pumping); microcurrent (µAT) claims to boost ATP for epithelial repair — weak clinical evidence.
Proliferative & remodelling phase
  • Continuous therapeutic ultrasound (3 MHz, 0.5–1.0 W/cm² for superficial structures like lateral epicondyle; 1 MHz for deep) — thermal effect increases collagen extensibility (pre-stretch) and perfusion.
  • Low-level laser (820–904 nm) for tendon injuries — evidence debated — DeLisa finds no benefit in lateral epicondylitis, while newer trials report short-term pain relief.
  • Extracorporeal shockwave therapy for insertional tendinopathies (plantar fasciitis, calcific supraspinatus) — the strongest modern evidence in this family.
  • Progressive loading exercise is the proven remodelling driver — modalities buy the pain-free window that allows it (e.g., eccentric Alfredson protocol for Achilles tendinopathy).
Fig 7 — Modality mapping onto healing phases — the one diagram that makes this answer examiner-proof.
Evidence caveats — the "evidence-based" part

Cochrane reviews find ultrasound no better than placebo for most soft-tissue injuries; shockwave and eccentric loading carry the strongest support; TENS has short-term analgesic benefit. So: justify every modality with a goal (pain window, tissue extensibility, oedema), set measurable reassessment endpoints, and stop what isn't working — that is the evidence-based behaviour, beyond brand loyalty to machines.

The word "evidence-based" is in the question for a reason: quoting at least ONE negative trial finding (e.g., "Cochrane: ultrasound vs sham in soft-tissue injury — no significant difference") is what distinguishes a postgraduate answer from a student listing machines.

5Recent advances

  • Charles et al. (2023) — a systematic review and meta-analysis of shockwave therapy found high-quality evidence of a large effect on pain and function in plantar fasciitis, but negligible effect in patellar and Achilles tendinopathy.
  • Challoumas et al. (2021) — a network meta-analysis of patellar tendinopathy concluded shockwave is not superior to sham; eccentric loading, with or without adjuncts, remains first-line treatment.
  • Karanasios et al. (2021) — a meta-analysis of lateral elbow tendinopathy found shockwave gave no clinically significant benefit over sham or corticosteroid injection.
  • Tripodi et al. (2021) — a systematic review and meta-analysis found that photobiomodulation (low-level laser) added to exercise significantly improves pain and function in tendinopathy compared with sham plus exercise, supporting laser as an exercise adjunct.
  • Challoumas et al. (2021) and Charles et al. (2023) — the consistent message remains that progressive exercise drives tendon remodelling and modalities such as shockwave only buy a pain-free window that allows it.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 5 (b–e).
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).
  3. Robertson VJ, Baker KG et al. Electrotherapy evidence reviews. Phys Ther / Aust J Physiother.
  4. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — tissue-healing & loading chapters.
  5. Karanasios S, Tsamasiotis GK, Michopoulos K, Sakellari V, Gioftsos G. Clinical effectiveness of shockwave therapy in lateral elbow tendinopathy: systematic review and meta-analysis. Clin Rehabil. 2021;35(10):1383–1398.

On the evaluation form — Q7: Electrotherapy in acute soft tissue injury

I. Subjective examination

Mr Farhan, 26 years old, footballer. Grade II hamstring strain (biceps femoris) 48 hours ago while sprinting. Chief complaint: posterior thigh pain, NPRS 5/10 on walking. Aggravating factors: walking, sitting and knee extension. Red-flag screen: no back pain and no distal symptoms (lumbar origin excluded). Vitals normal.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Developing posterolateral thigh bruising.

On palpation. Tender, indurated area 8 cm above the knee with local warmth; no palpable gap.

1. Motor assessment. Active knee ROM 20–90° (pain-limited); knee flexion 2/5, knee extension 4/5; girth +1 cm.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation and reflexes normal; straight leg raise reproduces thigh pain at 40°, unchanged by neck flexion — muscular, not neural.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Unable to jog or climb stairs. Outcome measures: NPRS 0–10; LEFS 0–80; time to a pain-free jog.

4. Gait analysis. Antalgic gait.

5. Balance. Preserved.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation.

7. Coordination. Not separately documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Active movementFlex/extend the knee through rangePain on contraction in one directionScreens tissue irritability — positive (pain-limited active ROM 20–90°)
Passive stretchOverpressure at end-range knee extensionPain on stretch, opposite to the painful movementContractile tissue under stretch — positive (pain on knee extension)
Resisted isometricKnee flexion in mid-range against resistancePain with a weak responseMusculotendinous lesion — positive (flexion 2/5 with pain)
Differentiated SLR / slumpNeural tension with sensitising additionsPain changed by neck or ankle movementNeurogenic source — negative (SLR pain unchanged by neck flexion)
10. Problem list

Impairments.

  • Pain 5/10; active knee ROM limited to 20–90°
  • Knee flexion 2/5; knee extension 4/5

  • Antalgic gait; unable to jog or climb stairs
