11. Functional diagnosis

Acute grade II biceps femoris strain with pain, knee-flexion weakness and range limitation, causing an antalgic gait and inability to run, climb stairs or play football.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): pain ≤2/10; swelling resolved; full pain-free active knee ROM; normal gait.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): knee flexion 5/5; hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio near 60%; pain-free sprinting; football by 8–12 weeks.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (day 0–3): ice 15 min every 2 h, compression, elevation, optimal loading; conventional TENS 30 min, 3 times/day; pain-free passive ROM only; no heat or stretching. Stage 2 (day 3–7): pulsed ultrasound 3 MHz, 0.2–0.5 W/cm², pulsed 1:4, 5 min daily; isometric sets 5 × 5-second holds. Stage 3 (wk 1–3): leg curls and PNF 3 × 10 on alternate days; high-seat cycling. Stage 4 (wk 3–6): soft-tissue mobilisation; eccentric Nordic hamstring lowers and bridge walk-outs, 3 × 6. Stage 5 (wk 6+): sport-specific training with a graded run.

14. Home programme

Daily pain-free ROM; post-warm-up stretching 3 × 30 s from week 2; eccentric work three times weekly.

Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Plan an ergonomic table for a software professional who has a condition of Trapezitis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 6a — Ergonomic interventions for work-related musculoskeletal disorders

★ Memory hook — Ergonomic table rule: eye level · elbows 90–100° · hips 90–110° · feet flat; micro-break every 30–60 min and the 20-20-20 rule for the eyes.

1Introduction

Trapezitis in a software professional is a work-related upper-limb disorder driven by sustained static upper-trapezius elevation and forward-head posture during long screen hours. This answer plans an ergonomic workstation (presented as a table), a break-and-movement prescription, and follow-up with outcome measures.

2Physiology

Postural control of the head and arm depends on the endurance of the cervicoscapular muscles and on the deep neck flexors and scapular stabilisers holding the scapula in a good position. When these muscles are conditioned and the posture is balanced, the upper trapezius does not have to work continuously against gravity.

3Pathophysiology

The problem

Trapezitis in a software professional is a classic work-related upper-limb disorder: static upper-trapezius elevation + forward head posture during 8–10 h of screen work → ischaemic overload and trigger points. The ergonomic plan removes the sustained postural demand; a RULA/rapid exposure assessment documents the risk before redesign.

4Answer

The ergonomic table (the heart of the answer)
ElementSpecificationWhy (link to trapezitis)
Monitortop at/slightly below eye level, 50–70 cm away, perpendicular to windowskills forward-head & sustained flexion
Chairlumbar support, seat height letting feet rest flat, hips 90–110°unloads the cervico-scapular chain
Armrestsheight so elbows rest at 90–100° with shoulders relaxedprevents chronic trap elevation — the direct culprit
Keyboard/mouseclose to body, elbows at sides, wrists neutral; document holder beside screenavoids reaching & trap activation
Deskelbow height; keyboard tray/standing-desk optionposition variation & neutral limbs
Laptopnever on the lap for long work — riser + separate keyboard/mouseforced neck flexion otherwise
Lightingambient + task light, anti-glare, contrast setprevents leaning-in postures
Phoneheadset — never shoulder-crunchingclassic acute trap overload
Fig 8 — Workstation sketch with the angles marked. Copy it with the four numbered postures beside the figure in the exam.
Breaks & movement prescription

Rest breaks of 2–5 min every 30–60 min, plus true micro-pauses of 20–30 s every 20–30 min of typing; the 20-20-20 rule for the eyes; trap-specific routine every hour: shoulder shrug-rolls ×10, chin tucks ×10, doorway pectoral stretch 30 s, scapular retractions ×10; hydration; headset and standing-desk alternatives to break monotony.

Follow-up

Reassess RULA score at 2 and 6 weeks; pain (VAS/NPS), NDI; combine with physiotherapy (postural re-education, trigger-point release, scapular strengthening — lower/middle trap and serratus); educate about early-warning symptoms so the patient self-corrects.

The question literally says "plan an ergonomic TABLE" — give a real table with element/specification/reason columns. The 'reason' column linking each element to trapezius overload is where the higher marks live.

5Recent advances

  • Hasani et al. (2022) — a cluster-randomised trial found that active ergonomic training plus workstation adjustment reduced upper-limb musculoskeletal pain and discomfort in computer workers.
  • Lee et al. (2021) — a randomised controlled trial found workstation adjustment significantly lowered neck, shoulder, upper-back and wrist/hand pain intensity in office workers over 36 weeks.
  • Waongenngarm et al. (2021) — a three-arm cluster-randomised trial found rest-break and postural-shift interventions cut the new onset of neck and low-back pain by 55–81% in high-risk office workers.
  • Johnston et al. (2021) — a cluster-randomised trial found combining ergonomics with neck-specific exercise reduced neck pain more than ergonomics plus general health promotion.
  • Andersen et al. (2012) — a cluster-randomised trial found that one hour per week of specific high-intensity neck and shoulder strength training significantly reduced neck and shoulder pain in office workers, whatever the time distribution.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 6 (a, c).
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — posture & work-related disorder chapters.
  3. OSHA Computer Workstations eTool / McAtamney & Corlett RULA (ergonomic standards).
  4. The role of active ergonomic training intervention on upper limb musculoskeletal pain and discomfort: a cluster randomized controlled trial. Applied Ergonomics. 2022;88:103275.

On the evaluation form — Q8: Trapezitis in a software professional

I. Subjective examination

Mr Rahul, 30 years old, software engineer; 8 months of upper trapezius pain, right side worse (NPRS 6/10 by evening), with tension headaches 2–3 times weekly; 9–11 h daily on a laptop. Aggravating factors: long desk sessions, stress, the cold AC draught; relieving factors: weekends. Red-flag screen: no arm radiation, no night pain. Vitals stable.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Forward head posture with rounded shoulders.

On palpation. Taut, tender trigger points in both upper trapezii and at the right scapular angle.

1. Motor assessment. Cervical ROM full but painful at end-range flexion and right side-flexion; upper trapezius 4/5; deep neck flexors weak; middle and lower trapezius 3/5.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation, reflexes and myotomes normal.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Desk tolerance 45 minutes. Outcome measures: NPRS 0–10; Neck Disability Index 0–50 (higher = worse); Headache Impact Test (purpose: headache burden).

4. Gait analysis. Normal.

5. Balance. Normal.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation.

7. Coordination. Not separately documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Trigger point palpationPincer grip, roll the taut bandTwitch response, referred temple painMyofascial trigger point — positive (taut, tender bands in both upper trapezii)
Passive stretchDepress the shoulder, side-flex the neck awayFamiliar pain at end-rangeMuscle shortening — positive (painful end-range flexion and right side-flexion)
Spurling's testExtension, rotation, side-flexion, axial compressionArm painExcludes radiculopathy — negative here
ULNT-1Upper limb neurodynamic test (median nerve bias)Symptom reproductionNeurogenic source — negative here
Scapular assistanceAssist upward rotation during elevationElevation pain reducesWeak scapular stabilisers — result not documented
10. Problem list

Impairments.

  • Myofascial trigger points in both upper trapezii and at the right scapular angle
  • Weak deep neck flexors and scapular stabilisers (middle and lower trapezius 3/5)
  • Painful end-range cervical flexion and right side-flexion

Functional limitations.

  • Desk tolerance limited to 45 minutes
  • Tension headaches 2–3 times weekly

Disabilities.

  • Reduced work output
11. Functional diagnosis

Myofascial upper trapezitis with active trigger points, weak deep neck flexors and scapular stabilisers, and faulty desk posture, causing early desk-work fatigue, recurrent tension headaches and reduced work output.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): pain ≤2/10; desk tolerance 2 hours with breaks.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): full pain-free 8-hour desk day; headaches ≤1 per month; scapular strength 4/5.

13. Treatment plan

Phase 1 (wk 1–2): hot pack, trigger point compression 30–60 s, stretching, posture education. Phase 2 (wk 2–4): upper trapezius stretch 3 × 30-second holds, 3 times/day each side; rows, Y-T-W raises, wall push-up plus 3 × 10, three times/week; craniocervical flexion 10 × 5 s twice daily. Phase 3 (wk 4–12): theraband and gym-ball endurance. Ergonomic plan: laptop on a stand, screen top at eye level; external keyboard and mouse close; elbows at 90°, wrists neutral; chair with lumbar support, feet flat; glare-free lighting away from the AC draught; micro-breaks every 30 minutes; 20-20-20 rule.

14. Home programme

Daily self-stretches; hourly chin tucks; theraband thrice weekly.

Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Physiotherapeutic strategies for Osteosarcoma.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Units 1–5 — rehabilitation across impairment, pain, function & advanced methods

★ Memory hook — Osteosarcoma pathway: neoadjuvant chemo → wide resection / limb salvage with megaprosthesis → adjuvant chemo; phase physiotherapy around the chemotherapy cycle, not just the surgery.

1Introduction

Osteosarcoma is the commonest primary malignant bone tumour of adolescents and young adults, usually arising near the knee. Physiotherapy runs alongside the oncology plan across pre-operative, post-operative and survivorship phases. This answer outlines the disease and its treatment, then the pre-, peri- and post-operative strategies, precautions and holistic care.

2Physiology

Bone is a metabolically active tissue that remodels continuously under load, and skeletal muscle responds to disuse and to chemotherapy by losing mass and strength; the bone–muscle unit around the knee is the target of pre-habilitation and rehabilitation after resection. Aerobic conditioning and respiratory training support the patient through the deconditioning effects of chemotherapy.

3Pathophysiology

Overview that matters to us

Osteosarcoma — the commonest primary malignant bone tumour of adolescents/young adults — arises typically at the distal femur/proximal tibia metaphysis (knee region ~60% of cases near the knee). Management: neoadjuvant chemotherapy → wide resection by limb-salvage surgery with megaprosthesis/endoprosthesis (or rotationplasty/amputation) → adjuvant chemo. Physiotherapy is needed across ALL phases, always inside the oncology team.

4Answer

Pre-operative & peri-operative

Baseline assessment (ROM, strength, function — MSTS score, TESS), patient education; pre-hab: maintain knee/hip ROM and quadriceps strength between chemo cycles, aerobic conditioning to counter chemo deconditioning, respiratory preparation, gait training on planned assistive device, psychological preparation.

Post-operative rehabilitation after limb salvage
  • Phase 1 (0–2 wk): pain management (TENS as adjunct, cryotherapy), oedema control, isometrics within the surgeon's protocol, protected weight-bearing (touch-down to partial per prosthesis fixation), chest physiotherapy during chemo-induced immunosuppression.
  • Phase 2 (2–6 wk): progressive active ROM of the knee, patellar mobilisation, scar/soft-tissue mobilisation, gradual weight-bearing progression, gait re-education, isotonic quadriceps/hamstring work.
  • Phase 3 (6 wk–months): strengthening in functional patterns, proprioceptive and balance training, endurance walk programme, return to low-impact function — usually NOT high-impact sport with a megaprosthesis; home-programme compliance training.
Precautions & complications

Protect against pathological/periprosthetic fracture (fall prevention, controlled loading), infection (pin/wound), extensor-mechanism insufficiency after distal-femoral resection, chemo side effects (fatigue, neuropathy, cardiotoxicity — adjust intensity), prosthetic loosening; avoid forceful passive stretching; monitor for recurrence symptoms in follow-up.

Holistic care

Energy-conservation pacing during chemo, nutritional counselling referral, psychosocial support (body image, school/work re-entry for adolescents), palliative and end-of-life physiotherapy when disease progresses — comfort, positioning, chest care; outcome tracking with TESS/MSTS and quality-of-life scales; in amputees, prosthetic rehabilitation as in Paper III Q8.

Fig 9 — The osteosarcoma rehab timeline laid over the chemo cycles — the drawing that proves you know therapy is phased around oncology, not just surgery.
High-scoring lines: "physiotherapy is phased around the CHEMOTHERAPY cycle, not just the surgery" and "high-impact sport is contraindicated after megaprosthesis." Examiners also love seeing a named outcome measure (TESS or MSTS) in the conclusion.

5Recent advances

  • Basteck et al. (2022) — the proGAIT pilot randomised controlled trial found an eight-week exercise programme produced small-to-medium gains in gait (Gait Deviation Index), TESS/MSTS scores and functional mobility in young osteosarcoma survivors with a knee megaendoprosthesis.
  • van Kouswijk et al. (2023) — a systematic review of exercise after lower-limb salvage surgery for sarcoma found very-low-certainty evidence of improved knee range of motion and function, and called for better-designed trials.
  • Cohen et al. (2026) — wearable-tracker work on physical activity in osteosarcoma patients shows activity is lowest on chemotherapy-infusion days, supporting exercise dosing tailored around the chemo cycle.
  • Yang et al. (2026) — digital-therapeutics-based rehabilitative exercise is emerging as a feasible adjunct after lower-extremity osteosarcoma surgery in adolescents.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Units 1–5 (integrative clinical application).
  2. Maxey L, Magnusson J. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. (reference 13).
  3. Wilk KE et al. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation. (reference 14).
  4. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10) — oncology rehabilitation chapter.
  5. Effects of an exercise intervention on gait function in young survivors of osteosarcoma with megaendoprosthesis of the lower extremity — results from the pilot randomized controlled trial proGAIT. Curr Oncol. 2022;29(10):7754–7767.
  6. Therapeutic validity and effectiveness of exercise interventions after lower limb-salvage surgery for sarcoma: a systematic review. BMC Musculoskelet Disord. 2023;24.

On the evaluation form — Q9: Osteosarcoma around the knee — post-surgical rehab

I. Subjective examination

Master Arjun, 16 years old. Osteosarcoma of the right distal femur — wide resection with a distal femoral endoprosthesis 4 weeks ago, after neoadjuvant chemotherapy; further cycles are planned. Chief complaints: knee stiffness, thigh weakness and walker gait; NPRS 3/10. Red-flag screen: fever reported on the same day as chemotherapy (possible neutropenia) — reported for medical review.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Well-healed scar, marked quadriceps atrophy, effusion; walker gait at partial weight bearing.

On palpation. Scar partly adherent; no local warmth or new mass.

1. Motor assessment. Knee ROM 10–70°; extensor lag 15°; quadriceps 3/5, hamstrings 3+/5; girth 4 cm lost at 15 cm above the patella.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation intact distally, including the saphenous territory; reflexes present.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Walker gait at 50% weight bearing; supervised stairs. Outcome measures: MSTS score — six domains (pain, function, emotional acceptance, supports, walking, gait), each 0–5, total 0–30; Toronto Extremity Restore Score (patient-reported physical function after extremity sarcoma treatment); LEFS 0–80.

4. Gait analysis. Walker gait at 50% weight bearing; stairs supervised.

5. Balance. Not separately documented at this assessment.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation.

7. Coordination. Not separately documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

Post-operative and chemotherapy records as per the surgical and oncology teams; no imaging or blood reports reviewed at this assessment. The same-day fever with possible neutropenia was reported for medical review.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Stroke (effusion) testMilk the pouch, stroke the guttersBulge reappearsReactive effusion — positive; modulate load
Extensor lag testStraight leg raise, lower slowlyHeel dropsQuadriceps insufficiency — positive (15° lag)
Scar mobilitySkin rolling over the scarTetheringAdhesions limiting ROM — positive (scar partly adherent)
Girth measurementCircumference 5/10/15 cm above the patellaAsymmetryTracks muscle loss — positive (4 cm lost at 15 cm)
10. Problem list

Impairments.

  • Knee ROM 10–70° with 15° extensor lag; quadriceps 3/5
  • 4 cm girth loss at 15 cm above the patella; scar adhesion; reactive effusion
  • Fatigue related to chemotherapy

Functional limitations.

  • Walker gait at partial weight bearing
  • Supervised stairs only

Disabilities.

  • Not attending school
11. Functional diagnosis

Post-resection distal femoral endoprosthesis status with knee stiffness, quadriceps weakness and extensor lag, scar adhesion and chemotherapy-related fatigue, limiting independent ambulation, stair use and school attendance.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): pain ≤2/10; ROM 0–90°; safe independent walker gait; quadriceps 3+/5.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): ROM 0–110°; quadriceps 4/5 without lag; cane ambulation; part-time school.

13. Treatment plan

Phase 1 (wk 4–8 post-op): quad sets 10 × 10-second holds, 3 times/day; active-assisted heel slides; patellar and scar mobilisation; gait re-education; sessions capped at 20–30 min, gentler during nadir weeks. Phase 2 (months 2–4): quadriceps and hip PRE 3 × 10 on alternate days; closed-chain work in 0–45° (mini squats, step-ups); no-resistance cycling; walker to crutches to cane. Phase 3 (months 4–6+): endurance walking, reciprocal stairs; lifelong precautions — no contact sports or high-impact running (per surgeon); encourage swimming and cycling; report new pain, swelling, fever or lumps immediately.

14. Home programme

Daily quad sets; heel slides 3 × 10; scar self-massage; walking 15 min; fatigue diary.

Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Types of meniscal tear. What are the causes and mechanism of injury to the meniscus? Plan PT intervention.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Units 1–3 — impaired mobility/performance & functional training in knee injuries

★ Memory hook — Meniscus: outer third = red-red zone (vascular, heals best), inner two-thirds avascular; bucket-handle tears lock the knee.

1Introduction

The menisci are C-shaped fibrocartilages that distribute load and stabilise the knee; their tears are described by pattern, cause and vascular zone. This answer covers the types of tear, the causes and mechanism of injury, the vascular zones that govern healing, and a phase-wise physiotherapy plan.

2Physiology

The menisci are C-shaped fibrocartilages that distribute load, absorb shock and contribute to joint stability and proprioception. Their healing potential depends on the blood supply: the peripheral third is vascular and the inner two-thirds are avascular.

Vascular zones

The red-red peripheral third is vascular (heals), the red-white middle has partial potential, the inner white-white two-thirds is avascular — this dictates repair versus partial meniscectomy versus conservative care.

3Pathophysiology

Types of meniscal tears
  • Bucket-handle — longitudinal vertical tear with central fragment displacement into the intercondylar notch; classic "locked knee."
  • Longitudinal (vertical) — along the circumference, common young athletes.
  • Radial — from free edge toward periphery (parrot-beak when oblique).
  • Oblique/flap — diagonal, symptomatic catching.
  • Horizontal cleavage — splits the meniscus into upper/lower laminae, common in older, degenerative menisci (often associated with cysts).
  • Complex/degenerative — multi-pattern tears in the aged meniscus.
Fig 10 — Bird's-eye view of the knee menisci with tear patterns. Two minutes to draw, worth a full mark in every knee-answer.
Causes & mechanism

Traumatic (young athletes): the foot is planted, the knee is flexed and loaded while the femur rotates on the fixed tibia — the meniscus is crushed and sheared between the condyle and plateau, tearing like a washer twisting under a bolt. Squatting-and-twisting in cricket, football cutting, kabaddi. Medial meniscus tears more often (firmly attached to the medial capsule, less mobile). Degenerative (40+): age-related chondrocalcinosis and mucoid degeneration tear from trivial activities (rising from a cross-legged squat) — horizontal/complex patterns. Risk factors: discoid meniscus, ACL insufficiency (unstable knee shears the menisci), repetitive deep squatting occupations.

4Answer

Physiotherapy intervention plan
  • Conservative (small, stable, degenerative tears — now the evidence default for degenerative tears): phase-wise — control effusion/pain (cryotherapy, TENS), restore ROM, quadriceps/hamstring strengthening (isometrics → closed-chain), proprioception, gait normalisation, return-to-sport criteria. Evidence (FIDELITY and METEOR trials) shows structured exercise matches arthroscopic partial meniscectomy for degenerative tears.
  • Post partial meniscectomy: rapid progression — day 1–3 quadriceps activation, full weight bearing as tolerated, ROM, closed-chain strengthening from week 1, running ~4–6 wk, sport ~6–8 wk.
  • Post meniscal repair: protected — brace limiting flexion (0–90° for ~4–6 wk), toe-touch to partial weight bearing 4–6 wk, no deep squats/deep flexion for 12–16 wk, progressive strength & proprioception; healing is the priority, speed comes later.
  • Outcome tracking: Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), Tegner activity scale, effusion and thigh-circumference measures.
Every examiner checks three things: the mechanism sentence (flexed-loaded-rotating knee), the locked-knee = bucket-handle link, and the conservative-vs-surgery evidence reversal for degenerative tears. Miss the last one and the answer reads a decade old.

5Recent advances

  • Noorduyn et al. (2022) — the five-year follow-up of the ESCAPE trial confirmed that exercise-based physical therapy is non-inferior to arthroscopic partial meniscectomy for knee function in degenerative meniscal tears, with comparable progression of knee osteoarthritis.
  • Kise et al. (2016) — a randomised controlled trial in the BMJ found supervised exercise therapy was not inferior to arthroscopic partial meniscectomy at two years and improved thigh muscle strength more in the short term, supporting exercise as a first-line option.
  • Sihvonen et al. (2018) — the FIDELITY trial found arthroscopic surgery no better than sham surgery for degenerative meniscal tears.
  • Berg et al. (2020) — a randomised-trial secondary analysis found exercise therapy and surgery produced comparable radiographic knee osteoarthritis progression, supporting exercise as the safe first-line treatment.
  • ESSKA–AOSSM–AASPT EU–US Meniscus Rehabilitation Consensus (2024) — post-repair rehabilitation continues to emphasise protected flexion limits (no deep flexion for 12–16 weeks) and criteria-based return to sport.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Units 1–3.
  2. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. (reference 1) — knee menisci.
  3. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4) — McMurray/Apley tests.
  4. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — post-meniscal surgery protocols.
  5. Noorduyn JCA, van de Graaf VA, Willigenburg NW, et al; ESCAPE Research Group. Effect of physical therapy vs arthroscopic partial meniscectomy in people with degenerative meniscal tears: five-year follow-up of the ESCAPE randomized clinical trial. JAMA Netw Open. 2022;5(7):e2220394.

On the evaluation form — Q10: Meniscal tear — rehabilitation after repair

I. Subjective examination

Mr Vikram, 25 years old, footballer. Twisting injury to the right knee 4 weeks ago — bucket-handle medial meniscus tear, repaired arthroscopically 2 weeks ago. Mechanism: twisting on a loaded, flexed knee with the tibia fixed; the medial meniscus tears more often because it is less mobile and anchored to the MCL. Chief complaints: guarded weight bearing; NPRS 3/10; no locking. Vitals normal.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Healed portal scars, effusion, quadriceps atrophy; crutch gait.

On palpation. Medial joint-line tenderness.

1. Motor assessment. Knee ROM 0–90°; quadriceps 3/5, hamstrings 3+/5; girth 2.5 cm lost.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation and reflexes normal; no neurovascular deficit.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Stairs step-to; hop tests deferred at this stage. Outcome measures: Lysholm 0–100 (higher = better); Tegner 0–10; IKDC 0–100.

4. Gait analysis. Crutch gait at partial weight bearing; stairs step-to.

5. Balance. Hop tests deferred (post-operative); formal balance testing not documented at this stage.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation.

7. Coordination. Not separately documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

Arthroscopy 2 weeks ago confirmed and repaired a bucket-handle medial meniscal tear; no current imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
McMurray's testFlexion, valgus, external rotation while extendingMedial joint-line click with painMedial meniscal tear — not re-tested at this post-repair assessment
Apley's grindProne, knee 90°; axial load with rotation vs distractionPain on compression, less on distractionMeniscal rather than ligamentous — not re-tested at this post-repair assessment
Thessaly testStand on one leg, knee 20°, rotate the bodyReproducible joint-line discomfortMeniscal tear — not re-tested at this post-repair assessment
Joint-line palpationPalpate both joint linesFocal posteromedial tendernessLocalises the torn zone — positive (medial joint-line tenderness)
Valgus stress testApply valgus stress to the kneeMedial joint-line gappingMCL laxity — negative (valgus stress stable, MCL intact)
10. Problem list

Impairments.

  • Medial joint-line pain (NPRS 3/10) with effusion
  • Knee ROM 0–90°; quadriceps 3/5; 2.5 cm girth loss

Functional limitations.

  • Crutch gait at partial weight bearing; step-to stairs
  • No running (hop tests deferred)

Disabilities.

  • Away from football
11. Functional diagnosis

Post-arthroscopic medial meniscal repair status with joint-line pain, effusion, quadriceps weakness and restricted knee flexion, resulting in partial-weight-bearing crutch gait and inability to run or play football.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): full extension; flexion ≥110° by week 4; quadriceps 4/5; weight bearing in a brace by week 4–6.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): full pain-free ROM; strength 5/5 at 90% of the left; return to sport at 4–6 months with Lysholm above 90.

13. Treatment plan

Phase 1 (wk 0–2, protection): hinged brace, touch-down weight bearing; passive ROM 0–90° only, flexion capped to protect the repair; quad sets 10 × 10 s hourly; cryotherapy. Phase 2 (wk 2–6): full weight bearing allowed; flexion to 120°; cycling from week 4. Phase 3 (wk 6–12): closed-chain resistance — leg press 0–60° then 0–90°, step-ups, 3 × 10 three times weekly; wobble-board proprioception. Phase 4 (months 3–4): jogging progression; return to sport at 4–6 months on pain-free ROM, 90% strength, symmetric hop tests and surgeon clearance.

14. Home programme

Hourly quad sets; heel slides; no deep squats, kneeling or fixed-foot twisting for 4–6 months.

Last-Hour Sheet · Paper IV — Physiotherapy Interventions

QP 8132 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1Muscle performance post wrist fracture

  • Staircase: isometric in cast → AROM → isotonic resisted → CKC/isokinetic/PNF → functional grip.
  • Progress ~5–10% when 12 reps easy; discharge grip within 10–15% of sound side (PRWE).

2Electrotherapy pain relief

  • Conventional TENS: 80–100 Hz, 50–100 µs = gate control (Aβ → SG closes gate).
  • Acupuncture-like: 2–4 Hz, 200–300 µs, twitch = opioid (naloxone-reversible, descending PAG-raphe).
  • IFT beat 90–130 Hz; HVPG for oedema; counter-irritation; placebo = real neurobiology.

3Balance after ankle sprain

  • Rationale: torn mechanoreceptors → re-sprain; training halves recurrence.
  • Ladder: floor SLS (EO→EC) → foam → wobble board → BOSU + SEBT → perturbation → hopping/cutting.
  • Discharge: SEBT symmetry ≥90%, hop tests ≥95%.

4Functional training post TKR

  • Day 0–3: quad sets, SLR, walker; wk 1–2 transfers, stairs; wk 2–6 mini-squats, step-ups, cycle; wk 6–12 outdoor, reciprocal stairs, driving.
  • "Up with the good, down with the bad." Indian ADLs: low toilet, cross-legged graded to implant flexion (110–125°). TUG <12 s to finish.

5Neurodynamics

  • Nerve must glide/elongate within interfaces; tests: ULNT1/2/3/4, SLR, slump.
  • Slider = one end releases as other moves (low tension, irritable patients); tensioner = both ends lengthen (strong dose). Short of symptom reproduction.

6Orthotics

  • Effects: support, immobilise, correct deformity, assist weak muscle, protect, pain relief.
  • Static: resting, cock-up, thumb spica, gutter, mallet. Dynamic: spring outrigger (radial palsy), knuckle-bender, turnbuckle.

7Evidence-based electrotherapy

  • Phases: inflammation 0–5 d; proliferation 5 d–3 wk; remodelling 3 wk–12 mo.
  • Acute: TENS/IFT + cryo + pulsed US/HVPG. Subacute: continuous US (3 MHz superficial, 1 MHz deep) + laser. Chronic: shockwave + eccentric loading.
  • Quote one negative trial (Cochrane: US vs sham — no difference); exercise is the driver, modalities buy the window.

8Ergonomics for trapezitis

  • Monitor top = eye level, 50–70 cm; chair lumbar support, hips 90–110°; armrests → elbows 90–100°, shoulders relaxed.
  • Keyboard close, wrists neutral; headset only; 2–5 min break every 30–60 min; 20-20-20 rule; hourly trap stretches.

9Osteosarcoma

  • Adolescent, distal femur/proximal tibia; chemo → limb salvage with megaprosthesis → chemo.
  • Prehab between cycles; post-op: protect (0–2 wk) → ROM/quads (2–6 wk) → loading/gait (6 wk–mo).
  • No high-impact sport with megaprosthesis; outcomes TESS/MSTS; energy pacing; psychosocial.

10Meniscal tears

  • Types: bucket-handle (locked knee!), longitudinal, radial, oblique/flap, horizontal cleavage, degenerative.
  • Mechanism: flexed, loaded knee + rotation (medial > lateral). Zones: red-red heals, red-white partial, white-white doesn't.
  • Conservative first for degenerative (FIDELITY/METEOR evidence); post-repair: flexion ≤90° 4–6 wk, no deep flexion 12–16 wk.
Six portable numbers: 80–100 (DeLisa 40–80) vs 2–4 Hz TENS; 90–130 Hz IFT beat (DeLisa 20–80); 20-20-20; TUG <12 s; 3 MHz superficial; 12–16 wk no deep flexion after repair. Two 2-word scores: "bucket-handle locked", "FIDELITY conservative".

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Describe the impaired mobility seen in ankle injuries.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 1 — interventions for impaired joint mobility

★ Memory hook — STIFF AND LOOSE — an injured ankle is hypomobile (lost posterior talar glide blocks dorsiflexion, and the capsular pattern is dorsiflexion more limited than plantarflexion) AND hypermobile (positive anterior drawer and talar tilt). Assess both, treat both.

1Introduction

Ankle injuries — most commonly inversion sprains of the anterior talofibular ligament, but also fractures, syndesmotic injuries and chronic instabilities — disturb mobility in two opposite directions, and a full answer must show both.

This answer therefore describes the impaired mobility of the ankle in two directions at once — stiffness and instability — and how each is assessed and treated.

2Physiology

Finally, the arthrokinematic problem: dorsiflexion requires the wide anterior part of the talus to roll and glide posteriorly between the malleoli

Normally the talocrural joint achieves about 20 degrees of dorsiflexion and needs at least 10 degrees for a normal terminal stance; accessory glides of the talus on the tibia and of the fibula on the tibia allow that range, and the ankle capsular pattern (dorsiflexion limited more than plantarflexion) reflects the shape of the mortise.

3Pathophysiology

Mechanism first: in the acute stage, effusion into the confined talocrural joint plus pain inhibition of the anterior tibial muscles splints the joint in a comfortable plantarflexed-inverted position, so active movement is lost globally. In the subacute stage, scar adhesion and shortening of the anterior capsule and the anterior talofibular ligament produce a true capsular pattern — remember the capsular pattern of the ankle is more restriction of dorsiflexion than plantarflexion.

; if the posterior talar glide is lost, the osteokinematic movement is blocked even when the capsule looks normal on table tests. Conversely, a ruptured ligament leaves the mortise too roomy, giving instability rather than stiffness.

Talocrural joint: loss of dorsiflexion dominates (often 10–20 degrees short of the normal 20 degrees); at least 10 degrees of dorsiflexion is essential for normal terminal stance, so the patient walks with a compensated abducted gait, early heel lift or a functional equinus. Subtalar joint: restriction of inversion and eversion follows sinus tarsi involvement or cast immobilisation, disturbing shock absorption on uneven ground — a real problem on Indian roads and potholed footpaths. Syndesmosis injury: end-range dorsiflexion is painful because the widened mortise jams the wider anterior talus; the squeeze test and loss of external rotation mark it. Accessory movements lost: posterior glide of the talus on the tibia, and glide of the fibula on the tibia at the distal tibiofibular joint. On the hypermobile side, a torn anterior talofibular ligament gives a positive anterior drawer, and a torn calcaneofibular ligament gives a positive talar tilt — the ligamentous laxity that drives recurrent sprains when proprioception is not retrained.

4Answer

Measure active then passive range with a goniometer (align along the fibula and fifth metatarsal); compare sides, since the uninjured ankle is the best control. Weight-bearing dorsiflexion by the knee-to-wall (lunge) test is more functional than table goniometry. Assess accessory glides and end-feel with the talus gliding posteriorly and the fibula gliding anteriorly. Grade ligamentous laxity with the anterior drawer and talar tilt tests, and confirm functional instability with single-leg stance, the star excursion balance test or a wobble-board balance timer. Always palpate the joint line for effusion and the sinus tarsi for tenderness.

Protect and settle first (relative rest, ice, compression, elevation), then restore arthrokinematics: grade I–II oscillatory posterior talar glides for pain, progressing to grade III–IV sustained glides with the joint at the end of available dorsiflexion. Convert to self-treatment quickly — knee-to-wall lunges, self-mobilisation with a strap, towel stretches, and eccentric calf work in the functional range. Rebuild proprioception progressively from double-leg to single-leg, stable to unstable surfaces, eyes open to closed, adding hopping and cutting when control returns. Tape or brace during the risky late phase. Progression logic: settle, glide, stretch, load, and retrain balance — in that order.

Verhagen and colleagues showed that a proprioceptive and balance training programme roughly halves the recurrence of ankle sprains — the strongest argument that impaired mobility must be treated together with impaired control. Conclusion: ankle injuries produce stiffness (effusion, capsular shortening, lost accessory glide) and instability (ligament laxity plus proprioceptive deficit) in the same joint; assessment must separate the two, because treatment of one without the other fails.

Fig 1 — Draw the talocrural joint and one arrow: no posterior talar glide, no dorsiflexion. This single mechanism line earns the middle marks of the answer.
Most students write only about stiffness. The examiner expects the two-sided answer — hypomobility AND ligamentous hypermobility — because "impaired mobility" covers both. Name the capsular pattern (dorsiflexion more limited than plantarflexion) to separate yourself from the pack.

5Recent advances

  • Vuurberg et al. (2018) — this evidence-based clinical guideline in the British Journal of Sports Medicine concluded that supervised exercise-based rehabilitation with functional support (brace or tape) is preferred over immobilisation after lateral ankle sprain, that mobilisation should be combined with exercise, and that surgery is reserved for those who fail comprehensive conservative care.
  • Gribble et al. (2016) — the International Ankle Consortium consensus standardised the definition and selection criteria for chronic ankle instability, enabling comparable trials and supporting early, supervised, exercise-based rehabilitation of this condition.
  • Yang et al. (2024) — a network meta-analysis of 44 trials in JOSPT found that combining balance and strengthening exercises, augmented with manual therapy or dry needling, gave the best function, dynamic balance and pain relief in chronic ankle instability, with tai chi ranking best for perceived stability.
  • Tang et al. (2024) — a meta-analysis in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders (20 studies, 682 patients) recommended balance training three times a week for 20–30 minutes over 4–6 weeks as the optimal dose for chronic ankle instability.
  • Marrón-Gómez et al. (2015) — this randomised trial in Physical Therapy in Sport showed that a single application of Mulligan mobilisation with movement or talocrural manipulation both improved weight-bearing dorsiflexion in chronic ankle instability, with effects lasting at least 48 hours.

6References

  1. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — ankle hypomobility and ligamentous instability sections.
  2. Verhagen et al., ankle-sprain recurrence, American Journal of Sports Medicine.
  3. O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation (10) — ankle and foot interventions.
  4. Vuurberg G, et al. Diagnosis, treatment and prevention of ankle sprains: update of an evidence-based clinical guideline. British Journal of Sports Medicine 2018.

On the evaluation form — Q1: Post-ankle-sprain stiffness / mobility impairment

I. Subjective examination

24-year-old badminton player. Chief complaints: persistent morning stiffness, pain and mild instability on uneven ground following an inversion injury 3 weeks ago (grade II lateral ankle sprain). Symptom analysis — site: ankle; onset: 3 weeks ago, inversion mechanism; type: stiffness with activity-related pain; severity: 3/10 on NPRS (0–10); aggravating factors: stairs and squatting; relieving factors: not reported; associated features: mild instability on uneven ground, no night pain or numbness. Vitals normal; the patient walks with a slight limp.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Residual anterolateral swelling over the ankle; mild calf wasting; no scars or bandages; shortened stance phase of gait on the involved side.

On palpation. Tenderness over the anterior talofibular and calcaneofibular ligaments and the joint line; no local warmth; no spasm or crepitus documented.

1. Motor assessment. ROM: dorsiflexion 10°, plantar flexion 35°, inversion and eversion restricted by one-third; capsular end-feel. MMT (MRC 0–5): dorsi- and plantar flexors 4, invertors 4, evertors 3+. Muscle girth: calf circumference 1.5 cm less than the sound side. Reflexes normal.

2. Sensory assessment. Dull sensation in the dorsal web space (superficial peroneal territory), improving; distal neurology otherwise normal.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Difficulty with stairs and squatting; unable to perform a single-leg heel raise; reduced star-excursion balance test reach on the involved limb. Outcome measures: NPRS 0–10; LEFS 0–80 (lower = greater disability); FAAM — ADL and sport function subscales; Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool for perceived instability.

4. Gait analysis. Antalgic gait with reduced push-off and a shortened stance phase on the involved side.

5. Balance. Impaired single-limb balance on the involved side, with reduced star-excursion reach and instability on uneven ground.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this ankle presentation.

7. Coordination. Poor ankle proprioception contributing to instability on uneven surfaces (documented as an impairment).

8. Investigations

No imaging reviewed at this assessment; X-rays and relevant investigations as per medical records.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Anterior drawerLeg stabilized with the knee flexed 20°; the foot is drawn forward on the stabilized tibiaExcess anterior talar shiftAnterior talofibular ligament laxity
Talar tiltAnkle held neutral; the talus is tilted into inversionExcess inversion laxityCalcaneofibular ligament laxity
Squeeze testThe calf is squeezed at mid-legSyndesmotic painTibiofibular syndesmosis injury
Kleiger's (external rotation) testThe foot is externally rotated with the leg fixedSyndesmotic painSyndesmosis injury

For this patient the record documents tenderness over the anterior talofibular and calcaneofibular ligaments, consistent with the grade II lateral sprain; laxity grades for the drawer and talar tilt tests are not documented, and no syndesmotic or Achilles tendon findings were recorded.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Pain
  • Restricted dorsiflexion
  • Weak evertors
  • Poor proprioception
  • Residual swelling

Functional limitations

  • Squatting
  • Stairs
  • Running

Disabilities

  • Cannot play badminton
11. Functional diagnosis

Post-grade-II lateral ankle sprain with pain, restricted dorsiflexion, weak evertors, poor proprioception and residual swelling, causing functional limitation in squatting, stairs and running and disability in badminton play.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). NPRS ≤1/10; full pain-free dorsiflexion; evertors MRC 4; single-leg stance 30 s.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Full pain-free ROM; MRC 5 in all groups; 10 heel raises; normal gait; graded return to badminton by 10–12 weeks.

13. Treatment plan

Phase 1 (weeks 3–6): anteroposterior and tibiofibular joint mobilizations grade III–IV (20×3), calf stretching, towel scrunches, cryotherapy after sessions. Phase 2 (weeks 6–10): theraband inversion/eversion 3×15, heel raises, wobble-board proprioception, hopping. Phase 3: agility ladder and sport-specific drills.

14. Home programme

Foot alphabet; calf stretch 30 s ×3 daily; band exercises and single-leg stance twice daily; ice after overload.

Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Write in detail about the role of various educational strategies in managing low back pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 2 — educational and behavioural strategies in pain management

★ Memory hook — ADVICE PLUS ACTION — education alone is weak; education plus graded exercise changes function. The message is 'hurt does not equal harm'.

1Introduction

Most low back pain is non-specific: no fracture, no nerve root compression, no sinister pathology. What decides the outcome is not the imaging but the patient's beliefs and behaviour — whether they fear the pain, rest excessively, or keep moving.

This answer explains why education is treatment, classifies the educational strategies, and shows how content is linked to behaviour change.

2Physiology

Pain is a brain output, not a direct readout of tissue damage: nociceptors signal potential threat, the dorsal horn gates the traffic, and descending pathways from the brainstem can turn that traffic up or down. Beliefs, attention, fear and expectation act on exactly these pathways — which is why an explanation that changes what a patient believes about their back also changes the pain they feel and the activity they dare to do. This is the neurophysiology that education is designed to reach.

3Pathophysiology

Education is therefore a genuine therapeutic tool within the biopsychosocial model: it targets the psychosocial flags (fear-avoidance beliefs, catastrophising, low self-efficacy) that convert an ordinary sprain into chronic disability. In the Indian clinic, where "complete bed rest for 15 days" is still commonly advised by well-meaning relatives, correcting beliefs early is high-yield treatment.

When fear-avoidance, catastrophising and low self-efficacy go uncorrected, protective rest becomes disuse, disuse produces deconditioning and central sensitisation, and an ordinary self-limiting sprain becomes chronic disabling low back pain — the very conversion that early education is meant to prevent.

4Answer

Individual advice in the consultation — stay active, avoid prolonged bed rest, keep working, and understand that "hurt does not equal harm". Back schools — structured group programmes of anatomy, posture, lifting technique and exercise, first formalised in Sweden; effective mainly in occupational settings when combined with exercise. Printed and audio-visual media — pamphlets, videos, mobile-phone messages; cheap and scalable but passive. Pain neurosciences education — explaining pain processing so the patient understands that pain reflects sensitivity of the nervous system, not ongoing damage; ideally delivered before or alongside exercise so movement is not feared. Group exercise classes with embedded education, and cognitive-behavioural informed classes (the UK Back Pain Exercise And Manipulation trial model), which combine supervised activity with belief change and have the best evidence for reducing disability. Yoga-based programmes deserve mention for our context — they deliver movement, breathing and relaxation in a culturally familiar package.

Whatever the delivery mode, the content must change behaviour: reduce fear-avoidance, teach graded activity and pacing rather than boom-and-bust cycling, set self-management goals, correct faulty beliefs about imaging findings ("disc degeneration is normal ageing, like grey hair"), and give clear flare-up plans so a bad day does not become a catastrophe. Education should always be paired with an active component — advice alone changes little; advice plus exercise changes function.

Systematic reviews find that education alone (especially pamphlets) produces small short-term effects, while structured programmes combining education with exercise — and pain neurosciences education before exercise — reduce pain and disability more meaningfully. Back schools show modest benefit in occupational cohorts. Bed-rest advice is actively harmful. Conclusion: education is the frame on which every other intervention for low back pain hangs; delivered early, matched to the patient's beliefs, and always paired with graded activity, it is among the most cost-effective treatments we own.

Fig 2 — Three delivery routes, one central box, one outcome. Draw this flow in under a minute and the structure of your answer is visible to the examiner.
The question says "various educational strategies", so marks sit in the MENU — list and classify at least five modes with one content line each. Close with the evidence line: advice alone is weak, education plus graded exercise is strong.

5Recent advances

  • Louw et al. (2016) — this systematic review of 13 randomised trials found that pain neuroscience education reduces pain, improves function and lowers disability, catastrophising and healthcare use in chronic musculoskeletal pain, supporting its use alongside active physiotherapy.
  • Ma et al. (2023) — an updated meta-analysis (17 RCTs, 1078 patients) confirmed that pain neuroscience education added to exercise or physiotherapy reduced short-term pain and disability more than exercise or physiotherapy alone; a single session over 60 minutes and group delivery worked best.
  • Wood & Hendrick (2019) — their systematic review found moderate-certainty evidence that adding pain neuroscience education to physiotherapy improves short-term disability.
  • Cuenca-Martínez et al. (2023) — an umbrella review showed pain neuroscience education adds benefit mainly when combined with exercise-based multimodal care, not as a stand-alone treatment.
  • Traeger et al. (2019) — this landmark JAMA Neurology randomised trial found that adding two hours of intensive patient education to first-line care did not improve pain in acute low back pain, showing that education alone is weak and must be paired with active management.

6References

  1. O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation (10) — education and back school content.
  2. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — functional activity education sections.
  3. McKenzie & May, The Lumbar Spine (24) — patient self-management and education principle.
  4. Wood L, Hendrick PA. A systematic review and meta-analysis of pain neuroscience education for chronic low back pain: short- and long-term outcomes of pain and disability. European Journal of Pain 2019;23(2):234–249.

On the evaluation form — Q2: Chronic low back pain — education-led management

I. Subjective examination

42-year-old IT professional with 8 months of intermittent low back pain without radiation. Pain 4/10 on NPRS (0–10), worse with sitting, eased by lying down. Symptom analysis — site: low back; onset: intermittent over 8 months; type: non-radiating back pain; severity: 4/10; aggravating factors: sitting; relieving factors: lying down. Believes his disc is “slipping” and avoids bending and lifting. Past medical/personal history: sedentary lifestyle, BMI 29. Red flags absent.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Slouched sitting posture with a forward head and reduced lumbar lordosis; no deformity, wasting or scars documented.

On palpation. Paraspinal spasm with L4–L5 tenderness; no bony step.

1. Motor assessment. ROM: lumbar flexion 50% of normal (fingers 30 cm from the floor); extension and side-flexion mildly painful and limited. MMT (MRC 0–5): trunk flexors 4, trunk extensors 4, gluteals 3+; poor bridge endurance.

2. Sensory assessment. SLR 80° bilaterally without radicular pain; dermatomes, myotomes, reflexes and saddle sensation normal.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Hands used for sit-to-stand; sitting tolerance 30–40 min; lifting tolerance 5 kg; stairs avoided. Outcome measures: ODI 0–100% (higher = greater disability); NPRS 0–10; Fear-Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire (FABQ) — physical-activity and work-related beliefs; Patient-Specific Functional Scale.

4. Gait analysis. No gait deviation documented; mobility limited by sitting and lifting tolerance as above.

5. Balance. Not documented; no imbalance reported.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation.

7. Coordination. Not documented; the neurological screen is normal.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Slump testSeated slump, knee extended, neck flexedPain eased by neck extensionNeurodynamic sensitivity
Prone instability testProne; pain on posterior shear re-tested with muscle activationPain decreases with activationSegmental lumbar instability
FABER (Patrick's) testFlexion–abduction–external rotation in supineLumbar or hip painLumbar or hip joint involvement

In this patient the SLR was 80° bilaterally without radicular pain (negative). Results for the remaining table tests are not documented; the clinical picture is of chronic low back pain with fear-avoidance behaviour.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Pain
  • Maladaptive beliefs
  • Fear-avoidance
  • Deconditioning

11. Functional diagnosis

Chronic low back pain with maladaptive beliefs, fear-avoidance, deconditioning and poor trunk endurance, limiting sitting, lifting and bending and reducing work output and social participation.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Pain ≤2/10; 60-minute sitting with micro-breaks; independent in a pacing diary and home exercises.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Full-time work without sick leave; lift 10 kg correctly; reduced FABQ score; independent self-management.

13. Treatment plan

Education is the core: (1) pain neurophysiology education in the local language replacing the “damaged disc” model; (2) activity pacing with graded exposure — weekly quotas for sitting, bending and walking; (3) back-school instruction on posture, lifting and workstation setup; (4) graded exercise over 8–12 weeks — core stabilization, gluteal and back-extensor strengthening, walking; (5) heat or TENS only as brief enablers.

14. Home programme

30 minutes of daily walking; abdominal bracing 10×3; bridge and bird-dog progressions; lumbar mobility exercises; pacing diary reviewed each visit; family included in goal-setting.

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Describe the role of anti-gravity muscles in maintaining postural stability.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 3 — postural stability and balance

★ Memory hook — SOLEUS, SPINDLE, STRATEGY — the tonic extensor chain (soleus first) supplies the force against gravity, the gamma-spindle loop supplies the sensitivity, and the CNS supplies the strategy.

1Introduction

Anti-gravity muscles are the tonic extensors that hold the skeleton upright against the pull of gravity: soleus (the workhorse of standing), quadriceps, gluteus maximus, the lumbar erector spinae, and — for the head — the neck extensors. They are phylogenetically the slow, fatigue-resistant, type-I fibre-rich muscles of the extensor thrust system; in decerebrate rigidity their tone is exaggerated, which is the classical proof that the nervous system is biased to keep the extensor chain ready. In quadrupeds the anti-gravity muscles are the limb extensors; in humans, standing upright, the same system must also fight gravity at every joint above the ground.

The answer then traces the mechanism, the postural-control strategies, assessment and training of this tonic extensor system.

2Physiology

Mechanism first. Standing is not a statue's pose: the body continuously sways over the base of support, and the anti-gravity muscles turn that postural sway into controlled sway. Low-level tonic activity in soleus and erector spinae holds a resting posture, driven by the gamma motor system, which keeps the muscle spindles sensitive so the tonic stretch reflex can respond within milliseconds to a perturbation. Postural tone is therefore a reflex background, continuously recalibrated by the cerebellum and vestibular nuclei against visual, vestibular and proprioceptive input. The result is a stable but adjustable column — a stick balanced on a moving hand, where the "hand" is the ankle strategy.

When balance is threatened, the anti-gravity muscles act in coordinated muscle synergy patterns, not one by one. Small sway on a firm surface: the ankle strategy — gastrocnemius-soleus and hamstrings on the posterior sway, tibialis anterior and quadriceps on the anterior sway. Faster or compliant-surface perturbations: the hip strategy — rapid trunk and thigh motion using the same extensor chain. Large displacements: the stepping strategy. Crucially, these muscles also fire BEFORE movement: anticipatory postural adjustments — the transversus abdominis and multifidus with the diaphragm pre-tension the trunk, and the soleus stiffens the ankle before the arm even lifts.

3Pathophysiology

Fatigue of the anti-gravity muscles shifts control to the hip strategy, increases sway velocity, and is a documented risk factor for falls in the elderly.

With ageing, sarcopenia, deconditioning or neurological disease, the tonic extensor reserve falls, the gamma-spindle loop loses sensitivity, and the anticipatory postural adjustments weaken — so sway velocity rises and a small perturbation that a young system absorbs becomes a fall.

4Answer

Static: Romberg test, sharpened Romberg, single-leg stance time (less than 10 seconds with eyes open flags falling risk in older adults), functional reach test, limits-of-stability platform measures. Dynamic: timed up-and-go, berg balance scale, or computerised posturography which quantifies sway path and strategy use. Test eyes open versus closed to separate the sensory contributions, and fatigue the muscles (repeated heel raises) to expose the reserve.

Train the reflex, not just the muscle: progressive balance work (stable to unstable, double to single leg, eyes open to closed), perturbation training, eccentric and endurance work for soleus and quadriceps, and core stability training that restores the anticipatory postural adjustments. Hislop, Daniels and Worthingham's covers the testing of these muscles' endurance; Guyton and Hall gives the reflex physiology. In conclusion: postural stability is a reflex-managed equilibrium in which the tonic extensor chain supplies the continuous force against gravity, the spindle-gamma system supplies the sensitivity, and the CNS supplies the strategy; treat instability by training all three layers.

Fig 3 — One stick figure, five yellow dots down the extensor chain, one gravity arrow. The examiner sees instantly that you know WHICH muscles and WHY they work together.
The three names that lift this answer from average to excellent: gamma motor system, anticipatory postural adjustment, and ankle strategy. Quote the reflex mechanism (spindle bias), then the strategies, then assessment and training — mechanism first, always.

5Recent advances

  • Sherrington et al. (2020) — the Cochrane-updated review of physical activity and falls prevention (116 studies, 25,160 participants) found high-certainty evidence that exercise reduces the rate of falls by about 23%; balance and functional training reduced falls by 24%, and programmes of 3 or more hours a week including balance exercises reduced falls by 42%.
  • Li et al. (2018) — this JAMA Internal Medicine randomised trial of 670 older adults found that a therapeutic tai ji quan balance programme reduced falls by 58% compared with stretching and by 31% compared with multimodal exercise, the largest fall-prevention exercise effect reported to date.
  • Albornos-Muñoz et al. (2024) — a randomised non-inferiority trial found the Otago Exercise Programme remains effective whether delivered in a group or individually, with higher adherence to individual training.
  • USPSTF (2024) — the US Preventive Services Task Force recommends exercise interventions to prevent falls in community-dwelling adults aged 65 years or older who are at increased risk.

6References

  1. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — postural reflexes and muscle spindle-gamma system.
  2. Hislop, Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing (7) — anti-gravity muscle testing positions.
  3. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — balance and postural stability training progression.
  4. Sherrington C, et al. Exercise for preventing falls in older people living in the community. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2019.

On the evaluation form — Q3: Postural instability — elderly faller (role of anti-gravity muscles)

I. Subjective examination

68-year-old retired teacher. Chief complaints: fear of falling with avoidance of outdoor walking; the “legs give way”; imbalance in the dark and on wet tiles; knee pain 2/10 on NPRS. Past medical history: two falls in the past year, one causing a wrist fracture; on antihypertensives; no vertigo. Symptom analysis — site: knees with general postural imbalance; onset: over the past year; severity: knee pain 2/10 on NPRS; aggravating factors: darkness, wet tiles; relieving factors: not reported. Vitals not recorded at this assessment.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Stooped kyphotic posture with the head forward and a wide-based stance; no wasting, oedema or scars documented.

On palpation. Soft quadriceps and calf muscles (reduced tone); tight thoracic paraspinals; no local tenderness, spasm or swelling documented.

1. Motor assessment. MMT (MRC 0–5): soleus 3+, quadriceps 3+, gluteus maximus 3, gluteus medius 3+, erector spinae 4. Cannot sustain heel raises; chair-stand performance below age norms.

2. Sensory assessment. Reduced vibration and position sense at the great toes; diminished ankle jerks — age-related distal sensory decline feeding impaired postural reflexes.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Difficulty rising from a chair (chair-stand below age norms); hand support needed on stairs; outdoor walking avoided. Outcome measures: Berg Balance Scale 0–56 (lower = greater fall risk); Timed Up and Go (seconds); Functional Reach Test for dynamic balance; Falls Efficacy Scale for fear of falling.

4. Gait analysis. Cautious, short-stepped gait without push-off; turns en-bloc; hand support on stairs.

5. Balance. Sway increases with the eyes shut; wide-based stance; delayed reaction to perturbation.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation; uses hand support on stairs as a balance strategy.

7. Coordination. Delayed postural reactions to perturbation.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

Romberg testFeet together, eyes closed for 30 sIncreased sway or a fallLoss of proprioceptive postural control
Single-leg stanceStanding on one leg, eyes openCannot sustain 10 sPoor static postural stability

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Weak anti-gravity muscles (soleus, quadriceps, glutei, spinal extensors)
