  • Self-image concerns
  • Risk of progression during the growth spurt
11. Functional diagnosis

Postural asymmetry with poor sitting endurance and self-image concerns secondary to adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, with a risk of curve progression during the remaining growth.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): performs a daily 20-minute exercise set independently; correct sitting posture for 30-minute study blocks.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): no progression on serial readings; 3 × 15 independent self-correction; brace compliance 18–20 hours daily if prescribed.

13. Treatment plan

Phase I (weeks 1–4): mirror feedback of curve correction; active self-correction 5 × 10-second holds, 3 times daily; hamstring and hip-flexor stretches 2 × 30 seconds daily. Phase II (weeks 5–12) — scoliosis-specific exercise (SEAS/Schroth-based): elongation and de-rotation in sitting, side-lying over a roll and standing; rotational angular breathing 10 breaths × 3; core stabilization (dead bug, bird-dog 3 × 10). Phase III: swimming and graded strengthening.

14. Home programme

Daily 20-minute set, brace wear as advised, monthly scoliometer review.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Write the principles and concept of the McKenzie technique.

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 4 — manual therapy schools including McKenzie

★ Memory hook — McKenzie law: centralise = continue, peripheralise = stop. Three syndromes D-P-D: Derangement (directional preference), Postural (correction), Dysfunction (end-range stretch).

1Introduction

Robin McKenzie's concept is that most spinal and extremity pain of mechanical origin behaves in a predictable, directional way: certain movements worsen it and the opposite movements abolish it. Assessment therefore uses repeated end-range test movements in a single direction — flexion in lying, extension in lying — observing the effect on the site of pain. The patient is assessed as a mechanical system, and the directional response found in the first session drives the entire treatment.

2Physiology

The intervertebral disc, facet joints, ligaments and muscles form a load-sharing system: in the neutral lordotic posture load is distributed evenly and the tissue tolerates sustained activity without pain. Normal tissue deforms elastically and recovers, and movement circulates nutrients into the avascular disc. This is why, in the absence of pathology, a change of position alone abolishes pain.

3Pathophysiology

Derangement syndrome: internal displacement of nuclear material; pain changes within a single session, flexion aggravates, rapid changes occur. Dysfunction syndrome: structurally shortened tissue stretched painfully; pain appears only at end range, does not centralise, improves over weeks. Postural syndrome: pain only from prolonged static loading of normal tissue, abolished by position change. OTHER (non-mechanical or chronic presentations such as CRPS, neural compromise) requires a different route — red flags and central sensitisation states, where McKenzie principles alone do not apply.

4Answer

Centralisation of symptoms is the heart of the method: when repeated movement abolishes distal or peripheral pain and draws it proximally toward the midline, the movement is therapeutic and the prognosis improves. Peripheralisation — pain travelling further down the limb — is a stop signal. Directional preference is the movement direction that centralises or abolishes pain; it is diagnostic and therapeutic simultaneously.

Treatment is patient-generated force first, therapist force only if needed — force progression goes from static positions (sustained) to dynamic movements, to patient overpressure, to clinician overpressure, to mobilisation and traction. Education is central: the patient learns which postures to adopt (lumbar lordosis) and which to avoid (slumped sitting, flexion in derangement), so self-management reduces recurrences. In dysfunction syndrome the principle inverts — the short tissue is stretched repeatedly at end range; in postural syndrome the cure is postural correction and endurance.

Fig 4 — The before-and-after centralisation box with the force-progression ladder beneath it. This one diagram carries the whole concept of the technique.

Once symptoms centralise and abolish, the patient maintains the directional-preference exercise and the postural habit: lumbar support in sitting, regular breaks from flexion, and a home programme of the recovery-of-function movements in the lost direction, restoring full flexion gradually once the derangement is stable.

Centralisation is a validated prognostic sign; McKenzie care shows short-term superiority over generic advice for acute low back pain and equals other active therapies long term. Conclude: assess by repeated movement, classify by behaviour, treat with the patient's own force in the preferred direction, and make the patient their own therapist.

Examiner's tip: the four syllabus words are centralisation, directional preference, classification and self-management — build each h4 around one of them and the examiner ticks in order.

5Recent advances

  • Halliday et al. (2019) — A systematic review found trials adhering to all three core MDT principles — classification, classification-based exercise and appropriate application of force — reported larger reductions in pain and disability than non-adherent trials.
  • Hennemann et al. (2024) — A meta-analysis of the McKenzie method delivered by credentialed therapists for chronic low back pain with directional preference found low-to-moderate certainty evidence of clinically important short-term pain and intermediate-term disability benefit.
  • Sanchis-Sánchez et al. (2020) — A meta-analysis concluded that MDT is no more effective than other active or passive physical-therapy approaches for chronic low back pain, so its value lies in accurate subgroup classification rather than as a universal treatment.
  • Edmond et al. (2019) — A cohort study of 801 patients found that adding graded activity or graded exposure was more likely to benefit those without a directional preference, while those with a directional preference did well on directional-preference exercise alone.
  • Lam et al. (2018) — A meta-analysis in the Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy found the McKenzie method (mechanical diagnosis and therapy) reduces pain and disability in low back pain, with the largest and most consistent gains when patients are classified by directional preference before treatment.

6References

  1. McKenzie R, May S. The Lumbar Spine: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Spine chapter.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Intervention sections.
  4. Halliday MH et al. Treatment effect sizes of mechanical diagnosis and therapy for pain and disability in low back pain: a systematic review. JOSPT. 2019.
  5. Lam OT et al. Effectiveness of the McKenzie method of mechanical diagnosis and therapy for low back pain: literature review with meta-analysis. JOSPT. 2018.
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Write down the role of physiotherapy in management of glenohumeral dysfunction in swimmers.

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 1 — interventions for muscle performance and neuromuscular control

★ Memory hook — GIRD plus dyskinesis equals swimmer's shoulder. Rebuild the chain C-S-T-C: Cuff (external rotation), Scapular control, Thoracic rotation, Core.

1Introduction

Swimmer's shoulder is the commonest overuse injury in competitive swimmers — a spectrum from rotator-cuff tendinopathy and subacromial pain to labral and instability problems driven by the repetitive overhead stroke. Because training volume is high and the shoulder is loaded near end-range thousands of times a week, physiotherapy must combine tissue healing with technique and load management, not local modalities alone.

2Physiology

Normal shoulder function depends on the rotator cuff centring the humeral head while the scapula provides a stable, upwardly rotating base; scapulohumeral rhythm and balanced rotator-cuff and periscapular activity keep the subacromial space open through elevation. Normal swimmers develop a physiological internal-rotation gain of about 18 to 20 degrees in the dominant arm, and the total rotational arc stays symmetrical.

3Pathophysiology

Swimmer's shoulder is an overuse problem of the shoulder girdle during the pull-through and recovery phases of freestyle. During recovery and hand entry the shoulder rotates under load; combined external rotation and abduction compresses the posterior-superior labrum and rotator cuff — internal impingement — while micro-instability from capsular laxity and fatigue lets the humeral head migrate. Fatigued periscapular muscles produce scapular dyskinesis: a dropped, protracted scapula that closes the subacromial space. Assess with the swimming history (stroke, weekly distance, hand-entry pattern), painful arc and Neer or Hawkins tests, labral provocation tests, scapular observation in repeated elevation, and documented glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD) with the side-lying comparison against total arc rotation.

4Answer

Relative rest from the aggravating volume, not total rest — swimmers decondition fast and can kick-train with a pull-buoy between the ankles. Modalities are optional adjuncts; the real work is pain-free maintenance of range, isometric cuff loading, and posture correction. Address the posterior capsule tightness with sleeper and cross-body stretches early.

Rehabilitate from inside out: rotator cuff strength with external rotation at 0 and 90 degrees abduction using elastic resistance, scapular control with retraction, low-row, prone Y-T-W and serratus wall slides, then closed-chain work and pyometric catching, and finally dry-land swim-specific strength — pull-ups, cable internal-rotation mimicking the pull-through. Correct GIRD to bring the total rotation arc to symmetry (sleeper stretch, cross-body adduction stretch and joint mobilisations in external rotation). Restore thoracic extension rotation for the breathing pattern and core strength to anchor the kinetic chain.

Fig 5 — The overhead arm at hand entry with the impingement zone marked, the rebuilding chain and the GIRD rule. Examining boards love the GIRD numbers 18 to 20 degrees of deficit.

Physiotherapy in swimmers fails without technique analysis: correct thumb-entry to fingertip-first entry, avoid midline crossover, balance the bilateral breathing, increase body roll. Coordinate with the coach on training-load modification — cutting only the painful sets, keeping the aerobic base.

Return to full training when the shoulder is pain-free through the full arc, external-rotation strength approximates the sound side (within 10 percent), and the scapula stays controlled after a fatigue set. Prevention is a season-long programme of cuff and scapular strengthening, GIRD surveillance, and a progressive rather than sudden increase in weekly distance.

Examiner's tip: half of every swimmer's-shoulder answer is NOT in the shoulder — GIRD, scapular dyskinesis and thoracic-core links are what fetch the full ten. Also name the phase of the stroke (hand entry, pull-through) when you describe the mechanism; vague "overhead activity" is a half-mark sentence.

5Recent advances

  • Yoma et al. (2022) — A scoping review found that a six- to eight-week programme of shoulder external-rotator and scapular-retractor strengthening plus pectoral stretching can reduce the incidence of shoulder pain in swimmers, and open-chain dry-land work is superior to water training for external-rotation strength.
  • Tavares et al. (2022) — A systematic review of therapeutic exercise for swimmer's-shoulder risk factors found favourable but low-quality evidence for improving strength, endurance and posture, with scapular dyskinesis and glenohumeral instability still under-studied.
  • Gharisia et al. (2021) — A randomised trial showed that a novel passive glenohumeral internal-rotation stretch (with clam-shell bridging) improved internal-rotation range as much as the modified sleeper stretch but reduced pain more.
  • Sajadi et al. (2019) — A six-week targeted corrective-exercise programme improved glenohumeral internal rotation in female adolescent swimmers with scapular dyskinesis.
  • Tavares et al. (2025) — A three-group randomised trial found a 12-week preventive shoulder programme (external and internal rotation at 90 degrees, scapular punches, T’s and Y’s) minimised the seasonal rotator-cuff strength imbalance in competitive swimmers, with weights and elastic bands equally effective.

6References

  1. Wilk KE, Brotzman SB. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation. Shoulder chapters.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Shoulder chapter.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Shoulder section.
  4. Yoma M et al. The effect of exercise therapy interventions on shoulder pain and musculoskeletal risk factors for shoulder pain in competitive swimmers: a scoping review. J Sport Rehabil. 2022.
  5. Effectiveness of therapeutic exercise in musculoskeletal risk factors related to swimmer's shoulder: a systematic review. Eur J Investig Health Psychol Educ. 2022.

On the evaluation form — Q5: Swimmer's shoulder

I. Subjective examination

A 19-year-old state-level freestyle swimmer (training mileage 30 km weekly) reports anterolateral right shoulder pain of six weeks' duration, with no trauma. Site: anterolateral right shoulder. Onset: gradual. Duration: six weeks. Type: overuse pain, occurring in the catch and pull-through phases of the stroke and now also present at night. Severity: 5/10 on NPRS during training, 2/10 at rest. Aggravating factors: swimming (catch and pull-through phases), lying on the shoulder at night. Relieving factors: rest. No neck-driven symptoms; no fever, weight loss or other red-flag features reported. Vital signs not recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Rounded shoulders with a forward head; scapular dyskinesis with inferior-angle winging on wall push-ups.

On palpation. Tenderness over the greater tuberosity, the anterior joint line and the medial scapular border; tight pectoralis minor.

1. Motor assessment. Painful arc on abduction between 60° and 120°; glenohumeral internal rotation 25° less than on the left. MMT: supraspinatus, external rotators, serratus anterior and lower trapezius 4/5, with upper trapezius dominance.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation normal; cervical dermatomal and myotomal screen normal — no neck-driven symptoms.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Dry-land push-ups show scapular winging; the catch phase of swimming is painful; the swimmer avoids breathing on the right side. Outcome measures: SPADI (0–100), QuickDASH (0–100) sports module, PSFS (0–10) for swimming tasks, and weekly training distance.

4. Gait analysis. Not formally analysed — an isolated right shoulder condition with no lower-limb involvement.

5. Balance. Not affected; not formally assessed.

6. Hand function. No hand dysfunction reported; no assistive devices used.

7. Coordination. Scapulohumeral coordination disturbed, evidenced by scapular dyskinesis with winging on wall push-ups.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Neer testPassive forward flexion, arm internally rotatedPain between 90° and 160°Subacromial impingement. Result in this patient: not documented.
Hawkins-Kennedy test90° flexion, forced internal rotationPain reproducedImpingement against the coracoacromial arch. Result in this patient: not documented.
Painful arcActive abduction in the scapular planePain between 60° and 120°Rotator cuff tendinopathy. Result in this patient: positive — pain between 60° and 120° documented.
Empty can (Jobe) testResisted abduction at 90° in internal rotationWeakness or painSupraspinatus involvement. Result in this patient: not formally documented; supraspinatus strength 4/5 on MMT.
Sulcus signDownward traction on the relaxed armGap below the acromionGeneralised laxity contributing to overload. Result in this patient: not documented.
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Rotator cuff overload with a painful arc (60–120°)
  • Glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (25°)
  • Scapular dyskinesis
  • Weak stabilisers — supraspinatus, external rotators, serratus anterior and lower trapezius 4/5
  • Tight pectoralis minor with upper trapezius dominance

Functional limitations

  • Cannot complete training sessions
  • Painful catch phase of the stroke
  • Avoids right-side breathing; winging on dry-land push-ups

Disabilities

  • Missed competition
11. Functional diagnosis

Right subacromial impingement with rotator cuff overload, glenohumeral internal rotation deficit and scapular dyskinesis, causing training intolerance in a competitive swimmer.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Pain reduced from 5/10 to 2/10 during daily activities; pain-free sleep; internal rotation deficit under 10°.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Full 30 km/week training, pain-free; SPADI reduced by 30%; normal scapulohumeral rhythm; return to racing by week 12.

13. Treatment plan

Phase I (weeks 1–2) — relative rest: training mileage cut to 50%; avoid butterfly and paddles; ice after sessions; sleeper stretch 3 × 30 seconds daily. Phase II (weeks 3–5) — scapular retraining: scapular setting, wall slides and prone Y-T-W 3 × 12; side-lying external rotation to theraband 3 × 15 daily. Phase III (weeks 6–12) — rotator cuff and kinetic-chain strengthening; graded return to training with volume increased 10–15% weekly; stroke correction with the coach (high-elbow catch, body rotation).

14. Home programme

Daily 15-minute band and stretch routine; icing after heavy sets.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Explain the role of assistive devices in the workplace.

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 6 — assistive devices at work and assistive technology

★ Memory hook — Prescribe a device by A-M-T-F: Analyse the job demands, Match the device to the task, Trial and train the worker, Follow up — a device the worker rejects is a device that sits in a cupboard.

1Introduction

An assistive device is any tool, product or technology that enables a person with an impairment to perform a task they would otherwise be unable to do, or to do it more safely. In the workplace they range along a spectrum: low-tech ergonomic aids (reachers, splints, adapted cutlery), mid-tech (ergonomic keyboards, voice-amplifiers, sit-stand desks, powered wheelchairs) and high-tech assistive technology (screen readers, voice-recognition software, environmental control units). Orthoses, prostheses and mobility aids used on the job are part of the same family.

2Physiology

The working body tolerates load best when joints stay near the neutral mid-range, when force is shared across large muscle groups, and when posture changes often enough for tissues to recover. Sustained static postures and repetitive end-range movements raise intramuscular pressure, reduce local blood flow and accelerate fatigue — which is why ergonomics aims to keep the worker within these physiological tolerances.

3Pathophysiology

Work-related musculoskeletal disorders arise when the physical demands of the job exceed the tissue capacity to adapt: sustained end-range lumbar flexion loads the disc and posterior ligaments, repetitive wrist extension and gripping strain the forearm tendons and first dorsal compartment, and constant standing loads the feet and spine. Cumulative exposure produces pain, weakness and lost workdays, and the resulting impairment in turn reduces the worker's tolerance of the very tasks that caused it.

4Answer

The device is prescribed only after an ergonomic job analysis: the physical demands of the post (lift, reach, keyboard hours, standing time), the environment, the impairment profile, and the worker's own goals. Match the device to the task, not to the diagnosis. Involve the worker in selection — a device the worker rejects is a device that will sit in a cupboard. Check safety, training time, maintenance and cost before finalising the recommendation.

Examples that earn concrete marks: reachers and long-handled tools for limited mobility after back injury; adjustable chair with lumbar support and footrest for the desk worker with chronic low back pain; angled or split keyboards and vertical mice for carpal-tunnel and WRMSD presentations; standing desks and anti-fatigue mats; lifting aids such as hoists and transfer boards in hospitals; jar openers, one-handed boards and splints in food or assembly work; amplified phones and visual alarms for hearing impairment.

Fig 6 — Labelled ergonomic workstation with the assessment chain. Simple boxes with the device names beside the body part they protect are enough; the examiner wants names, not art.

Voice-recognition software for the worker with severe WRMSD of the hand or high spinal involvement; screen readers, magnification and Braille displays for visual impairment; eye-gaze systems and environmental controls for severe motor loss; powered mobility with work-specific modifications; prosthetic myoelectric hands for amputees returning to office or technical work. In the Indian context, also mention accessibility under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016, which obliges employers to provide reasonable accommodation.

Benefits: earlier and safer return to work, retention of employment and income, reduced re-injury and compensation cost, improved productivity and morale. Barriers: cost, employer attitudes, lack of trial and training, poor follow-up. Evidence: provision of ergonomic devices with workplace assessment reduces WRMSD symptom progression and lost workdays compared to advice alone; work-hardening programmes that embed the actual devices and tasks of the job return more workers to sustained employment. Conclude: the device is the visible half — the assessment, training and follow-up are what make it work.

Examiner's tip: structure this answer as classify, assess, match, train, follow up — and give at least six named devices with one condition each. Generic phrases like "helps the worker" carry no marks.

5Recent advances

  • Sundstrup et al. (2020) — A systematic review found strong evidence that workplace strength training reduces musculoskeletal disorders in workers with physically demanding jobs, but only limited or no benefit for participatory ergonomics and multifaceted interventions in isolation.
  • Skamagki et al. (2026) — An updated systematic review of workplace interventions for chronic musculoskeletal disorders found that multicomponent approaches combining exercise, ergonomics and education gave the most consistent benefits, that digitally delivered exercise was comparable to face-to-face delivery, and that work-related outcomes remained limited and inconsistent.
  • Sormunen et al. (2022) — A randomised trial of participatory ergonomics plus occupational physiotherapy counselling did not show additional benefit over counselling alone for preventing work disability in low back pain.
  • Santos et al. (2025) — A systematic review and meta-analysis found ergonomic interventions reduce work-related musculoskeletal pain (notably in the lower back, upper back, neck and wrist) but with small, context-dependent effects, so devices work best as part of a multicomponent programme rather than in isolation.
  • Gram et al. (2014) — A 20-week cluster randomised trial of 351 office workers found workplace neck and shoulder strength training reduced neck pain and headache, and the benefit was similar whether or not the sessions were supervised.

6References

  1. Maxey L, Magnusson P. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. Work and ADL chapters.
  2. Chui L et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Work conditioning section.
  4. Sundstrup E et al. A systematic review of workplace interventions to rehabilitate musculoskeletal disorders among employees with physically demanding work. J Occup Rehabil. 2020.
  5. Workplace interventions for chronic musculoskeletal disorders: a systematic review. BMJ Open. 2025.

On the evaluation form — Q6: Worker with MSK disorder — workplace assistive devices

I. Subjective examination

A 42-year-old assembly-line worker reports low back pain of two years' duration and right wrist discomfort of four months' duration. Severity: mid-shift backache 5/10 on NPRS (0–10). Heavy lifting and repetitive gripping are difficult. There is recurrent sick leave. No rest or night paraesthesia; no red-flag features documented. Vital signs not recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Assessed at the workstation: stooped lifting, forward head posture, and sustained wrist extension while standing on concrete flooring.

On palpation. Lumbar paraspinal tenderness at L4–L5 and tenderness over the first dorsal compartment of the right wrist.

1. Motor assessment. Lumbar ROM full but painful at end-range flexion; core strength 4/5; right grip 30% weaker; forearm flexibility reduced.

2. Sensory assessment. Median, ulnar and radial nerve screens normal; no rest or night paraesthesia.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Lifts 8 kg with correct technique until mid-shift; wrist-intensive work tolerated for only 2 hours. Outcome measures: NPRS (0–10), ODI (0–100%), QuickDASH (0–100) work module, PSFS (0–10), and monthly sick-leave days.

4. Gait analysis. Not formally documented; gait not reported as affected.

5. Balance. Not documented.

6. Hand function. Repetitive gripping and wrist-intensive grasping/releasing on the line difficult, tolerated 2 hours only; no assistive devices in use at presentation.

7. Coordination. Not affected.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

No specific special test results were documented in the case record; the examination findings noted above (lumbar and first dorsal compartment tenderness, painful end-range lumbar flexion, grip weakness) stand as recorded.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Lumbar and forearm overload
  • Weak core and wrist stabilisers
  • Sustained end-range postures

Functional limitations

  • Limited lifting tolerance
  • Limited assembly/wrist work tolerance (2 hours)

Disabilities

  • Reduced productivity
  • Recurrent sick leave
11. Functional diagnosis

Work-related lumbar and forearm (first dorsal compartment) overload secondary to sustained end-range postures at the workstation, with reduced lifting and assembly tolerance.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Mid-shift pain reduced from 5/10 to 2/10 with workstation changes; independent correct lifting technique.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Full shift with pain below 2/10; lifts 12 kg using aids; ODI down 20 points; no MSK-related sick leave.

13. Treatment plan

Phase I (weeks 1–2): worksite visit — trolley, lumbar cushion, anti-fatigue mat; lifting and neutral-wrist training; 3 micro-break stretches every 30 minutes. Phase II (weeks 3–6): core stabilisation (plank 3 × 30 seconds, dead bug, bird-dog daily); eccentric wrist strengthening 3 × 15. Phase III (weeks 7–12): work hardening with graded tasks; resistance training twice weekly; device-compliance review.

Workplace assistive devices to be prescribed:

DevicePurposeExample
Ergonomic chair with lumbar supportMaintains lumbar lordosis when seatedAdjustable chair, lumbar cushion
Sit-stand workstationAlternates posture, cuts static loadingHeight-adjustable desk

Daily stretch and band routine; continued device use at home.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. What are the tendon transfer techniques for median nerve injury? Add a note on physiotherapy management.

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 4 — neurological concepts including tendon transfer and re-education

★ Memory hook — Opposition transfers are P-E-F: Palmaris longus (Camitz), Extensor indicis proprius, Flexor digitorum superficialis of the ring finger — and name each donor WITH its insertion (abductor pollicis brevis).

1Introduction

A tendon transfer re-routes the muscle-tendon unit of a working muscle to the insertion of a paralysed one. The classic requirements: the donor muscle must be expendable, of adequate strength (grade 4 plus) and similar amplitude; joints must be mobile and supple; the transfer should run a straight line in a single direction; and it should be synergistic with the movement it replaces. Correctable contractures and adequate soft-tissue cover come first — no transfer survives a stiff, scarred bed.

2Physiology

The median nerve supplies the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis and the superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis), the radial two lumbricals, and sensation to the radial three-and-a-half digits; opposition combines thumb abduction, flexion and pronation to bring the pulp against the other fingers. After a tendon transfer the transferred muscle-tendon unit heals by tendon-to-tendon and tendon-to-bone union, regaining gliding as early controlled motion begins, while the cortex re-learns the new muscle-to-movement pairing.

3Pathophysiology

Median nerve injury denervates the thenar muscles and the radial lumbricals: a low lesion (below the anterior interosseous branch) loses opposition, abduction and radial-digit sensation, while a high lesion additionally weakens the flexor pollicis longus and the flexor digitorum profundus to the index, giving the ape hand and a weak pinch. Without opposition the thumb cannot reach the fingers, precision grip fails, and trophic and sensory changes follow in the median territory.

4Answer

A low median injury paralyses the thenar intrinsic muscles, so thumb opposition and abduction are lost, and sensation over the radial three and a half digits is absent. The standard transfers: the FDS of the ring finger (Royle-Thompson) routed subcutaneously to the abductor pollicis brevis insertion; the Camitz transfer, in which the palmaris longus with a strip of palmar aponeurosis is passed to the APB — quick, single-incision, and best in carpal tunnel thenar wasting; the extensor indicis proprius split and transferred to the first dorsal interosseous and APB for opposition plus pinch; and a slip of abductor digiti minimi (Huber) for thenar bulk in the visible thumb-position deficit. The goal is a thumb that can abduct, rotate and reach the fingers — the opponensplasty in one word.

Above the elbow, FPL and FDP to the index are lost too, so flexion of the thumb interphalangeal joint and index distal joint go in addition to opposition and sensibility. Reconstruct: brachioradialis or extensor carpi radialis longus to FPL for thumb flexion; side-to-side tenodesis of the index FDP to the middle-finger FDP for index flexion; and the same opposition transfers as above, plus an FCR or ECRL addition when a strong donor is needed. Sensation can be improved by neurovascular island flaps in selected cases.

Fig 7 — Two arrows from palmaris longus and ring FDS converging on the APB insertion, with the high-lesion transfers in the side box. A wrist circle with two labelled arrows is a full-marks diagram.

Pre-operatively, maintain the prerequisites: full passive joint range, soft-tissue mobilisation for scar and oedema, strengthen the donor muscles consciously (the patient must be able to fire FDS or palmaris longis on command), and desensitise and protect the anaesthetic zones. Post-operatively the transferred tendon is protected in a thumb-spica splint for three to four weeks, then controlled mobilisation begins.

The heart of physiotherapy: the transferred muscle still contracts in its old pattern, so re-education trains the new action — the patient flexes the ring finger (donor action) and simultaneously watches and feels the thumb abduct. Use biofeedback, mirror work and repeated attempted opposition until the movement becomes a single unconscious synergy. Then progress through graded resistance to functional pinch, precision grip and activities of daily living; sensory re-education for the median territory proceeds in parallel.

Well-selected opposition transfers achieve functional pinch in most hands, though power and fine sensory discrimination never equal the original. Conclude: surgery re-routes the tendon, physiotherapy rewires the movement — the transfer earns its function on the treatment table.

Examiner's tip: name the donor AND the insertion for each transfer (FDS of ring finger TO abductor pollicis brevis) — a transfer without its insertion is half a mark. And never forget the physiotherapy half of the question: splint, donor-contraction re-education, then strengthening.

5Recent advances

  • Novak & von der Heyde (2015) — A review in Seminars in Plastic Surgery concluded that combined motor and sensory (sensorimotor) re-education is essential after nerve and tendon reconstruction, using bilateral and mirror-guided training to rebuild cortical motor patterns.
  • Sultana et al. (2013) — A systematic review in the Journal of Hand Therapy found early mobilisation (started within a week) after hand tendon transfer is safe, with no tendon ruptures or pull-outs, and improves range of motion, grip and pinch strength in the first four weeks compared with immobilisation.
  • Rath et al. (2010) — A randomised controlled trial found early active mobilisation after tendon transfer caused no tendon pull-out and shortened rehabilitation time by about two weeks compared with conventional immobilisation.
  • Silfverskiöld & May (1995) — A series of hand and forearm tendon transfers mobilised actively within three days achieved 69 to 78 percent of their final range of motion within a month, showing that early active movement speeds recovery without rupture.

6References

  1. Saunders RJ. Hand and Upper Extremity Rehabilitation. Nerve injury chapters.
  2. Cooper C. Fundamentals of Hand Therapy. Tendon transfer sections.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Peripheral nerve injuries.
  4. Opponensplasty for nerve palsy: a systematic review. 2023.
  5. Functional evaluation of early tendon transfer for thumb opposition in median nerve palsy. J Clin Orthop Trauma. 2020.

On the evaluation form — Q7: Median nerve injury — tendon transfer

I. Subjective examination

A 24-year-old man, six weeks after a deep right forearm laceration (high median nerve injury), is unable to oppose the thumb and reports a clumsy grip with numbness and cold intolerance in the radial three-and-a-half digits. He is right-handed. Tendon transfer (ring-finger FDS to APB, brachioradialis to FPL) is planned. No red-flag features or vital signs documented.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Thenar flattening with an "ape hand" deformity; trophic skin changes over the affected digits.

On palpation. Well-healed, mobile scar; no other palpation findings documented.

1. Motor assessment. MMT (MRC 0–5): thumb opposition and APB 0/5; FPL 2/5; index flexors reduced; pronator quadratus weak; ulnar-innervated muscles 5/5. Muscle girth: thenar girth 1 cm less than on the left.

2. Sensory assessment. Absent light touch over the radial three-and-a-half digits (median nerve distribution); two-point discrimination more than 10 mm (normal up to 6 mm); Tinel's sign advancing at the scar.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Right-hand dominant but currently uses the left hand; unable to button, write or pick up coins. Outcome measures: MMT (0–5) for opposition and pinch; two-point discrimination (normal up to 6 mm); QuickDASH (0–100); PSFS (0–10).

4. Gait analysis. Not relevant — an isolated right forearm/hand condition.

5. Balance. Not relevant.

6. Hand function. Grasping, releasing and precision handling of the right hand impaired — cannot button, write or pick up coins; no thumb opposition; uses the left hand for daily tasks; no assistive device documented.

7. Coordination. Precision coordination of the right hand impaired (clumsy grip).

8. Investigations

Electrodiagnostic studies and any imaging as per medical records; no reports reviewed at this assessment.

Impairments

  • Loss of thumb opposition and pinch (opposition and APB 0/5)
  • Weak FPL (2/5) with reduced index flexion and weak pronator quadratus
  • Sensory loss over the radial three-and-a-half digits with trophic changes

11. Functional diagnosis

Right high median nerve lesion with loss of thumb opposition and pinch, thenar wasting and sensory loss in the median distribution, for which tendon transfer is planned; physiotherapy is directed at pre-operative conditioning and post-operative re-education of the transferred tendons.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Pre-operative conditioning — full passive opposition, supple scar, oedema-free hand; independent splint use; precautions taught.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Transfer power 3+/5 with a new opposition pattern by week 12; QuickDASH improved by 25 points; independent ADLs.

13. Treatment plan

Pre-operative (2–3 weeks): opponens splint; passive thumb and wrist ROM 10 reps 4 times daily; sensory re-education and scar massage twice daily; wax bath. Post-operative Phase I (0–3 weeks): below-elbow cast with the thumb held in opposition; active use of free joints; elevation. Phase II (3–6 weeks): guarded re-education — ring-finger flexion produces thumb opposition, 10 reps hourly; gentle passive ROM. Phase III (6–12 weeks): putty strengthening 3 × 15 daily; pinch and dexterity drills; wean the splint by week 10; return to work by week 12.

14. Home programme

Motor imagery, texture discrimination, scar mobilisation.

Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Describe the role of myofascial release in trapezitis.

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 4 — myofascial schools of manual therapy

★ Memory hook — Sequence the answer R-L-S: Release the trigger point, Lengthen the muscle, Strengthen the lower trapezius so the upper fibres stop doing everyone's work.

1Introduction

Trapezitis — myofascial pain of the upper trapezius — is one of the commonest causes of neck-shoulder ache and tension headache, especially in desk workers and those who carry load on one shoulder. Because the upper trapezius is a postural and accessory muscle it is easily overloaded, and myofascial release targets the taut band and its trigger point to restore comfortable length and movement.

2Physiology

Normal muscle maintains length and tone through balanced actin-myosin overlap and adequate local blood flow; after contraction it relaxes fully and recovers. The upper trapezius normally works with the middle and lower trapezius and the deep neck flexors to support the head, so balanced scapular and cervical muscle activity keeps the muscle within its physiological range.

3Pathophysiology

Trapezitis is overload of the upper trapezius: sustained low-grade contraction from desk posture, phone-on-shoulder habits, emotional stress and poor workstation ergonomics keeps the muscle in continuous activity, exhausting its local circulation. The resulting myofascial trigger point is a hyperirritable spot in a taut band, explained by the integrated hypothesis: an energy crisis — ischaemia releases sensitising substances that lower the local pain threshold and sustain abnormal acetylcholine release, producing the taut band, which further compresses the local vessels. The patient feels aching at the point plus the classic referral to the temple, angle of jaw or between the scapulae.

4Answer

Diagnose on palpation: a taut band in the upper trapezius, an exquisite spot, reproduction of the patient's recognised pain, a local twitch response to snapping palpation, and restricted, painful cervical rotation or side-flexion with or without a positive stretch test. Screen for perpetuating factors — sleep, workstation, spectacles, stress — because a trigger point with perpetuating factors never stays released.

MFR works on the fascia-muscle complex by sustained, low-load, gentle pressure and elongation rather than forceful kneading. For the upper trapezius: direct release with gentle thumb or knuckle pressure applied at 90 degrees to the taut band, held until tissue softening (typically 60 to 90 seconds); skin rolling over the cervicothoracic fascia to restore fascial mobility; positional release — find the tender point, move the neck into the position of ease and hold, letting the point quieten; and sustained stretch with the head side-flexed away and gently rotated toward, held for the full release time. Follow every release with active use of the range gained: the muscle must learn the new length.

Fig 8 — Neck circle with the taut band, the trigger point and its referral arrows to temple and jaw. Drawing the referral pattern correctly is the clinical fingerprint of this answer.

Treat in the order that matches the assessment: release the trigger point, lengthen the muscle, then retrain. Two to three sessions per week over three to four weeks with a home programme of heat, self-pressure with a ball, and stretching. Adjuncts that combine well: spray-and-stretch with ethyl chloride or ice, post-isometric relaxation, dry needling for stubborn points, ergonomic correction of the workstation, breathing retraining for stress-related elevation, and strengthening of the mid and lower trapezius so the upper fibres stop doing everyone's work.

MFR and sustained-pressure techniques show short-term reductions in pain and improved neck range and disability versus placebo in neck-pain trials, with the strongest effect when combined with exercise; dry needling adds short-term benefit. Conclude: MFR releases the taut band, but only posture correction and lower-trapezius retraining keep it released — treat the fire, then remove the fuel.

Examiner's tip: the sequence "release — lengthen — strengthen" is the spine of this answer. Also write the referral pattern of the upper trapezius (temple, jaw, ipsilateral neck) — examiners ask for it in vivas more often than the techniques themselves.

5Recent advances

  • Navarro-Santana et al. (2020) — A systematic review and meta-analysis found dry needling reduces pain intensity and pain-related disability in the short term versus sham or waiting list, with no significant effect on pressure-pain threshold or cervical range of motion.
  • Stieven et al. (2021) — A randomised trial showed that a single session of dry needling or myofascial release produced local and distant pressure-pain-threshold gains superior to sham in upper-trapezius trigger points.
  • Lew et al. (2021) — A meta-analysis found dry needling and trigger-point manual therapy (ischaemic compression, pressure release) equally effective for pain and function in neck and upper-back myofascial pain syndrome.
  • Alattar & Alzahrani (2024) — A randomised trial showed that adding dry needling of upper-trapezius trigger points to usual physiotherapy improved disability, cervical range and depression at follow-up, though immediate post-session pain was higher.
  • Fryer & Hodgson (2005) — A randomised, sham-controlled study found a single 60-second application of manual pressure release to latent upper-trapezius trigger points significantly raised the pressure-pain threshold, providing an evidence base for the ischaemic-compression component of myofascial release.

6References

  1. Butler DS, Jones MA. Mobilisation of the Nervous System / myofascial approaches.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Soft-tissue intervention chapter.
  3. Shacklock M. Clinical Neurodynamics. Mechanosensitivity chapters.
  4. Effectiveness of dry needling for myofascial trigger points associated with neck pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. 2020.
  5. Comparison of dry needling and trigger-point manual therapy in patients with neck and upper back myofascial pain syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis. 2021.

Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. How do you manage pain in fracture cases based on educational and behavioral strategies?

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 2 — educational and behavioural management of pain

★ Memory hook — Fracture pain is managed by E-B-G: Education (pain neuroscience), Behaviour (relaxation, pacing, operant reinforcement), Graded exposure — all working through the dorsal-horn gate.

1Introduction

Fracture pain is acute nociceptive pain with an inflammatory phase, then movement-related pain during healing, and — if mishandled — a transition to chronic pain with fear of movement, guarded patterns and disuse. The gate control theory explains the opening: descending anxiety and attention amplify the signal; confidence and understanding close the gate. Educational and behavioural strategies exploit exactly this — they change what the patient does and expects, which changes what the nervous system transmits.

2Physiology

Normal fracture healing passes through inflammation (days 1 to 5), soft callus (to about three weeks) and hard callus with remodelling (to about three months), during which controlled loading actually stimulates union while immobilisation protects alignment. Pain in this period is acute nociceptive pain — an appropriate alarm from the healing tissue — and the dorsal-horn gate can be opened or closed by attention, anxiety and expectation.

3Pathophysiology

When movement-related pain is interpreted as danger, a fear-avoidance cycle develops: guarding and disuse weaken the limb, the pain persists, and the patient becomes increasingly disabled — the transition from acute to chronic pain. Central sensitisation, catastrophising and low pain self-efficacy sustain this state, so the fracture heals but the patient does not return to function.

4Answer

Pain-neuroscience education first: explain in the patient's language that pain is an alarm produced by the brain on the basis of danger, not a meter of tissue damage — a healing fracture that is protected by a cast is safe to move. Show the healing timeline (inflammation days 1 to 5, soft callus to about 3 weeks, hard callus to about 3 months) so the patient interprets twinges correctly. Give clear rules: weight-bearing status, dos and don'ts, red flags. Set expectations for mobilisation pain and control pathways, teach relaxation breathing to be used before and during painful procedures such as cast removal and pin-site care, and give the patient a written home plan — knowledge that is not written down does not travel home.

Relaxation and breathing retraining, progressive muscle relaxation of uninvolved segments, guided imagery and distraction for procedural pain; cognitive restructuring to catch catastrophising thoughts ("the bone is breaking again"); pacing to break the boom-bust cycle of overdoing on good days; operant strategies — the family is taught to reinforce function ("well done for walking to the gate") and not to reinforce pain behaviour (not rushing with a tray every time the patient winces); goal-setting and self-monitoring with a simple diary; and positive reinforcement tied to achievement, not to suffering.

Fig 9 — The Melzack-and-Wall gate with the fracture-specific openers and closers. One diagram links education, relaxation and graded exposure to a single mechanism — that is how a 10-marker reads like a story.

After immobilisation, many patients show fear-avoidance: they equate pain with damage and stop moving. Assess with the Tampa Scale and map their fear hierarchy, then expose them in graded steps — from pain-free isometrics, to assisted range, to weight-bearing, stairs and return to work — each step mastered before the next. Time-contingent rather than pain-contingent scheduling ("walk ten minutes at 8 am daily") prevents the patient being ruled by the pain meter. Combine with goal-setting for functional milestones and progress visible to the patient.

Pain neuroscience education reduces pain and disability and fear in musculoskeletal cohorts; behavioural graded activity matches or beats standard physiotherapy for return-to-function after injury. Conclude: in fracture care, the pharmacologist controls the chemistry of pain, but the physiotherapist controls the psychology and behaviour of pain — education that the patient can repeat back is the cheapest analgesic on the ward.

Examiner's tip: the examiner set this question under educational and behavioral strategies, so do NOT spend half the answer on TENS and cryotherapy — one sentence on adjuncts is enough, then build the marks on gate control, pain education, pacing, operant reinforcement and graded exposure.

5Recent advances

  • Kim & Lee (2020) — A systematic review and meta-analysis found pain neuroscience education significantly improves kinesiophobia and pain in chronic musculoskeletal pain, with the effect larger when combined with other treatment.
  • Murillo et al. (2023) — A secondary mediation analysis of a randomised trial found that reductions in kinesiophobia and central-sensitisation-related distress after pain-neuroscience education plus exercise mediated later gains in disability, medication intake and quality of life.
  • Huang et al. (2022) — A network meta-analysis found multimodal protocols combining physical and psychological treatment the most likely to be effective for kinesiophobia, ahead of unimodal physical or psychological therapy alone.
  • Xu et al. (2020) — A systematic review and meta-analysis found multimodal therapy combining physical and psychological approaches reduces kinesiophobia more than single-modality therapy, an effect that decreases with age.
  • Wood et al. (2019) — A systematic review and meta-analysis found that adding pain neuroscience education to usual physiotherapy produces moderate-quality short-term improvements in pain and disability in chronic low back pain.

6References

  1. Melzack R, Wall PD. Pain mechanisms: a new theory. Science 1965.
  2. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Pain chapters.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Pain management chapter.
  4. Effects of pain neuroscience education on kinesiophobia in patients with chronic pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Phys Ther Rehabil Sci. 2020.
  5. Reductions in kinesiophobia and distress after pain neuroscience education and exercise lead to favourable outcomes: a secondary mediation analysis of a randomised controlled trial. 2023.

Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Explain the physiotherapy intervention for improving endurance in individuals with a sedentary lifestyle.

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 1 — interventions for endurance impairment (Unit 3: physical activity promotion)

★ Memory hook — Quote two number-sets and nothing can fail you: 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity per week plus strengthening on two days (WHO 2020), and the 10-percent-per-week progression rule — then write FITT as four labelled boxes, not one paragraph.

1Introduction

A sedentary lifestyle is now one of the leading modifiable risks for chronic disease: nearly one third of adults worldwide are physically inactive, and prolonged sitting is independently associated with poorer cardiovascular and metabolic health. Improving endurance in the sedentary adult is therefore a core physiotherapy task — it reverses deconditioning and restores the capacity to meet the demands of daily life.

2Physiology

Endurance depends on the integrated capacity of the heart, lungs, blood and skeletal muscle to deliver and use oxygen: central factors (stroke volume and cardiac output) and peripheral factors (capillary and mitochondrial density and oxidative enzymes). Regular aerobic training enlarges stroke volume, raises capillary and mitochondrial density, improves insulin sensitivity and shifts muscle toward fat oxidation — adaptations that begin within weeks and continue for months.

3Pathophysiology

A sedentary lifestyle produces deconditioning through central and peripheral mechanisms: a lower stroke volume and cardiac output reserve, reduced capillary and mitochondrial density in muscle, and a shift toward glycolytic fatigability. Insulin sensitivity falls, visceral fat accumulates, and the patient fatigues on one flight of stairs. The good news is the trainability — even modest volumes of activity reverse much of this, and the WHO's position that some activity is always better than none.

4Answer

Screen with a physical-activity readiness questionnaire (PAR-Q+) and risk-factor profile; flag the sedentary middle-aged desk worker with hypertension or diabetes for medical clearance before vigorous training. Baseline tests that need no lab: resting and exercise heart rate, the six-minute walk test, a submaximal step or cycle test (Astrand or Chester), a sit-to-stand test for strength endurance, and simple anthropometry. Record the baseline — the whole motivational architecture of the programme depends on being able to show change.

Prescribe by the FITT framework. Frequency: five days per week of moderate, or three of vigorous, aerobic activity. Intensity: begin at 40 to 50 percent of heart-rate reserve or a Borg RPE of 10 to 12, progressing to 60 to 70 percent; use the talk test as the field check. Time: start at 20 to 30 minutes of accumulated moderate activity — three 10-minute walks count — progressing to 150 to 300 minutes per week as the WHO 2020 guidelines recommend, plus muscle-strengthening on two or more days. Type: walking is the Indian default — cheap, safe, and sociable — with cycling, swimming, or home-based step-ups and dance as alternatives that survive the monsoon and the office calendar.

Fig 10 — The four FITT boxes over a rising 12-week staircase. This figure answers both halves of the question in one image: what to prescribe and how to progress.

Add circuit training with body-weight resistance (sit-to-stand, step-ups, wall push-ups, resistance band rows) at 12 to 20 repetitions, two days per week — endurance of the postural and locomotor muscles, not just the heart. Progress by roughly 10 percent per week in duration first, then intensity; monitor with RPE, morning resting heart rate, session adherence and symptom review, and step counters or phone apps as objective feedback. Include warm-up, cool-down and safety education.

Adherence decides the outcome: match the intervention to the patient's stage of change, use motivational interviewing, goal-setting and self-monitoring, embed activity into daily routine (stairs, walking to the market, cycle commutes), and use social supports and follow-up. Conclude with the WHO 2020 message — some activity is better than none, more is better still — and the physiotherapist's skill of converting a deconditioned patient into someone who keeps moving.

Examiner's tip: quote two numbersets and nothing can fail you — 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity per week plus strengthening on two days (WHO 2020), and the 10-percent-per-week progression rule. Then write FITT as four separate labelled boxes, not one paragraph.

5Recent advances

  • Bull et al. (2020) — The WHO 2020 guidelines recommend that all adults do 150 to 300 minutes of moderate, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous, aerobic activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening on two or more days, and, for the first time, advise limiting sedentary time.
  • Milanović et al. (2015) — A meta-analysis in Sports Medicine found high-intensity interval training and continuous endurance training both produce large gains in VO2max in healthy adults, with interval training slightly superior and more time-efficient.
  • Bacon et al. (2013) — A meta-analysis found interval training raised VO2max by about 0.5 L/min in sedentary and recreationally active adults, showing that short, high-intensity programmes are an effective, time-efficient way to build endurance.
  • Wicks et al. (2023) — A systematic review and meta-analysis in Age and Ageing found physiotherapist-led, exercise-based telerehabilitation is non-inferior to face-to-face rehabilitation and better than no intervention for improving strength, walking endurance and quality of life in older adults, at lower cost.

6References

  1. WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour, 2020.
  2. ACSM's Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Aerobic endurance chapters.
  4. Bull FC et al. World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. Br J Sports Med. 2020.
  5. Physical activity guidelines 2020: comprehensive and inclusive recommendations to activate populations. Lancet. 2020.

On observation. BMI 29 with central adiposity; round-shouldered posture.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Breathless on two flights of stairs; evening fatigue; cannot jog for a minute. Outcome measures: 6-minute walk test (6MWT) distance and Borg RPE (6–20) every 4 weeks; resting pulse; PSFS (0–10) for stairs.

4. Gait analysis. Gait normal in quality but with poor endurance; pauses on two flights of stairs.

5. Balance. Not formally assessed.

6. Hand function. Not relevant; no hand complaints reported; no assistive devices used.

7. Coordination. Not affected.

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

11. Functional diagnosis

Deconditioning with poor aerobic endurance and reduced calf flexibility in a sedentary adult, limiting stair climbing and participation in family activity.

12. Goals

Phase II (weeks 5–8): 40 minutes, or jog-walk (1 minute jog / 2 minutes walk × 10); stairs twice weekly; 2 strength sessions (squats, push-ups, rows 2–3 × 12). Last-Hour Sheet · Paper IV

QP 8132 · 05-Jun-2024 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1THR — functional training

  • Posterior approach precautions: no flexion past 90, no adduction past midline, no internal rotation in flexion — first 6 weeks.
  • Stairs: up with the sound, down with the operated; stick in the opposite hand.
  • Gluteus medius weakness = Trendelenburg; train the task, not the muscle alone.

2AKA — electrotherapy advances

  • TENS 80-100 Hz for stump pain; evidence for phantom pain still unproven (no RCTs) — say so.
  • Mirror therapy + graded motor imagery = strongest evidence for phantom limb pain.
  • Phantom motor execution: myoelectric pattern recognition, about 15 sessions.
  • NMES maintains residual quadriceps — the future prosthetic bed.

3Scoliosis — posture correction

  • Cobb angle = angle between the most tilted end vertebrae; thresholds 10, 20, 40-45 degrees.
  • Schroth block: elongate — de-rotate — rotational angular breathing — stabilise.
  • PSSE per SOSORT: specific beats generic exercise.

4McKenzie technique

  • Centralisation = symptoms move proximally = better prognosis; peripheralisation = stop.
  • Syndromes: derangement, dysfunction, postural, OTHER.
  • Force progression: static — dynamic — overpressure — therapist force; patient self-treats.

5Swimmer's shoulder

  • Internal impingement + micro-instability + scapular dyskinesis — name all three.
  • GIRD: internal rotation deficit more than 20 degrees with total-arc asymmetry = stretch programme.
  • Rebuild chain: external-rotation cuff — scapula — thorax — core — swim-specific.

6Assistive devices at work

  • Sequence: job demands analysis — worker assessment — match — trial — train — follow up.
  • Low tech: reacher, split keyboard, vertical mouse, lumbar chair, sit-stand desk, hoist.
  • High tech: voice recognition, screen reader, eye-gaze, myoelectric hand.

7Median nerve transfers

  • Low lesion: FDS ring to APB (Royle-Thompson); Camitz = palmaris longus to APB; EIP; Huber.
  • High lesion adds: brachioradialis or ECRL to FPL; index FDP side-to-side.
  • Re-education rule: think donor action, get thumb opposition; thumb-spica 3-4 weeks.

8Trapezitis — MFR

  • Integrated hypothesis: ischaemia — energy crisis — taut band — trigger point.
  • Referral: temple, angle of jaw, between scapulae.
  • Release — lengthen — strengthen; 60-90 second holds; fix the workstation too.

9Fracture pain — education and behaviour

  • Melzack and Wall, Science 1965: fear opens the gate, education and movement close it.
  • Tools: pain neuroscience education, pacing, breathing, operant reinforcement, graded exposure.
  • Time-contingent, not pain-contingent scheduling.

10Endurance in the sedentary

  • WHO 2020: 150-300 min moderate or 75-150 min vigorous per week + strength 2 days.
  • FITT: 5 days, 40-70 percent HRR, 20-30 min, walking first.
  • Progress about 10 percent per week; adherence = motivational interviewing + self-monitoring.
keep-if-nothing-else: the minimum cargo for the exam hall.

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Describe the impaired endurance seen in bed ridden patients with spinal cord injury.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Exercise physiology and management of the immobile patient (spinal cord injury).

★ Memory hook — Bed rest steals the pump, the pipes and the pressure — in SCI the damage is faster because the nervous system that runs them is already cut.

1Introduction

Endurance is the ability to sustain a physical task over time and reflects integrated cardiorespiratory, vascular, muscular and autonomic function. In a bed-ridden patient with spinal cord injury (SCI) this system is challenged twice over: once by the lesion itself and again by prolonged recumbency. The result is a steep fall in aerobic capacity, early fatigue and poor activity tolerance that delays rehabilitation and raises long-term cardiovascular risk.

2Physiology

Normal endurance depends on peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak), the product of cardiac output and the arteriovenous oxygen difference. Cardiac output depends on stroke volume, heart rate and venous return, maintained by the leg muscle pump and sympathetic vasoconstriction. Muscle contributes oxidative capacity through mitochondria, capillaries and type I fibres; VO2peak is about 35-45 ml/kg/min in trained people and 25-30 in sedentary adults.

3Pathophysiology

Immobility alone causes deconditioning: within days there is a fall in plasma volume, reduced left ventricular mass and compliance, loss of the leg muscle pump, reduced capillary density and a shift of muscle fibres towards fast, glycolytic type IIx. In SCI these changes are amplified and lesion-specific. A lesion above T6 removes supraspinal sympathetic control, causing neurogenic chronotropic incompetence (a blunted heart-rate response), impaired vasomotor tone and orthostatic hypotension; loss of the leg pump and venous pooling further reduce venous return, while cardiac atrophy lowers stroke volume. High lesions also impair respiratory function and cough. Spasticity, pressure ulcers, pain and depression reduce activity further. The net effect is a VO2peak that may fall to 10-20 ml/kg/min, with a disproportionate rise in perceived exertion, fatigue at low workloads and reduced endurance for transfers and arm work.

4Answer

Impaired endurance in the bed-ridden SCI patient is assessed and treated in the same framework.

Assessment. Record heart rate, blood pressure (watch for autonomic dysreflexia), respiratory rate and perceived exertion (RPE/Borg); use the 6-minute arm test or arm-crank ergometry for VO2peak, with the Fatigue Severity Scale for function.

Management (early, while on bed rest).

  • Positioning and early passive/active-assisted range of motion, four to six times daily, to preserve joint and muscle length.
  • Respiratory muscle training and incentive spirometry to preserve ventilation and cough.
  • Supine arm-crank ergometry using a bed-mounted ergometer, starting at 40-60% of predicted heart-rate reserve for 15-20 minutes, progressing to 30 minutes, three to five times weekly.
  • Functional electrical stimulation (FES) cycling or FES rowing of the paralysed legs to restore the muscle pump, increase venous return and recruit oxidative fibres; 30-45 minutes, three times weekly.
  • Graded tilt-table or standing programme to re-train orthostatic tolerance; abdominal binders and compression stockings as adjuncts.

Dosage and progression. Apply overload with recovery; evidence-based SCI guidelines recommend at least two aerobic and two strength sessions weekly. Progress duration before intensity and monitor autonomic signs.

Outcome measures. VO2peak/peak power, 6MAT distance, RPE at a fixed load, Fatigue Severity Scale and functional independence scores.

5Recent advances

  • Hodgkiss et al. (2023) — A PLOS Medicine systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression confirmed that exercise improves VO2peak, relative VO2peak and peak power output in SCI, with upper-body aerobic and resistance training among the most effective modes.
  • Pelletier et al. (2015) — A 16-week randomised controlled trial in Spinal Cord showed that following the SCI physical-activity guidelines raised relative VO2peak by about 17% and upper-body strength by 11.5-38.9%, validating the minimum exercise dose for the deconditioned patient.
  • Martin Ginis et al. (2018) — The evidence-based scientific exercise guidelines for adults with SCI (Spinal Cord) recommend at least 20 min of moderate-to-vigorous aerobic exercise twice weekly plus strength training of the major muscle groups twice weekly.
  • Lutfy et al. (2021) — Pilot-tested supine arm-cycle ergometry (the multi-purpose arm cycle ergometer, M-PACE) to safely reduce deconditioning during the four to six weeks of complete bed rest after flap surgery for pressure injuries in SCI.

6References

  1. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. Philadelphia: F.A. Davis; 2018.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. Philadelphia: F.A. Davis; 2019.
  3. American College of Sports Medicine. ACSM's Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription. 11th ed. Wolters Kluwer; 2021.
  4. Martin Ginis KA, van der Scheer JW, Latimer-Cheung AE, et al. Evidence-based scientific exercise guidelines for adults with spinal cord injury. Spinal Cord. 2018;56(4):308-321.
  5. Dolbow DR, Gorgey AS, et al. Exercise and health-related risks of physical deconditioning after spinal cord injury. Top Spinal Cord Inj Rehabil. 2017.

Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Describe the physiological mechanism of analgesia effect in the management of pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Pain mechanisms and electrotherapeutic/physiotherapeutic modulation of pain.

★ Memory hook — Pain is turned down at two gates: one in the spinal cord (gate control) and one in the brainstem (descending control).

1Introduction

Analgesia is the reduction of the perception of pain without loss of consciousness. Physiotherapists produce analgesia through several overlapping physiological mechanisms rather than by a single switch. Understanding these mechanisms explains why techniques as different as TENS, manual therapy, exercise, acupuncture and cryotherapy all relieve pain, and how to choose and dose them.

2Physiology

Nociception has four stages: transduction (a noxious stimulus becomes an electrical signal in free nerve endings), transmission (conduction along A-delta and C fibres to the dorsal horn and then via the spinothalamic tract), modulation (alteration of the signal at the spinal cord and brainstem) and perception (the subjective experience). The dorsal horn is a key control point. Melzack and Wall's gate control theory (1965) proposed that large-diameter A-beta fibres, excited by touch or non-noxious stimulation, activate inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) that presynaptically inhibit the A-delta and C fibres carrying nociceptive input, closing the gate. The brain also sends descending control: the periaqueductal grey matter (PAG) and the rostral ventromedial medulla project to the dorsal horn through serotonergic and noradrenergic pathways, and activate the endogenous opioid system. Endogenous opioids - endorphins (mu receptors), enkephalins (delta) and dynorphins (kappa) - inhibit transmitter release (including substance P) and hyperpolarise neurons, raising the pain threshold. Diffuse noxious inhibitory controls (DNIC), measured clinically as conditioned pain modulation, form another endogenous inhibitory system.

3Pathophysiology

When nociceptive input is intense or prolonged the modulation systems fail. Repeated C-fibre firing causes wind-up and central sensitisation, with increased excitability of dorsal-horn neurons, enlarged receptive fields, hyperalgesia (painful response to mildly painful stimuli) and allodynia (pain from non-painful stimuli). Descending inhibition may become less effective, and peripheral sensitisation lowers nociceptor thresholds through inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins, bradykinin and substance P. This is the state of persistent musculoskeletal and neuropathic pain that physiotherapy must modulate.

4Answer

Each physiotherapeutic agent works through one or more of these mechanisms.

  • Conventional (high-frequency) TENS - 80-120 Hz, low intensity, comfortable paraesthesia; selectively excites A-beta fibres and closes the spinal gate (segmental, fast onset, short duration).
  • Acupuncture-like (low-frequency) TENS - 2-10 Hz, high intensity, visible muscle twitch; activates A-delta fibres, the PAG and endogenous opioid release (mu and delta), giving slower onset but longer-lasting analgesia; reversed by naloxone.
  • Burst TENS - combines both mechanisms, stimulating A-beta and A-delta fibres.
  • Interferential and other currents - stimulate large fibres and reduce nociceptive transmission; the rhythmical, non-painful input closes the gate.
  • Manual therapy and mobilisation - stimulate mechanoreceptors and activate descending inhibition; part of the effect is contextual and expectation-driven.
  • Exercise and aerobic activity - produce exercise-induced hypoalgesia through endogenous opioids, endocannabinoids and descending inhibition.
  • Acupuncture/dry needling - A-delta stimulation, DNIC and endogenous opioid release.
  • Cryotherapy and thermotherapy - reduce nociceptor firing, slow conduction and reduce oedema, reducing peripheral input.

Clinical implications. Choose the mechanism that matches the pain state: segmental TENS for acute localised pain, acupuncture-like or burst TENS for chronic pain, exercise-induced hypoalgesia for widespread persistent pain. Apply electrodes over the painful segment or the related dermatome and check sensation. Reassess after each session and combine modalities with active therapy, since pain relief alone does not restore function.

5Recent advances

  • Sluka et al. (2018) — Described exercise-induced hypoalgesia and its opioid, endocannabinoid and descending-inhibition mechanisms, supporting exercise as an analgesic in its own right.
  • Hoegh & Bannister (2024) — A Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy review of the descending pain modulatory system explained how counter-stimulation techniques such as acupuncture and manual therapy, plus patient expectation and context, influence pain.
  • Johnson et al. (2022) — The meta-TENS systematic review and meta-analysis of 381 randomised trials (BMJ Open) found moderate-certainty evidence that strong non-painful TENS at the site of pain reduces pain intensity versus placebo, supporting TENS as a physiotherapy adjunct.
  • Naugle et al. (2012) — A meta-analytic review in the Journal of Pain showed that acute aerobic, isometric and dynamic-resistance exercise all reduce experimentally induced pain, with isometric exercise producing the largest hypoalgesic effect.
  • Dailey et al. (2020) — A randomised controlled trial showed that TENS reduced movement-evoked pain and fatigue in women with fibromyalgia.

6References

  2. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2018.
  3. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. St. Louis: Elsevier; 2021.
  4. Melzack R, Wall PD. Pain mechanisms: a new theory. Science. 1965;150(3699):971-979.

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Describe the concept of functional rehabilitation following total knee replacement.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Rehabilitation following joint replacement surgery.

★ Memory hook — A knee replacement buys you the joint; only functional rehabilitation teaches you how to use it.

1Introduction

Total knee replacement (TKR) relieves pain and restores alignment in advanced knee arthritis, but it only provides a pain-free, stable joint - it does not by itself restore movement, strength or the ability to walk, climb stairs and work. Functional rehabilitation is a structured, goal-directed, phase-based programme that translates the new joint into real-life activity, guided by the patient's goals.

2Physiology

The knee is a modified hinge whose function depends on the interplay of the extensor mechanism (quadriceps and patella), the hamstrings, the joint capsule and the surrounding proprioceptors. The quadriceps is the key muscle: its strength determines stair climbing, rising from a chair and normal gait. Normal knee flexion for daily living is 0-110 degrees, and full extension is essential to avoid a flexed, inefficient gait. Healing after TKR proceeds through the inflammatory, proliferative and remodelling phases, and bone ingrowth into the cement or porous surface takes weeks. Because the patient is weight-bearing early, rehabilitation must protect the implant while progressively loading the soft tissues.

3Pathophysiology

TKR creates a predictable set of impairments: post-operative pain and swelling, quadriceps weakness and arthrogenic muscle inhibition (the joint refuses to let the muscle fire fully), restricted range of motion, a risk of arthrofibrosis (excessive scar formation) if movement is not regained early, altered proprioception and gait, and reduced function. If extension is not regained quickly, the patient develops a flexed-knee gait with increased energy cost; if flexion stalls, stair and toilet transfers are difficult. Persistent weakness and kinesiophobia delay return to activity.

4Answer

Functional rehabilitation follows four overlapping phases, individualised to the patient's goals.

Phase 1 - Pre-operative (prehabilitation). Education about the procedure and expected milestones, quadriceps and range-of-motion exercises, cardiovascular conditioning and smoking cessation. Pre-operative education reduces anxiety and improves early outcomes.

Phase 2 - Acute post-operative (day 0-3). Control pain and swelling (cryotherapy 15-20 minutes several times daily, elevation, compression, adequate analgesia); ankle pumps and active-assisted knee flexion/extension; isometric quadriceps, straight-leg raise and terminal knee extension to counter arthrogenic inhibition; sit-to-stand and safe transfer practice; begin walking with a frame or crutches and full weight-bearing as allowed. Goal: safe mobilisation and 0-90 degrees of movement.

Phase 3 - Early functional (weeks 2-6). Progress strengthening (open- and closed-chain quadriceps, hamstrings, hip abductors and calf), stationary cycling, step and stair practice, balance and proprioceptive work, and gait re-education. Aim for 0-120 degrees of flexion and independent household mobility.

Phase 4 - Advanced and return to function (weeks 6-12 and beyond). Progressive resistance training, endurance work (walking, cycling, aquatics), agility and task-specific training for work, driving, gardening or sport. Outcome is judged by function, not by the implant.

Dosage. Exercise should be performed most days, with strengthening three to five times weekly, one to three sets of 8-15 repetitions, progressed by load and complexity. Supervised rehabilitation is most intense in the first six weeks and then tapered.

Outcome measures. Range of motion, quadriceps and hamstring strength, timed up-and-go (TUG), 30-second sit-to-stand, 6-minute walk test, stair test, and patient-reported measures such as the Oxford Knee Score, WOMAC, KOOS and the Hospital for Special Surgery (HSS) knee score.

5Recent advances

  • Jiao et al. (2023) — A randomised controlled trial showed that enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)-based quantitative rehabilitation training improved knee function, shortened hospital stay and improved satisfaction after TKR.
  • Tousignant et al. (2015) — A non-inferiority randomised controlled trial in the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery showed that in-home telerehabilitation was not clinically inferior to face-to-face rehabilitation after total knee arthroplasty (WOMAC), supporting remote delivery of supervised exercise.
  • Piqueras et al. (2013) — A randomised controlled trial in the Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine found that an interactive virtual telerehabilitation programme after TKR was at least as effective as conventional outpatient physiotherapy.
  • Gränicher et al. (2020) — A pilot randomised controlled trial in Archives of Physiotherapy found that preoperative physiotherapy improved the level of physical activity before and after TKA and reduced analgesic use and overall costs.

6References

  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2019.
  3. Brotzman SB, Manske RC, eds. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation: A Team Approach. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2018.
  4. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation and Intervention. 5th ed. McGraw-Hill; 2020.
