Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Describe the principles of Butler's mobilization and methods of performing the lower limb tissue tension tests.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Neural tissue mobilisation / neurodynamics.

★ Memory hook — Treat the nerve like a delicate thread through a tight sleeve: slide it, do not tug it.

1Introduction

David Butler's concept of neural mobilisation (neurodynamics) treats the nervous system as a continuous, mechanically sensitive and mobile tissue. Injury, inflammation or entrapment makes a nerve mechanosensitive, so normal movement becomes painful. Butler's approach uses graded movement to restore the nerve's ability to glide and tolerate load. The lower limb tissue tension tests identify this mechanosensitivity and guide treatment.

2Physiology

Peripheral nerves must stretch and glide relative to their bed. During limb movement a nerve both elongates (tension) and slides within its sheath (excursion); sciatic excursion during a straight-leg raise is about 10-12 mm. Nerves tolerate modest elongation of roughly 6-8% before intraneural blood flow is impaired. Neurodynamic tests load the neural and surrounding non-neural tissues, and sensitising movements add load to the nervous tissue to confirm neural involvement.

3Pathophysiology

Mechanosensitivity develops when a nerve is compressed, stretched, inflamed or its surrounding tissue is injured; inflammatory mediators sensitise the nerve and dorsal root, so tension provokes pain. Common situations are lumbar radiculopathy, piriformis-related sciatica, tarsal tunnel syndrome and post-operative or scar-related restriction. In these states the neurodynamic test reproduces the patient's symptoms, the involved side differs from the uninvolved side, and structural differentiation (adding or removing a distal or proximal movement) changes the response.

4Answer

Principles of Butler's mobilisation.

  • The nervous system is treated as a continuum; the site of symptoms is not always the site of the problem.
  • Techniques are graded from least to most provocative, and are always within the patient's tolerance.
  • Sliders move the nerve in one direction while the opposite end moves away, producing excursion with little increase in tension - used when the nerve is very sensitive.
  • Tensioners move both ends apart, increasing neural tension - used later to build tolerance.
  • Slow, rhythmic, oscillatory movement is preferred; avoid prolonged end-range stretch.
  • Assess before and after every session (symptom response and test range) and progress load gradually.
  • Combine with education and active movement; avoid aggravating positions such as prolonged sitting or slump.

Lower limb tissue tension (neurodynamic) tests.

TestNerve / structureHow performed
Straight leg raise (Lasègue)Sciatic nerve, L4-S3 rootsSupine; passively raise the straight leg with the knee extended; positive if symptoms reproduce between 30 and 70 degrees.
Slump testMeninges, spinal cord, sciatic nerveSitting; thoracic and lumbar flexion, then cervical flexion, knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion; symptoms relieved by cervical extension confirm neural involvement.
Bragard / sensitised SLRSciatic nerveLower the leg slightly from the painful SLR angle then add ankle dorsiflexion; reproduction confirms neural tension.
Bowstring testTibial and common peroneal nervesAt the SLR limit, flex the knee slightly and press in the popliteal fossa over the nerve.
Femoral nerve stretch (prone knee bend)Femoral nerve, L2-L4Prone; passively flex the knee, then extend the hip; anterior thigh symptoms reproduce.
Slump with knee extension / tibial nerve testTibial nerveSlump position plus ankle dorsiflexion and eversion to load the tibial nerve.

Record the range at which symptoms appear, whether they are the patient's familiar symptoms, and whether sensitising movements change them. Repeat the same test after treatment to measure the response.

5Recent advances

  • Basson et al. (2017) — A systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy found that neural mobilisation (slump and straight-leg-raise mobilisation) significantly reduced pain and disability in people with neurogenic low back pain.
  • Neto et al. (2017) — A systematic review of lower-body-quadrant neural mobilisation confirmed reductions in pain and disability in low back pain and improved flexibility in healthy adults.
  • Cuenca-Martínez et al. (2022) — An umbrella review with meta-meta-analysis in Physical Therapy found moderate-to-large effects of neural mobilisation on pain and disability in musculoskeletal disorders and on mechanosensitivity in asymptomatic people.
  • Pellicciari et al. (2019) — A study of contralateral limb mobilisation in the slump position (Acta Biomedica) showed increased ipsilateral knee-extension range, supporting the neurodynamic principle of treating the opposite limb.

6References

  2. Shacklock M. Clinical Neurodynamics: A New System of Musculoskeletal Treatment. Edinburgh: Elsevier; 2005.
  3. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. Elsevier; 2021.
  4. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2018.

Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Describe the role of cognitive behavioral therapy for a subject with neck pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Biopsychosocial management of neck pain.

★ Memory hook — Neck pain lives in the tissues, but it grows in the thoughts - CBT treats the thoughts.

1Introduction

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is a structured, goal-oriented psychological approach that targets the thoughts, beliefs and behaviours that maintain pain and disability. In neck pain - especially chronic, non-specific and whiplash-associated neck pain - fear of movement (kinesiophobia), catastrophising and passive coping drive avoidance, deconditioning and persistence of pain. CBT is therefore not an alternative to physical therapy but a partner to it, helping the patient re-engage with activity.

2Physiology

Pain is not a simple reflection of tissue damage; it is produced by the brain in a biopsychosocial context. Descending modulation from the brainstem can either inhibit or facilitate nociception, and psychological state influences this balance. Stress and anxiety increase sympathetic activity and muscle guarding, and negative beliefs about pain amplify the perceived threat, sensitising the system. Normal cervical function depends on mobility, deep flexor and extensor endurance, and proprioceptive control, all of which deteriorate with inactivity driven by fear.

3Pathophysiology

In chronic neck pain, central sensitisation and impaired descending inhibition make the pain system hypersensitive. Kinesiophobia leads to avoidance of movement and work, which causes muscle weakness, reduced endurance and further disability. Catastrophising (ruminating on the worst outcome) and low self-efficacy predict poor recovery, and in whiplash-associated disorders these psychological factors are among the strongest predictors of chronicity. The goal of CBT is to break this fear-avoidance cycle.

4Answer

Role and components of CBT in neck pain.

  • Education and reconceptualisation - explain the biopsychosocial model and pain neuroscience so the patient understands that hurt does not always equal harm.
  • Cognitive restructuring - identify and challenge unhelpful thoughts ('my neck is fragile', 'movement will damage me') and replace them with realistic beliefs.
  • Graded exposure and graded activity - gradually reintroduce feared movements, postures and tasks, setting a baseline and progressing by time and load rather than by pain.
  • Relaxation and coping skills - diaphragmatic breathing, progressive muscle relaxation and pacing to reduce muscle guarding and stress.
  • Goal setting and self-management - collaborative, meaningful goals and problem-solving to build self-efficacy.
  • Behavioural activation - reducing pain behaviour and increasing healthy, functional behaviour.

Delivery and dosage. CBT is usually delivered in 6-12 individual or group sessions of 45-60 minutes, weekly or twice weekly, either by a psychologist or by a physiotherapist trained in psychologically informed practice. It is most effective when integrated with exercise and manual therapy in a multimodal programme, and when it addresses work-related and ergonomic factors.

Outcome measures. Neck Disability Index (NDI), Numerical Pain Rating Scale, Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia (TSK), Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS), Pain Anxiety Symptoms Scale, and measures of quality of life and work ability.

Clinical message. CBT is most valuable in chronic or whiplash-associated neck pain with high fear, catastrophising or distress. It reduces kinesiophobia, anxiety and depression and improves function; its effect on pain intensity itself is modest, so it should always be combined with active physical rehabilitation.

5Recent advances

  • Javdaneh et al. (2020) — A randomised controlled trial showed that scapular exercise combined with cognitive functional therapy was superior to scapular exercise alone for reducing chronic neck pain and kinesiophobia.
  • Monticone et al. (2022) — Designed a randomised controlled trial of a multidisciplinary programme combining task-oriented exercise with CBT for working patients with chronic neck pain, with one-year follow-up.
  • Monticone et al. (2015) — A Cochrane review of cognitive-behavioural treatment for subacute and chronic neck pain found low-quality evidence of benefit, mainly for kinesiophobia and psychological outcomes when CBT was combined with other treatment.
  • Ploutarchou et al. (2023) — A systematic review with meta-analysis in Cognitive Behaviour Therapy found low-certainty evidence of short-term pain reduction with CBT and clinically significant improvements in kinesiophobia, anxiety and depression when CBT formed part of a multimodal programme.
  • Ragab et al. (2019) — A randomised study adding CBT to physical therapy for chronic cervical radiculopathy reported greater improvement in pain anxiety, neck disability and range of motion than physical therapy alone.

6References

  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2019.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Write in detail about extra corporeal shock wave therapy used for tissue healing.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Electrotherapy / therapeutic modalities for tissue healing.

★ Memory hook — Shock waves are controlled micro-trauma: they wake a sleeping tendon and make it heal itself.

1Introduction

Extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT) delivers high-energy acoustic (pressure) waves to a tissue from outside the body. Originally used to break kidney stones (lithotripsy), it is now an established non-invasive modality for chronic tendinopathies and other musculoskeletal conditions that have failed standard care. Its value lies in stimulating the body's own repair processes rather than simply masking pain.

2Physiology

Tendon healing passes through an inflammatory phase (days), a proliferative phase (weeks, with tenocyte proliferation and type III collagen) and a remodelling phase (months, with maturation to type I collagen and realignment). ESWT is applied at an energy flux density measured in millijoules per square millimetre (mJ/mm2). Low-energy ESWT stimulates healing, whereas excessive energy can itself cause structural injury, so dose matters. The acoustic wave creates mechanical stress at tissue interfaces and triggers a biological cascade.

3Pathophysiology

In chronic tendinopathy the tendon is degenerative rather than simply inflamed: disorganised collagen, increased matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and cytokines, neovessels with accompanying nerve ingrowth and failed healing. ESWT disrupts this failed cycle through mechanotransduction - converting mechanical energy into a cellular response - and by inducing controlled micro-trauma that restarts healing.

4Answer

Mechanisms of action.

  • Mechanotransduction - the pressure wave is converted into biochemical signals in tenocytes and other cells.
  • Neovascularisation - release of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and other growth factors promotes new capillary formation and improves blood supply.
  • Tenocyte stimulation - increased tenocyte proliferation, upregulation of proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), transforming growth factor beta-1 (TGF-beta1) and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), and accelerated collagen synthesis and maturation.
  • Matrix and cytokine modulation - reduced MMP-1, MMP-13 and IL-6, contributing to metabolic normalisation.
  • Disruption of calcification - breaks down calcium deposits in calcific tendinitis.
  • Analgesia - altered nociceptor input and central mechanisms reduce pain.

Types. Focused ESWT (f-ESWT) concentrates energy at a defined focal point; radial ESWT (r-ESWT) spreads a lower-energy pressure wave over a larger area and is simpler and cheaper. Evidence does not clearly favour one over the other for most tendinopathies.

Dosage parameters. Energy flux density typically 0.1-0.3 mJ/mm2 for low-energy and up to about 0.5 mJ/mm2 for high-energy treatment; 1,500-3,000 pulses per session; frequency around 4-15 Hz; three to five sessions at weekly intervals. Parameters are set according to the tendon, the tissue depth and patient tolerance.

Indications. Chronic plantar fasciitis, calcific and non-calcific rotator cuff tendinopathy, lateral epicondylalgia, Achilles and patellar tendinopathy, and delayed fracture or tendon-bone healing. Contraindications and precautions include application over malignancy, infection, open wounds, over the lung or major nerves and vessels, coagulopathy, pregnancy, and in children over growth plates. Transient skin reddening, bruising and discomfort are common and usually minor.

Clinical use. ESWT is usually an adjunct to loading exercise, not a stand-alone cure. Best results occur when it is combined with progressive eccentric and concentric exercise and load management. The evidence is strongest for plantar fasciitis and mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy and weaker for insertional Achilles tendinopathy.

5Recent advances

  • Paantjens et al. (2022) — A systematic review in Sports Medicine - Open found that adding ESWT to a tendon-loading programme produced clinically important improvement in mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, but could not support its use for insertional Achilles tendinopathy.
  • Charles et al. (2023) — A systematic review and meta-analysis in Frontiers in Immunology found high-quality evidence of a large effect for plantar fasciitis, but only low-to-moderate evidence with small effects for patellar and Achilles tendinopathy.
  • Majidi et al. (2024) — A systematic review and meta-analysis in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation of 45 trials found that ESWT significantly reduced pain across tendinopathies, with the largest effects for plantar fasciitis and rotator cuff tendinopathy.

6References

  2. Prentice WE. Therapeutic Modalities in Rehabilitation. 5th ed. McGraw-Hill; 2017.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2018.

  5. Biological effects of extracorporeal shockwave therapy in tendons: a systematic review. 2022.
  6. The effectiveness of shockwave therapy on patellar tendinopathy, Achilles tendinopathy and plantar fasciitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Immunol. 2023;14:1193835.
  7. External stimulation: a potential therapeutic strategy for tendon-bone healing. Front Bioeng Biotechnol. 2023;11:1150290.
Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Describe work related musculoskeletal disorders seen in rock drillers.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Occupational health and work-related musculoskeletal disorders.

★ Memory hook — The drill shakes the hand, the hand shakes the nerve, and the nerve shakes the whole arm.

1Introduction

Rock drillers use heavy, hand-held percussive and rotary tools that expose them to intense hand-arm vibration, repetitive gripping, awkward postures, whole-body vibration and heavy manual handling. The resulting work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) are a well-recognised occupational problem, dominated by hand-arm vibration syndrome (HAVS) but also including disorders of the shoulder, elbow, wrist and spine. These are dose-related and largely preventable.

2Physiology

Hand-transmitted vibration is measured as the frequency-weighted, eight-hour energy-equivalent acceleration (A(8)) and governed by the ISO 5349 standard. Vibration at the frequencies generated by percussive drills (largely 20-500 Hz) is absorbed mainly by the fingers and hand but lower-frequency components travel to the arm, shoulder and neck. Repeated gripping and vibration cause vascular, neurological and musculoskeletal changes. Sustained static grip, awkward wrist and shoulder positions and whole-body vibration during drilling add further load.

3Pathophysiology

HAVS has three components. The vascular component is vibration-induced white finger: episodic blanching of the fingers after cold exposure, caused by vasospasm of the digital arteries and arterioles. The sensorineural component is vibration-induced neuropathy, with numbness, tingling, reduced tactile and thermal sensation and impaired dexterity. The musculoskeletal component includes reduced grip strength, carpal tunnel syndrome, tenosynovitis, epicondylalgia, shoulder tendinopathy and degenerative joint changes, and vibration exposure is associated with cysts and osteoarthritis. The condition is dose-dependent: prevalence and severity rise with years of exposure, and a classic study of rock drillers found vibration white finger in about half, with a median latent period of roughly seven to eight years and blanching in up to 80% of those exposed for sixteen years or more. Whole-body vibration and awkward postures contribute to low back and neck pain.

4Answer

Recognising the disorders. Stage HAVS using the Stockholm workshop scales for the vascular (white finger) and sensorineural components, and record the history of exposure, latency and cold provocation. Measure grip strength, and test sensation (vibration and thermal thresholds). Screen for carpal tunnel syndrome, lateral epicondylalgia, shoulder impingement and spinal pain.

Prevention and exposure control (first-line).

  • Reduce vibration at source: choose low-vibration tools, maintain and service equipment, and use the correct tool for the task.
  • Limit exposure time and rotate workers so that daily A(8) stays within ISO 5349 limits; avoid piecework that drives over-exposure.
  • Use anti-vibration gloves and supports, and warm, dry gloves to reduce vasospasm.
  • Keep hands warm, avoid smoking (which worsens vasoconstriction) and avoid cold after exposure.
  • Health surveillance with regular examination so that early signs are detected and the worker is redeployed before permanent damage.

Physiotherapy management.

  • Advise on stopping or reducing exposure and on self-monitoring of white-finger attacks.
  • Graded strengthening and endurance training of the forearm and shoulder muscles; tendon gliding and nerve mobilisation for the upper limb.
  • Desensitisation and sensory re-education for the sensorineural component.
  • Ergonomic advice on grip technique, wrist posture, rest breaks and tool handling; work-station and task redesign.
  • Treat secondary conditions - carpal tunnel, epicondylalgia, shoulder tendinopathy and spinal pain - with the appropriate modality and exercise.
  • Educate on the importance of early reporting, since once the vascular damage is established it is largely irreversible.

Outcome measures. Stockholm staging, grip strength, monofilament and vibration thresholds, symptom diaries and work-ability measures.

5Recent advances

  • Tanveer et al. (2025) — A cross-sectional study in the Journal of Hand Therapy reported a high prevalence of hand-arm vibration syndrome in mine workers at the Khewra salt mines, with hand discolouration, tingling and loss of grip strength among the most common symptoms.
  • Bovenzi et al. (1994) — Studies of quarry drillers and stone workers showed a dose-response relation for vibration-induced white finger, with prevalence rising with the lifetime vibration dose.
  • Marufa et al. (2023) — A pre-experimental study in the Physical Therapy Journal of Indonesia found that neurodynamic (neural) mobilisation significantly reduced sensorineural symptoms on the Stockholm Workshop Scale in workers with HAVS, supporting manual therapy in physiotherapy management.
  • Tekavec et al. (2023) — A clinical study in Occupational and Environmental Medicine found that the International Consensus Criteria regrade HAVS severity lower than the Stockholm Workshop Scale and stressed assessing small and large nerve fibres and cold intolerance, refining physiotherapy assessment.

6References

  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. Elsevier; 2021.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2019.

Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Write in detail about the work conditioning program for mason following a rotator cuff injury.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Work conditioning / vocational rehabilitation.

★ Memory hook — Do not just treat the shoulder - rebuild the mason, task by task.

1Introduction

A mason performs heavy overhead and repetitive work: laying bricks above shoulder height, carrying blocks, mixing and lifting mortar and gripping trowels. After a rotator cuff injury these demands exceed the shoulder's capacity, so a clinic-based programme alone is not enough. Work conditioning is a structured, work-oriented, progressive programme that rebuilds the strength, endurance and task tolerance needed for the mason's job and returns the worker safely to duty.

2Physiology

The rotator cuff - supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis and teres minor - centres the humeral head and provides dynamic stability, while the deltoid produces the lifting force. Overhead work loads the cuff and subacromial space, and repeated lifting needs both strength and endurance. Tendon healing passes through inflammatory, proliferative and remodelling phases, tolerating increasing load over time. Cardiovascular fitness and general work capacity also determine how many hours a mason can sustain.

3Pathophysiology

Rotator cuff injury ranges from tendinopathy and partial tears to full-thickness tears, producing pain, weakness (especially with elevation and external rotation), night pain and functional loss. In a mason this means difficulty lifting a brick, working overhead and sustaining a full shift; deconditioning and fear of movement add to the disability. Unmanaged, weakness and poor scapular control perpetuate subacromial irritation and prevent return to work.

4Answer

Assessment and job demands analysis first. Measure pain (NPRS), range of motion, cuff and scapular strength, and function (DASH, SPADI, Constant score). Perform a functional capacity evaluation (FCE) and a job-demand analysis of the mason's tasks - weights lifted, heights worked, repetition, duration and postures - to set objective return-to-work targets.

Programme structure. Work conditioning is usually delivered three to five days per week, two to four hours per day, for four to eight weeks, combining physical conditioning with simulated work tasks.

  • Pain and symptom control - relative rest, activity modification, appropriate modalities and education, without prolonged immobilisation.
  • Mobility - restore glenohumeral and scapulothoracic range, then thoracic mobility.
  • Strengthening - progressive cuff and scapular strengthening, then larger pushing, pulling and overhead patterns; begin with isometrics, progress to bands, then free weights, one to three sets of 8-15 repetitions, three to five times weekly.
  • Endurance and cardiovascular conditioning - arm ergometry, circuit training and general aerobic work to build shift tolerance.
  • Work simulation / job-specific training - graded lifting (brick boxes or weighted crates from floor to waist, then chest, then overhead), carrying, reaching, trowel use, and sustained overhead work; increase weight, repetitions and duration gradually.
  • Ergonomics and education - correct lifting mechanics, keeping loads close, using scaffolds and hoists, pacing, and the value of graded activity.
  • Psychosocial support - address fear-avoidance, catastrophising and work confidence, with CBT or psychologically informed practice where needed.

Progression and return-to-work criteria. Progress by time before load, and by load before speed. Return to work when strength is at least about 80% of the uninvolved side, pain is controlled, the worker can complete the simulated task at the required weight and duration, and cardiovascular fitness is adequate. Use modified duties or a graded return (partial hours, no overhead work) as a bridge.

Outcome measures. DASH/QuickDASH, SPADI, grip and shoulder strength, FCE task performance, pain scores, and work-ability or lost-time measures.

5Recent advances

  • Cullen et al. (2017) — A systematic review in the Journal of Occupational Rehabilitation found strong evidence that multi-domain return-to-work interventions (combining health care, service coordination and work modification) reduce lost time for musculoskeletal conditions.
  • Cheng & Hung (2007) — A randomised controlled trial found that workplace-based work hardening returned 71% of workers with work-related rotator cuff disorder to work versus 37% for clinic-based work hardening, and lowered self-reported shoulder problems.
  • Dyer et al. (2022) — A clinical practice guideline in the Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy recommended an active, task-oriented rehabilitation programme plus early, multi-stakeholder return-to-work planning for adults with rotator cuff disorders.
  • Schaafsma et al. (2013) — A Cochrane review of physical conditioning as part of a return-to-work strategy found that workplace-based or workplace-visited programmes may reduce sickness absence, especially in chronic back pain.
  • Skamagki et al. (2026) — A systematic review in BMJ Open of workplace interventions for chronic musculoskeletal disorders found that multicomponent programmes combining exercise, ergonomics and education gave the most consistent benefits.

6References

  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2019.

Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Describe the management and rehabilitation following total Patellectomy.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Rehabilitation following knee surgery / extensor mechanism.

★ Memory hook — No patella, no lever - so you must rebuild the brake and the spring with muscle.

1Introduction

Total patellectomy is the complete removal of the patella, now performed only as a last resort for severe patellofemoral destruction, comminuted fracture, infection or tumour. It is radical because the patella is the fulcrum of the extensor mechanism. Management is therefore both surgical (reconstruction) and rehabilitative, aiming to restore extension, strength and function despite the lost lever.

2Physiology

The patella increases the moment arm of the quadriceps, centralises the extensor mechanism and protects the front of the knee. Removing it reduces the quadriceps lever arm by roughly a third and lowers extensor efficiency, so more quadriceps force is needed for the same task. Normal knee function depends on the quadriceps (extension, shock absorption, stair and sit-to-stand control) and the hamstrings (flexion and dynamic stability). Healing after patellectomy involves repair of the reconstructed extensor mechanism, and the surrounding muscles must compensate for the lost patella.

3Pathophysiology

Loss of the patella produces a characteristic set of problems: reduced extensor moment arm and quadriceps strength (reported losses of 45-60% in some series), extensor lag or difficulty achieving full extension against gravity, reduced range of motion (active flexion often around 110 degrees), anterior knee pain, instability, altered gait (with compensatory early soleus activity) and reduced function. Weakness of the hamstrings correlates with poorer outcomes, and loss of quadriceps function of more than about 40% is associated with functional impairment.

4Answer

Post-operative rehabilitation is phase-based and must protect the reconstructed extensor mechanism while rebuilding strength.

Phase 1 - Protection and early motion (weeks 0-2). Immobilise or brace as the surgeon directs; control swelling with cryotherapy, elevation and compression; isometric quadriceps and hamstring setting; ankle pumps; passive and active-assisted knee flexion within safe limits; and protected weight-bearing. Goal: protect the repair, control pain and swelling, and begin muscle activation.

Phase 2 - Early strengthening (weeks 2-6). Progress active-assisted to active range of motion; straight-leg raises; terminal knee extension; closed-chain work such as mini-squats and step-ups as tolerated; patellar-mobilisation equivalent is not applicable, but soft-tissue and scar mobilisation around the knee is important. Begin gait re-education.

Phase 3 - Progressive strengthening and function (weeks 6-12). Progressive resistance training for quadriceps and, importantly, the hamstrings; eccentric quadriceps work; proprioceptive and balance training; stationary cycling; stair practice. Aim for full functional range and good eccentric control.

Phase 4 - Advanced and return to activity (3-6 months and beyond). Sport- or job-specific training, plyometrics as appropriate, and endurance work. Quadriceps and hamstring strengthening continues for many months.

Key principles.

  • Strengthen the hamstrings as well as the quadriceps - hamstring function is a strong predictor of a good outcome.
  • Train eccentric control and full knee extension against gravity.
  • Restore a normal gait pattern to reduce energy cost and compensations.
  • Reinforce the extensor mechanism, where the surgeon has reconstructed it, before aggressive loading.

Outcome measures. Range of motion, isokinetic quadriceps and hamstring strength, extensor lag, gait analysis, the Lower Extremity Functional Scale (LEFS), Knee Society Score and functional tests (sit-to-stand, stairs, 6-minute walk).

5Recent advances

  • Tozzi et al. (2026) — A case report of physical rehabilitation after total patellectomy described recovery to 110 degrees of active flexion, quadriceps strength of about 57% of the other side, independent gait and large gains on the Lower Extremity Functional Scale.
  • Kuster & Blatter (1996) — An isokinetic study in Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy showed that loss of quadriceps function greater than 40% after patellectomy correlates with proportional hamstring loss and a poorer functional result, so peak flexion torque can guide rehabilitation targets.
  • Watkins et al. (1983) — A classic isokinetic study in the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery quantified the quadriceps and hamstring strength deficits after patellectomy, establishing the muscle-function losses that physiotherapy must target.

6References

  1. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2018.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2019.
  3. Brotzman SB, Manske RC, eds. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation: A Team Approach. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2018.
  4. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation and Intervention. 5th ed. McGraw-Hill; 2020.
  5. Cavaignac E, Pailhe R, Reina N, et al. Total patellectomy in knees without prior arthroplasty: a systematic review. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2014;22(12):3083-3092.

Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Write in detail about management of complex regional pain syndrome following Colles fracture.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Management of persistent pain / neuropathic pain syndromes.

★ Memory hook — After a wrist fracture, keep the hand moving and the brain connected - or CRPS moves in.

1Introduction

Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is a disproportionate, persistent pain condition that can follow a Colles fracture of the distal radius. Type 1 (previously reflex sympathetic dystrophy) occurs without nerve injury; type 2 has evidence of nerve injury. CRPS combines pain, sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/oedema, motor and trophic changes and is a clinical diagnosis. Because the hand becomes painful, stiff and neglected, early recognition and movement-based rehabilitation are the keys to a good outcome.

2Physiology

After a distal radius fracture the hand depends on early movement to maintain oedema control, joint mobility, tendon gliding and sensory input; normal recovery involves controlled inflammation, callus formation and remodelling. Nociceptive input from the fracture and immobilisation, and reduced sensory and motor activity, set the scene in which central and peripheral sensitisation can develop.

3Pathophysiology

CRPS is now understood as a disorder of the central nervous system as much as the periphery. Mechanisms include peripheral and central sensitisation, inflammatory mediator release, autonomic dysfunction (abnormal vasomotor and sudomotor control), cortical reorganisation with a disrupted 'body map' of the hand, and disuse. The result is spontaneous and evoked pain, hyperalgesia and allodynia, oedema, temperature and colour change, sweating changes, trophic changes (skin, hair, nail) and motor signs (weakness, tremor, dystonia). Immobilisation, neglect of the limb and pain-related fear perpetuate the cycle. Diagnosis uses the Budapest criteria: continuing pain disproportionate to the event, with at least one symptom in three of four categories and one sign in two, with no better explanation.

4Answer

Principles. Start early, explain the condition clearly, keep the limb moving, and treat the whole person. Physiotherapy is the mainstay alongside medical and psychological management.

Pain neuroscience education - help the patient understand that the pain is real but is produced by an over-protective nervous system, reducing fear and encouraging movement.

Graded motor imagery (GMI) - a three-stage sequence in the classic order: (1) left/right limb laterality recognition, (2) imagined movements, (3) mirror therapy; this targets cortical reorganisation.

Mirror therapy - the patient watches the reflection of the moving unaffected hand, giving visual feedback of normal movement.

Desensitisation and sensory re-education - graded exposure to textures, vibration and touch to reduce allodynia, plus tactile discrimination training.

Oedema control - elevation, compression, retrograde massage and active movement.

Movement and function - gentle active and active-assisted range of motion of the wrist and hand, tendon gliding, and graded functional activity, avoiding prolonged immobilisation. Add aerobic exercise, which has an analgesic effect and is used as pain-exposure therapy.

Modalities - TENS for pain modulation. Avoid aggressive passive stretching and painful modalities.

Psychological support - CBT for fear, catastrophising and depression.

Medical and interventional - analgesia, gabapentinoids or tricyclics, bisphosphonates, and sympathetic blocks or spinal cord stimulation in refractory cases. Vitamin C is used prophylactically after wrist fracture.

Dosage and progression. GMI is performed twice daily in short sessions, progressing over weeks; desensitisation is graded from least to most provocative, guided by tolerance rather than pain alone.

Outcome measures. Pain intensity (NPRS), the Budapest criteria checklist, hand oedema, wrist and hand range of motion, grip strength, the Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) score, and quality of life.

5Recent advances

  • Shafiee et al. (2023) — A systematic review and meta-analysis of rehabilitation for CRPS found low-quality evidence that graded motor imagery and mirror therapy may produce large improvements in pain and disability, and that pain-exposure therapy and aerobic exercise added to physical therapy may reduce pain.
  • Smart et al. (2022) — A Cochrane review of physiotherapy for pain and disability in CRPS types I and II found only low-certainty evidence, highlighting the need for higher-quality trials of multimodal, movement-based physiotherapy.
  • Donati et al. (2024) — A systematic review in Biomedicines reported that graded motor imagery and mirror therapy reduced pain (on average about 20 points on the Neuropathic Pain Scale) and improved function in CRPS.
  • Griffiths et al. (2023) — An integrative review of person-centred upper limb CRPS (Hand Therapy) concluded that movement, desensitisation and graded functional activity remain the mainstays, with psychological and functional outcomes under-addressed.
  • Harden et al. (2022) — The fifth edition of the CRPS practical diagnostic and treatment guidelines (Pain Medicine) set out contemporary multidisciplinary management.

6References

  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2019.

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Discuss the interventions to improve muscle performance following flexor tendon repair of the hand.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Hand and Tendon Rehabilitation

★ Memory hook — Repair the tendon, then make it glide before you make it strong.

1Introduction

Flexor tendon injuries of the hand, especially in zone II (Bunnell's "no man's land"), are among the most demanding problems in hand rehabilitation. Surgery restores continuity, but the final result depends on rehabilitation that restores tendon glide, prevents adhesion and rupture, and rebuilds muscle performance — that is, strength, endurance and coordinated grip. Muscle performance after repair is therefore the product of controlled early motion, graded loading and functional retraining, not of immobilisation.

2Physiology

Tendon healing passes through three overlapping phases: an inflammatory phase (0–7 days), a fibroblastic or proliferative phase (5–21 days) and a remodelling phase (beyond 21 days). The repaired tendon is nourished both intrinsically (synovial fluid diffusion through the vincula and sheath) and extrinsically (from the surrounding tissues). Controlled tension and motion align collagen fibres along lines of stress, raise tensile strength and discourage adhesions, whereas prolonged immobilisation allows adhesions to mature and muscle to waste. Flexor muscles are also highly sensitive to disuse: within weeks of immobilisation there is measurable loss of cross-sectional area, strength and endurance, so mobilisation is simultaneously a tendon and a muscle intervention.

3Pathophysiology

When motion is inadequate or excessive, complications appear. Adhesions between tendon and sheath cause loss of glide and flexion contractures; excessive load causes gap formation or rupture, which is most likely in the first 7–10 days when repair strength is lowest; and immobilisation produces muscle atrophy, joint stiffness and a weak, poorly coordinated grip. Zone II repairs are the most vulnerable because both flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus lie within a tight fibro-osseous tunnel.

4Answer

Interventions are organised into four overlapping phases. The therapist works with the surgeon, since the allowed load depends on the number of core suture strands (typically four to six for early active motion).

Phase 1 (0–3/4 weeks) — protection and glide. A dorsal blocking orthosis holds the wrist in 20–30° extension, MCP joints in 50–70° flexion and IP joints in extension. Oedema is controlled with elevation and compression. The classic programme (modified Duran) uses passive finger flexion with active finger extension; the Kleinert programme uses a dynamic traction splint. Place-and-hold (active hold in the passively flexed position) and tenodesis (wrist extension with finger relaxation, wrist flexion with finger flexion) encourage glide. Exercise is performed 10 repetitions every hour, in 4–6 sessions daily.

Phase 2 (3–6 weeks) — early active motion. Active finger flexion is begun through a partial range (the first third to two-thirds), because the tendon is smoothest and bending forces are lowest in mid-range. Tang's passive-active protocol recommends at least 40, ideally 60–80, cycles of active flexion per session — roughly 200–300 cycles daily — before progressing to full range by weeks 4–6. The orthosis is weaned.

Phase 3 (6–12 weeks) — strength and differential glide. Full active range is regained, and gentle resistance, blocking exercises to isolate FDS and FDP, tendon-gliding exercises and grip strengthening are added. Resistance begins at 3 sets × 10 repetitions and progresses weekly.

Phase 4 (beyond 12 weeks) — work conditioning. Progressive resistance training, endurance work, power and pinch grip and job-specific tasks restore muscle performance for daily living and occupation.

ImmobilisationNoneMinimalUnreliable repair/patient

Place-and-holdActive hold in flexed positionModerate2–6 strand repairs

Outcome measures: total active motion (TAM) and the Strickland formula, grip and pinch strength (Jamar dynamometer), and the DASH questionnaire track muscle and hand performance.

5Recent advances

  • Mortada et al. (2024) — systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 studies (1414 patients) showing early active motion gives greater range of motion than passive protocols after zone II repair, with comparable re-operation rates, so strongly repaired tendons can be mobilised actively.
  • Starr et al. (2013) — systematic review of 34 studies found early passive protocols had a lower rupture rate but greater loss of digital motion, while early active protocols gave better motion, supporting active mobilisation as suture technique and repair strength improved.
  • Tang (2021) — the Nantong partial-range active flexion protocol glides the repaired tendon through only the initial one-third to two-thirds of flexion, where bending forces are lowest, protecting the repair while preventing adhesions.
  • Peck et al. (2014) — the Manchester short splint permits earlier wrist motion than the traditional forearm-based splint, reducing PIP flexion contracture and improving the digital flexion arc without increasing rupture.
  • Groth (2004) — the "Pyramid of Progressive Force Application" grades eight exercises from lowest to highest tendon load and guides progression by tissue response rather than by time alone.

Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Explain the educational and behavioural strategies in managing osteoarthritis of knee pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Osteoarthritis — Education and Behaviour

★ Memory hook — OA is not wear-and-tear; it is load-and-learn.

1Introduction

Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a whole-joint, biopsychosocial condition, not simply a worn-out cartilage surface. Education and behavioural strategies are now recognised as core treatments, alongside exercise, because pain and disability in OA are shaped as much by beliefs, fear, coping and self-management as by the joint itself. The physiotherapist's task is to change how the patient understands and lives with OA, not only to strengthen the quadriceps.

2Physiology

Normal cartilage is avascular and nourished by synovial fluid through cyclic loading and unloading. Regular, moderate joint movement improves cartilage nutrition, strengthens periarticular muscle, improves proprioception and maintains joint range. Mild inflammation is part of normal tissue repair. These facts matter because they underpin the message that sensible activity protects rather than harms the knee.

3Pathophysiology

In OA, cartilage fibrillation, subchondral bone remodelling and synovitis produce nociceptive input. Persistent pain leads to central sensitisation, pain catastrophising, kinesiophobia and fear-avoidance, which reduce activity, decondition the quadriceps and worsen disability — a self-reinforcing cycle. The therapist therefore treats the maladaptive beliefs and behaviours, not just the joint.

4Answer

Educational and behavioural strategies work best when combined with exercise and delivered over several sessions.

Education. Pain neuroscience education explains that pain is a protective output of the nervous system rather than a direct readout of damage; that OA is not a fixed "wear-and-tear" process; and that graded activity is safe. Arthritis education is a core treatment in the OARSI 2019 guidelines. Simple, reassuring explanations, written material and clear prognosis reduce fear and improve adherence.

Self-management programmes. Structured programmes such as the Arthritis Self-Management Programme teach patients to monitor symptoms, pace activity, use heat or cold, manage flare-ups and solve problems. OARSI 2019 conditionally recommends self-management programmes across all comorbidity subgroups.

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). CBT targets unhelpful thoughts and behaviours through cognitive restructuring, activity pacing, graded activity, relaxation and coping-skills training. OARSI 2019 recommends CBT with an exercise component, particularly for patients with widespread pain or depression.

Behaviour-change techniques. Goal setting (specific, measurable, achievable), motivational interviewing, self-monitoring with activity diaries or apps, feedback, prompts and relapse-prevention planning all increase exercise adherence. Shared decision-making and a therapeutic alliance improve outcomes.

Weight and lifestyle. Dietary weight management combined with exercise is a core treatment for knee OA; even modest weight loss reduces knee load and pain. Aquatic exercise, Tai Chi and yoga are safe adjuncts.

DomainStrategyTarget
EducationalPain neuroscience education, arthritis educationBeliefs, understanding
BehaviouralCBT, pacing, graded activity, self-monitoringCoping, adherence
Self-managementStructured programmes, flare-up plansIndependence
LifestyleWeight management, mind–body exerciseJoint load, general health

Outcome measures: WOMAC or KOOS, numeric pain rating, the Pain Catastrophising Scale, Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia and measures of adherence and self-efficacy.

5Recent advances

  • OARSI (2019) guideline — makes arthritis education and structured land-based exercise core treatments for knee OA, with CBT and self-management programmes conditionally recommended across comorbidity groups.
  • NICE (2022) guideline — the NG226 guideline recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to the person, combined with an education or behaviour-change package as core care for osteoarthritis, and reassures patients that exercise-related pain does not mean joint harm.
  • Nelligan et al. (2021) — a randomised trial of 206 people found a self-directed web-based strengthening programme supported by automated behaviour-change text messages improved knee pain and function at 24 weeks compared with information alone.
  • Supe et al. (2023) — a randomised trial showed pain neuroscience education added to exercise via telerehabilitation reduced pain catastrophising and pain intensity in knee OA, supporting education as an active treatment.
  • Hurley et al. (2007) — structured self-management programmes retain benefit on pain and quality of life in knee OA and are now embedded in stepped-care pathways.

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. How do you apply the functional concepts in rehabilitation of adhesive capsulitis of shoulder.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Shoulder Rehabilitation

★ Memory hook — Freezing means calm it, frozen means stretch it, thawing means use it.

1Introduction

Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is a painful, progressive loss of glenohumeral movement caused by capsular fibrosis and contracture, usually in three overlapping phases — freezing (painful), frozen (stiff) and thawing (recovering). Because the disability is functional (dressing, reaching, sleeping), rehabilitation must be stage-matched and functionally oriented, not simply a set of passive stretches.

2Physiology

The glenohumeral joint is a mobile ball-and-socket whose stability depends on the capsule, the coracohumeral ligament and the rotator interval. Normal movement requires arthrokinematics (roll and glide) and a scapulohumeral rhythm of roughly two degrees of humeral to one degree of scapular motion. Capsular extensibility is maintained by regular end-range movement; when this is lost, connective tissue shortens and the muscle and capsular mechanoreceptors alter their input.

3Pathophysiology

In frozen shoulder, fibroblastic proliferation and myofibroblast activity, driven by cytokines such as TGF-beta and PDGF, thicken and contract the capsule, reducing joint volume and producing pain and stiffness. Pain and capsular tightness alter scapular mechanics, rotator cuff activation and proprioception, so the shoulder becomes functionally limited. Diabetes and thyroid disease are common associations and worsen prognosis.

4Answer

Functional rehabilitation is organised by stage, with the functional goal (for example dressing, hair care, reaching a shelf, hand behind back) agreed with the patient from the outset.

Freezing (painful) phase. The priority is pain relief and maintaining range, not aggressive stretching. Use gentle pendular exercises, active-assisted range, pain-free mobilisation (Maitland grades I–II), scapular mobility, and modalities such as heat, laser or TENS. Vigorous mobilisation is avoided because it aggravates inflammation.

Frozen (stiff) phase. With pain settling, the aim shifts to regaining range. Progress to end-range mobilisation (grades III–IV), sustained stretching of the posterior capsule (cross-body adduction, sleeper stretch), anterior capsule stretch, and proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF) patterns. Mobilisation-with-movement (Mulligan) and muscle energy techniques are useful. Cane or wand exercises, wall slides and pulleys let the patient self-stretch at home, 3–4 sessions a day of 10–15 minutes.

Thawing phase. Range returns spontaneously; the focus is on strengthening the rotator cuff and scapular stabilisers and on functional, task-specific practice — reaching overhead, behind the back, dressing and carrying.

Functional concepts applied throughout. Train movements the patient actually needs (hand behind back for toileting and dressing, hand to mouth for feeding, overhead reach for shelves). Use task-specific practice, closed- and open-chain exercise, scapular stabilisation and rotator cuff rehabilitation, and home exercises in the functional ranges. Outcome measures include the SPADI and DASH questionnaires and goniometry of flexion, abduction and rotation.

PhasePain/stiffnessPriorityMain methods
FreezingHigh pain, early stiffnessPain relief, maintain rangePendulum, grade I–II mobilisation, modalities
FrozenLow pain, marked stiffnessRegain rangeGrade III–IV mobilisation, PNF, stretching, MWM
ThawingMinimal pain, improving rangeStrength, functionRotator cuff and scapular strengthening, task training

5Recent advances

  • Rangan et al. (2020) — the UK FROST multicentre randomised trial found physiotherapy with steroid injection, manipulation under anaesthesia and arthroscopic capsular release were not clinically superior to one another, supporting a trial of conservative, stage-matched physiotherapy first.
  • Page et al. (2014) — the Cochrane review of 32 trials (1836 participants) synthesised the evidence on manual therapy and exercise for adhesive capsulitis, showing mobilisation with supervised exercise gives worthwhile short-term gains in pain and function.
  • Zhang et al. (2021) — an updated network meta-analysis ranked capsular distension (hydrodilatation) highly for short-term pain relief and function, with extracorporeal shockwave and laser therapy showing promise.
  • Lin et al. (2022) — a pilot randomised trial showed proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation improved shoulder range and reduced pain, with MRI evidence of reduced coracohumeral ligament and capsular thickening.
  • Itoi et al. (2016) — the ISAKOS Upper Extremity Committee consensus prefers the term "frozen shoulder" over "adhesive capsulitis", since true adhesions are not present, and guides treatment by clinical stage.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. How would you analyze the selection of exercises to improve postural stability and balance in chronic ankle instability.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Ankle and Foot Rehabilitation

★ Memory hook — Find the deficit, then train that deficit — stable to unstable, eyes open to closed.

1Introduction

Chronic ankle instability (CAI) is the persistence of "giving way", pain and reduced function after lateral ankle sprain. It combines mechanical instability (ligament laxity) with functional instability (impaired proprioception and neuromuscular control). Exercise selection to improve postural stability and balance must therefore be driven by a careful assessment of the specific deficits, then progressed systematically from easy to demanding.

2Physiology

Postural control depends on sensory input from muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, joint and cutaneous receptors, integrated centrally and expressed through feed-forward and feedback muscle activation. The ankle evertors (peroneals) and dorsiflexors are critical for resisting inversion, and their reaction time and strength determine how well the joint is protected. Balance is thus a sensorimotor skill, trainable through repetition.

3Pathophysiology

After sprain, ligament laxity, damaged mechanoreceptors, delayed peroneal reaction time, reduced dorsiflexion range, altered arthrokinematics and, in some patients, cortical sensorimotor changes produce recurrent instability and reduced dynamic balance. The therapist must identify which component dominates in each patient, because this determines which exercises are chosen.

4Answer

Step 1 — Assess the deficits. Use the Star Excursion Balance Test or Y-Balance Test for dynamic balance, single-leg stance (eyes open/closed, firm/foam) for static balance, the Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (CAIT) and Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) for self-reported function, and isokinetic or handheld dynamometry for evertor and dorsiflexor strength.

Step 2 — Match exercise to deficit.

  • Static balance deficit: single-leg stance progressions.
  • Dynamic balance deficit: reach tasks, wobble board, BOSU.
  • Reactive deficit: perturbation, hop-and-stick, drop landings.
  • Strength deficit: peroneal and dorsiflexor resistance work.

Step 3 — Progress the challenge. Move from bilateral to unilateral, eyes open to eyes closed, firm to unstable surface, static to dynamic, single task to dual task (adding a cognitive task), and finally to sport-specific and plyometric work. Dosage of roughly 4–6 weeks, three times weekly, three to four sets per exercise, is supported by the literature.

Deficit foundExercise choiceProgression
Static balanceSingle-leg stanceEyes closed → foam → perturbation
Dynamic balanceSEBT reaches, wobble boardStable → unstable surface
Reactive controlHop-and-stick, drop landingPlanned → unplanned direction
StrengthPeroneal/dorsiflexor resistanceIsometric → dynamic → eccentric

Step 4 — Reassess and progress. Re-test balance and function regularly; progress only when the current level is mastered without pain or giving way, and maintain a long-term home programme, because gains partly decline after six months.

5Recent advances

  • Mollà-Casanova et al. (2021) — a meta-analysis of 15 trials confirmed balance training significantly improves function, instability and dynamic balance in CAI, and is superior to general exercise for functional outcomes.
  • Koshino & Kobayashi (2023) — a systematic review and meta-analysis of conservative interventions found both balance and strength training improve static and dynamic balance in CAI, supporting exercise-based rehabilitation as first-line care.
  • Hou et al. (2022) — a one-year prospective study showed three months of supervised balance training improved postural control and strength in CAI, but some gains declined by six months, and high Beighton scores and initial inversion weakness predicted re-sprain, so dorsiflexion and eversion strengthening should be added.
  • Wang et al. (2023) — a meta-analysis of dual-task training in CAI found it improved dynamic balance and reduced centre-of-pressure area, supporting the addition of cognitive tasks to balance work.
  • Sierra-Guzmán et al. (2018) — a randomised trial found whole-body vibration added to balance training improved sensorimotor balance outcomes in recreational athletes with CAI.

  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. Elsevier; 2021.

Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Describe the functional training methods in treatment of musculoskeletal conditions.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Functional Training

★ Memory hook — Train the task, not just the tissue.

1Introduction

Functional training is a task-oriented, activity-based approach in which the patient practises the movements and activities they actually need, rather than isolated muscle actions alone. It is a top-down strategy: instead of only strengthening an impairment, it trains the whole functional task, promoting transfer to daily life, work and sport. In musculoskeletal rehabilitation it is used across fracture, joint replacement, back pain, tendon and sports injuries.

2Physiology

Functional training rests on motor learning and neuroplasticity. Skills are acquired through repeated, meaningful practice with feedback, and the nervous system reorganises in response to that practice. Training is specific: the body adapts to the exact task, load and context trained, so the closer the exercise is to the real task, the greater the transfer. Progressive overload, practice variability and part-to-whole learning drive adaptation.

3Pathophysiology

Musculoskeletal injury produces pain, weakness, loss of range and altered movement strategies. Prolonged protection and fear of movement (kinesiophobia) lead to deconditioning and maladaptive movement habits, so patients may regain strength without regaining function. Functional training directly addresses this gap by retraining the tasks that are limited.

4Answer

Functional training methods are applied along a continuum, from isolated to integrated to truly functional work.

Task-oriented training. The patient practises real, meaningful tasks — reaching, lifting, carrying, dressing, stair climbing, working — with difficulty graded to the current ability.

Motor skill training. For chronic low back pain, person-specific training changes how the patient performs a pain-provoking activity (for example, bending to pick up an object), using motor-learning principles rather than strength exercises alone.

Occupational and work simulation. Job-specific tasks, lifting technique and work conditioning prepare the patient for return to work.

Progressive functional exercise. Isolated strengthening is integrated into functional patterns; closed-chain, balance, perturbation and plyometric exercises are added as tolerated.

Graded activity and graded exposure. Activity is increased in a planned way to overcome fear-avoidance and build tolerance.

Principles. Specificity, overload, progression, individualisation, feedback, practice variability and part-to-whole sequencing govern the programme. Outcome measures include the Patient-Specific Functional Scale, DASH, WOMAC and job-related measures.

LevelExamplePurpose
IsolatedQuadriceps settingRestore activation
IntegratedSit-to-standCombine muscle groups
FunctionalStair climbing, liftingDaily-life transfer
Work/sportJob simulation, plyometricsReturn to role

5Recent advances

  • Monticone et al. (2021) — a randomised controlled trial showed task-oriented exercises based on patients' specific job activities plus occupational therapy produced clinically important, durable improvements in disability, pain and quality of life after surgically treated proximal humeral fracture.
  • Dudonienė et al. (2023) — a randomised trial found task-oriented exercise superior to conventional physiotherapy for hip function and dynamic balance in early rehabilitation after total hip replacement.
  • van Dillen et al. (2021) — a randomised trial found person-specific motor skill training in functional activities produced greater and more durable functional improvement than strength and flexibility exercise in chronic low back pain.
  • Nieves-Silva et al. (2025) — a systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 trials reported functional task training significantly improves balance (Berg Balance Scale), mobility (Timed Up and Go) and endurance (6-minute walk test) in older adults.
  • Newington et al. (2024) — a systematic review of work-participation interventions for upper-limb musculoskeletal conditions found exercise-based, task-focused programmes had the most consistent benefit for return to work.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. How do you distinguish and prioritize the selection of different manual therapy methods for chronic non-specific neck pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Spine — Manual Therapy

★ Memory hook — Classify first, then choose the technique — and always pair it with exercise.

1Introduction

Chronic non-specific neck pain is neck pain without a specific pathological cause. Manual therapy is one component of a multimodal, classification-based approach and is never used in isolation. Distinguishing between the available manual therapy methods, and prioritising them, depends on the patient's impairment classification, irritability and stage, and on safety screening.

2Physiology

Manual therapy produces neurophysiological rather than purely mechanical effects: mobilisation and manipulation stimulate joint and muscle mechanoreceptors, modulate dorsal horn and descending pain-inhibitory pathways, and may transiently alter muscle tone and pain sensitivity. Cervical and thoracic techniques also influence segmental mobility and sensorimotor control, which is why they are combined with exercise and education.

3Pathophysiology

Persistent neck pain involves altered motor control, reduced segmental mobility or hypermobility, myofascial trigger points, and central sensitisation with psychosocial contributors. The JOSPT neck pain guideline classifies patients into mobility deficits, movement coordination impairments, headache and radiating pain, because the appropriate manual therapy differs for each.

4Answer

Distinguishing the methods.

  • Mobilisation vs manipulation: mobilisation uses low-velocity, graded oscillatory or sustained movements (Maitland grades I–V); manipulation is a single high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust beyond the physiological range.
  • Region: cervical versus thoracic mobilisation/manipulation; thoracic manipulation is often added for cervical mobility deficits.
  • Technique family: Maitland mobilisation, Mulligan sustained natural apophyseal glides (SNAGs), muscle energy technique, myofascial release and soft-tissue massage, and neural mobilisation.
  • Target tissue: articular (joint glides), myofascial (soft-tissue techniques) or neural (neurodynamic techniques).

Prioritising the selection.

  • By classification: mobility deficits → cervical and thoracic manipulation or mobilisation; movement coordination impairments (including whiplash) → mobilisation with a progressive exercise programme using cognitive behavioural principles; cervicogenic headache → C1–2 SNAG or upper cervical mobilisation/manipulation; radiating pain → intermittent mechanical cervical traction plus mobilisation.
  • By irritability: highly irritable conditions start with grade I–II mobilisation; less irritable conditions tolerate grade III–IV and manipulation.
  • By safety: screen for upper cervical instability, vertebrobasilar insufficiency and red flags before any thrust technique.
  • Always combined: manual therapy plus exercise and education, because manual therapy alone gives only short-term benefit.
FeatureMobilisationManipulation
VelocityLowHigh
AmplitudeGraded (I–V)Low, single thrust
Patient comfortGenerally comfortableMay cause brief soreness
Typical useIrritable or stiff jointsNon-irritable mobility deficits

5Recent advances

  • Blanpied et al. (2017) — the JOSPT neck pain clinical practice guideline recommends a multimodal approach (thoracic and cervical manipulation or mobilisation, mixed exercise and education) for chronic neck pain with mobility deficits, rather than relying on passive techniques alone.
  • Gross et al. (2015) — the Cochrane review of 51 trials (2920 participants) found cervical manipulation and mobilisation give similar benefit and thoracic manipulation improves pain and function, but manipulation carries rare serious risk, so mobilisation is preferred.
  • Bussières et al. (2016) — the Canadian chiropractic clinical practice guideline recommends multimodal manual therapy including manipulation, mobilisation and soft-tissue therapy for persistent neck pain, with high-dose massage over no treatment.
  • Cleland et al. (2007) — developed a clinical prediction rule identifying patients with neck pain likely to benefit from thoracic spine thrust manipulation, supporting classification-based matching of technique to patient.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Elaborate the neurological concepts and functional methods in rehabilitation of musculoskeletal dysfunctions.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Neurological Concepts in MSK Rehabilitation

★ Memory hook — Pain lives in the brain; retrain the brain to retrain the movement.

1Introduction

Musculoskeletal dysfunction is not only a tissue problem. Persistent pain and injury change the nervous system — altering cortical body maps, sensorimotor control and movement strategies. Rehabilitation therefore applies neurological concepts (neuroplasticity, pain neuromatrix, sensorimotor integration) together with functional methods (task-oriented training, motor control retraining, graded motor imagery) to restore both movement and the brain's representation of it.

2Physiology

The sensorimotor cortex contains detailed maps of the body that are refined by use and can reorganise with learning or disuse. Motor learning occurs through practice, feedback and repetition, supported by neuroplastic mechanisms such as synaptic strengthening and cortical reorganisation. Descending pathways from the brain modulate pain, and normal movement depends on accurate sensory input, intact body schema and coordinated feed-forward control.

3Pathophysiology

Chronic pain and injury produce maladaptive neuroplasticity: altered cortical representation of the affected part, cortical disinhibition, disrupted body schema, sensory loss (for example reduced two-point discrimination) and learned non-use. These changes persist even after tissue healing and explain why some patients remain painful and functionally limited despite a healed injury.

4Answer

Neurological concepts applied.

  • Pain neuroscience education: explain pain as a protective output of the nervous system, reducing threat and fear.
  • Neuroplasticity: use repeated, meaningful practice to drive beneficial reorganisation.
  • Sensorimotor integration: restore accurate sensory input and coordinated motor output.
  • Central sensitisation: graded, non-threatening input to reduce nervous system sensitivity.

Functional methods.

  • Graded motor imagery (GMI): sequential laterality training (left/right recognition), explicit motor imagery, then mirror therapy — used in complex regional pain syndrome, chronic shoulder pain and after joint replacement.
  • Sensory retraining: tactile localisation, two-point discrimination and graphesthesia training to restore body maps.
  • Motor control retraining: re-educating movement patterns and segmental control.
  • Task-oriented and functional training: practising meaningful activities to embed new strategies.
  • Cognitive functional therapy: combining movement retraining with behavioural and cognitive approaches.
ConceptMethodExample condition
Pain neuromatrixPain neuroscience educationChronic low back pain
Cortical reorganisationGraded motor imageryCRPS, chronic shoulder pain
Body schemaSensory discrimination trainingChronic pain, post-surgery
Motor learningTask-oriented trainingPost-fracture, joint replacement

Dosage and progression: GMI is commonly delivered over about six weeks, two weeks per stage; sensory and motor retraining uses short, frequent, pain-free sessions that progress as tolerance improves. Outcome measures include pain ratings, two-point discrimination, the DASH and function-specific scales.

5Recent advances

  • Moseley (2004) — introduced graded motor imagery, a movement-representation technique using laterality, motor imagery and mirror therapy to achieve cortical reorganisation and reduce pain.
  • Louw et al. (2016) — a systematic review of randomised trials found pain neuroscience education reduces pain, improves function, lowers disability, reduces psychosocial factors and cuts healthcare use in chronic musculoskeletal pain.
  • Bagg et al. (2022) — the RESOLVE randomised trial found pain education integrated with graded sensorimotor precision training significantly reduced pain intensity in chronic low back pain at 18 weeks.
  • Candiri et al. (2023) — a randomised trial found graded motor imagery added to rehabilitation after total knee arthroplasty improved pain, motor imagery ability, pain catastrophising and kinesiophobia.
  • Wand et al. (2010) — showed that two-point discrimination and graphesthesia (cortical sensory tests) are impaired over the lumbar spine in chronic low back pain, supporting their use as clinical markers of cortical body-map disruption.

  4. Moseley GL, Butler DS. Fifteen years of explaining pain: the past, present and future. J Pain. 2015;16(9):807–813.
