  6. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation and Intervention. 5th ed. McGraw Hill; 2020.
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. How do you determine the importance of physical agents in rehabilitation of low back pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Physical Agents and Electrotherapy

★ Memory hook — Physical agents are helpers, not heroes — active exercise leads.

1Introduction

Physical agents in low back pain (LBP) include thermal agents (heat, cold), electrotherapeutic agents (TENS, interferential, electrical muscle stimulation), mechanical agents (traction, ultrasound, laser) and electromagnetic agents. Determining their importance means placing them correctly within the evidence-based, biopsychosocial management of LBP: they are adjuncts that may give short-term symptom relief, while exercise, manual therapy and education remain the core.

2Physiology

Thermal agents work by altering tissue temperature and blood flow: superficial heat increases extensibility and reduces spasm, while cold reduces acute inflammation and pain. TENS acts largely through the gate-control mechanism and descending inhibition; ultrasound produces thermal and non-thermal (cavitation, microstreaming) effects; traction distracts spinal segments. These are physiological effects on symptoms, not on the underlying course of LBP.

3Pathophysiology

LBP is classified as acute, subacute or chronic, and as nociceptive, neuropathic or centrally sensitised. Most acute LBP is self-limiting; chronic LBP often has biopsychosocial contributors. Physical agents target symptoms and short-term irritability, but do not address deconditioning, fear-avoidance or central sensitisation — hence their limited role.

4Answer

How to determine importance.

  1. Follow the guidelines. The JOSPT 2021 LBP guideline and the WHO 2023 guideline make exercise, manual therapy and education the priorities; physical agents are adjuncts.
  2. Match agent to stage and classification. Acute, highly irritable LBP may benefit from short-term heat or TENS for comfort; chronic LBP needs active exercise, not passive agents.
  3. Use evidence honestly. Heat has modest short-term benefit; TENS evidence is mixed and it is not recommended as routine care by the WHO 2023 guideline; ultrasound is not recommended; traction is not recommended for chronic LBP with leg pain (conflicting evidence) but may help a selective radicular subgroup.
  4. Combine with active therapy. Agents should enable exercise and function, not replace them, and should not foster passive dependence.
  5. Respect patient preference and safety, and reassess effect; discontinue agents that give no measurable benefit.
AgentMechanismEvidence in LBP
Superficial heatBlood flow, extensibility, spasm reliefShort-term relief
TENSGate control, descending inhibitionMixed; not routine (WHO 2023)
UltrasoundThermal/non-thermal tissue effectsNot recommended
TractionSegmental distractionNot for chronic LBP with leg pain; selective radicular use
Laser / interferentialPhotobiomodulation / currentAdjunct, limited evidence

Typical dosage: TENS 80–150 Hz or 2–4 Hz, 20–30 minutes; superficial heat 15–20 minutes; lumbar traction approximately 25–40% of body weight, intermittent. Agents are timed to precede exercise so that movement is easier.

5Recent advances

  • JOSPT/AOPT (2021) guideline — recommends exercise and manual therapy as core interventions for low back pain and states mechanical traction should not be used for chronic LBP with leg pain because it adds no benefit.
  • WHO (2023) guideline — for chronic primary low back pain conditionally recommends structured exercise and education, and conditionally recommends against routine traction, therapeutic ultrasound and TENS.
  • NICE (2016) guideline — the NG59 guideline recommends group exercise programmes for low back pain and advises against ultrasound, TENS, PENS and acupuncture, embedding active rehabilitation and de-emphasising passive electrotherapy.

6References

  1. George SZ, Fritz JM, Silfies SP, et al. Interventions for the management of acute and chronic low back pain: revision 2021. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2021;51(11):CPG1–CPG60.
  2. World Health Organization. WHO guideline for non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults in primary and community care settings. Geneva: WHO; 2023.
  3. Watson T, ed. Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice. 12th ed. Elsevier; 2008.
  4. Robertson V, Ward A, Low J, Reed A. Electrotherapy Explained: Principles and Practice. 4th ed. Butterworth-Heinemann; 2006.
  5. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. FA Davis; 2018.
  6. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. Elsevier; 2021.
Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Discuss the application of electric currents for tissue healing.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Electrotherapy — Tissue Healing

★ Memory hook — The body makes its own current of injury — we just copy it.

1Introduction

Electrical stimulation (ES) for tissue healing uses externally applied current to imitate the endogenous bioelectric currents that the body generates around an injury. By mimicking the natural "current of injury", ES accelerates and supports the healing of chronic wounds and injured musculoskeletal tissues. It is an evidence-supported adjunct in wound care and is applied to tendon, ligament and bone healing.

2Physiology

Every wound generates an endogenous electric field — the skin battery — that guides cells to migrate into the wound (galvanotaxis) and drives repair. Electrical current influences cell migration, proliferation, cytokine and growth-factor secretion (for example VEGF, FGF), angiogenesis, bacterial control and keratinocyte and fibroblast activity. These cellular effects map onto the inflammatory, proliferative and remodelling phases of healing.

3Pathophysiology

In chronic wounds and some musculoskeletal injuries, healing stalls — often in the inflammatory phase — because of poor perfusion, infection, diabetes or impaired fibroblast function. Without the normal bioelectric signal, cells migrate poorly, angiogenesis is reduced and the wound does not close. Exogenous ES restores the missing electrical cue.

4Answer

Current types and their application.

  • Direct current (DC): continuous unidirectional flow, useful for galvanotaxis and iontophoresis; polarity matters, and continuous DC can irritate skin.
  • High-voltage pulsed current (HVPC): monophasic twin-peak pulses, the most studied for wound healing; often used with the cathode over the wound in the inflammatory phase and the anode later.
  • Low-intensity/microcurrent: very low amplitude, mimics endogenous currents.
  • Pulsed and interferential current: used for tendon, ligament and soft-tissue healing and pain.
  • Pulsed electromagnetic fields / capacitive coupling: used for bone and fracture healing.

Wound-healing protocol (typical). HVPC at approximately 100–150 pulses per second, amplitude 100–500 microamps to a few milliamps (enough to produce a comfortable sensation), for 45–60 minutes, three to seven times a week, with the active electrode placed over or near the wound. For DC, amplitude is typically in the hundreds of microamps.

Musculoskeletal tissue healing. Pulsed or interferential currents are applied around injured tendon or ligament to support proliferation and reduce pain; PEMF is used for delayed union and fracture healing.

Current typeKey effectTypical use
DCGalvanotaxis, polarityWound, iontophoresis
HVPCCellular migration, antibacterialChronic wounds, oedema
MicrocurrentMimics endogenous currentWounds, tissue repair
Pulsed/interferentialProliferation, pain reliefTendon, ligament
PEMFOsteogenesisBone, fracture healing

Precautions and contraindications: avoid over the pregnant uterus, over the heart in patients with pacemakers, over malignant tissue, over thrombophlebitis and in areas of impaired sensation; ensure correct polarity and check skin regularly.

5Recent advances

  • Rajendran et al. (2021) — a review of 30 studies concluded electrical stimulation improves chronic wound healing by limiting inflammation, increasing perfusion, controlling bacteria, and promoting fibroblast migration, angiogenesis and keratinocyte activity, with pulsed current most used.
  • Arora et al. (2020) — the Cochrane review of electrical stimulation for treating pressure ulcers found adding it to standard care probably increases the proportion of ulcers healed within 12 weeks.
  • Koel & Houghton (2014) — a meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials found adding electrical stimulation to standard wound care increased the four-week percentage area reduction by about 27%, supporting it as an evidence-based adjunct to wound care.
  • Avendaño-Coy et al. (2022) — a meta-analysis of randomised trials found electrical microcurrent therapy reduced wound surface area, shortened healing time and reduced pain, with no increase in adverse effects.

6References

  1. Watson T, ed. Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice. 12th ed. Elsevier; 2008.
  2. Robertson V, Ward A, Low J, Reed A. Electrotherapy Explained: Principles and Practice. 4th ed. Butterworth-Heinemann; 2006.
  3. Kloth LC. Electrical stimulation technologies for wound healing. Adv Wound Care. 2014;3(2):81–90.
  4. Arora M, Harvey LA, Glinsky JV, et al. Electrical stimulation for treating pressure ulcers. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020;(1):CD012196.
  5. Khouri C, Kotzki S, Roustit M, et al. Hierarchical evaluation of electrical stimulation protocols for chronic wound healing: an effect size meta-analysis. Wound Repair Regen. 2017;25(5):883–891.
  6. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. FA Davis; 2018.
Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Explain the current designs in assistive technology for work related musculoskeletal disorders.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Ergonomics and Assistive Technology

★ Memory hook — Change the task first, the tool second, the worker last.

1Introduction

Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) are the leading occupational health problem, driven by repetitive movement, sustained posture, high force, vibration and psychosocial stress. Assistive technology for WMSDs spans ergonomic redesign, wearable devices and, most recently, industrial exoskeletons and smart sensing. Current designs aim to reduce the biomechanical load on the back, shoulders, knees and upper limbs while preserving function and safety.

2Physiology

WMSDs arise from cumulative load on muscles, tendons, nerves and joints. Reducing the external moment at a joint (for example the lumbar spine during lifting), lowering muscle activation and sharing load between the device and the body are the physiological goals. Devices work best when they reduce peak and cumulative tissue stress without introducing new stresses elsewhere.

3Pathophysiology

Repetitive strain and sustained awkward postures cause tendon overload (tendinopathy), muscle fatigue, nerve compression and joint degeneration. The mismatch between task demands and human strength or endurance produces injury. Assistive technology addresses this mismatch directly.

4Answer

Current designs.

  • Passive exoskeletons: use springs, dampers or counterbalance mechanisms (no power) to support posture; common for the back, shoulder and knee in construction, assembly and logistics.
  • Active exoskeletons: use electric motors, pneumatics or hydraulics to provide powered assistance; some are adaptive, sensing load in real time.
  • Soft exosuits: textile-based devices that assist movement with less bulk.
  • Wearable sensors and smart PPE: inertial sensors and EMG biofeedback that monitor posture and load and warn the worker.
  • Adaptive control: force-myography and machine-learning controllers adjust support to the lifted mass in real time.
  • Ergonomic aids and adaptive tools: height-adjustable workstations, lift assists, powered tools and ergonomic seating.

Assessment and prescription. Risk is assessed with tools such as REBA, RULA, the NIOSH lifting equation and the Key Indicator Method. Devices are selected by body region and task (overhead work, stooping, kneeling, lifting) and evaluated with objective measures (EMG, kinematics, forces) and subjective measures (discomfort, usability).

FeaturePassive exoskeletonActive exoskeleton
Power sourceNone (springs)Motors/pneumatics
WeightLighterHeavier
AdaptabilityFixed supportAdaptive/real-time
Typical useStooping, overhead, kneelingLifting, dynamic tasks

Principles. Follow the hierarchy of controls: engineering and administrative controls first, with exoskeletons as a supplement (like PPE), not the only measure. Ensure correct fit and training, monitor for new hazards (pressure, hyperextension, instability) and guard against over-reliance and workload creep. Combine devices with job rotation and ergonomic redesign.

5Recent advances

  • NIOSH (2022) — its science bulletin on exoskeletons in construction summarises research showing passive back-support exoskeletons reduce lumbar muscle activity and discomfort, and knee-assistive exoskeletons reduce knee muscle activation during kneeling.
  • de Looze et al. (2016) — a review of 26 industrial exoskeletons found passive low-back devices reduce back muscle activity by 10–40% and active devices by up to 80%, while discomfort, device weight and poor anatomical fit still limit real-world use.
  • Golabchi et al. (2022) — proposed a three-dimensional framework for evaluating industrial exoskeletons based on efficacy metrics, target tasks and supported body postures.
  • Sierotowicz et al. (2022) — demonstrated adaptive control of a shoulder exoskeleton using force myography and machine learning, adjusting support to the lifted mass in real time and reducing muscle activity.
  • Cardoso et al. (2024) — a systematic review of 49 studies (2014–2024) found passive and active devices reduce WMSD risk factors but highlighted ergonomic limitations, user discomfort and the need for real-world evaluation, stressing the hierarchy of controls, correct fit and training.

6References

  1. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. FA Davis; 2018.
  2. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation and Intervention. 5th ed. McGraw Hill; 2020.
  3. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH). Exoskeletons: potential for preventing work-related musculoskeletal injuries and disorders in construction workplaces. NIOSH Science Blog; 2022.
  4. De Bock S, Ghillebert J, Govaerts R, et al. Benchmarking occupational exoskeletons: an evidence mapping systematic review. Appl Ergon. 2022;98:103582.
  5. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. FA Davis; 2019.
  6. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. 4th ed. Wolters Kluwer; 2012.

Simple answers

110 marks

List the methods of training to improve muscle performance in post-traumatic fracture at the wrist joint.

Full answer →

Show the exercises in the order the fracture heals, not just a random list of methods.

  • What earns marks: show phase logic — training must follow fracture healing (immobilisation, then after the cast, then remodelling), not a random list · name one method from each family — isometric, isotonic, CKC, isokinetic, PNF — plus grip and function · give the grip-strength target (within 10-15% of the uninjured side) and use PRWE as an outcome.
  • Principle first: after a distal-radius / Colles' wrist fracture, muscle performance is rebuilt in a healing-driven order — immobilisation, then post-immobilisation, then remodelling.
  • Treatment moves from isometric (no joint motion, protects the fracture site) to active/isotonic, to resisted, to functional training.
  • Progression is decided by callus maturity, pain and effusion.
  • Isometric (during the cast / early healing): work the muscles that cross the immobilised joint.
  • Use tendon-gliding isometrics for the wrist flexors and extensors.
  • Cast-squeezing routine: gentle graded holds of 6-10 s x10, kept within pain limits.
  • These prevent muscle wasting and help pump out oedema.
  • Also work the shoulder, elbow and full hand outside the cast to keep the whole chain active.
  • Teach active finger movement (AROM) of the free fingers every hour.
  • Isotonic and isoinertial progression: once X-ray union and pain allow, start active, then active-assisted, then dynamic (isotonic) contractions against gravity.
  • Then add graduated resistance — wrist curls, reverse wrist curls, pronation/supination with a small dumbbell or elastic band.
  • Add eccentric emphasis later for tendon tolerance.
  • Progressive-resistance rule (DeLorme/Zinovieff or daily adjustable): 2-3 sets of 8-12 at 60-75% of estimated 1RM.
  • Progress the load by about 5-10% when 12 repetitions become easy.
  • CKC: closed-kinetic-chain weight-bearing — palm-down table pressing, quadruped rocking, wall push-ups — loads the wrist with co-contraction and less shear.
  • Isokinetic dynamometry at 6-12 weeks: constant-speed training gives objective, accommodated resistance and documented torque curves.
  • PNF: rhythmic stabilisation around the wrist for endurance of the stabilisers; contract-relax for wrist-flexion range restriction.
  • Functional and grip progression: grip — putty progression (soft to firm), pinch boards, towel wringing.
  • Dexterity — pegboards, coins, writing; then task-specific loading (carrying a bucket, turning a jar).
  • Outcome tracking: dynamometric grip strength (target within 10-15% of the uninjured side) and PRWE score.

The staircase: each step = one healing phase; progress when pain-free and callus mature; track grip within 10-15% of sound side (PRWE).

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 1a.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — resistance exercise chapters.
  • Hislop H et al. Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing. (reference 7).
  • Hoppenfeld S, Murthy VL. Treatment and Rehabilitation of Fractures. (reference 16).
210 marks

Explain the mechanism of pain relief using electrotherapy modalities.

Full answer →

Explain HOW each modality relieves pain — the mechanism with its settings, not just "TENS closes the gate".

  • What earns marks: give the mechanism AND the parameters for each modality — the exam trap is writing only "TENS closes the gate" · the opioid mechanism (2-4 Hz, naloxone-reversible) carries the second half of the marks · finish with a one-line conclusion.
  • Segmental gate control — the workhorse: TENS floods the large-diameter Aβ afferent fibres.
  • These excite the substantia gelatinosa interneurons of the dorsal horn.
  • This closes the gate on pain transmission to the T cells (Melzack and Wall).
  • Conventional TENS: high frequency 80-100 Hz, short pulse duration 50-100 μs, amplitude strong but comfortable.
  • It gives rapid onset and short carry-over, and is best for acute pain.
  • Endogenous opioid (descending) system: low-frequency acupuncture-like TENS — 2-4 Hz, 200-300 μs, high intensity enough to produce rhythmic muscle contraction.
  • This drives C-afferent / muscle-afferent input to hypothalamic-PAG activation.
  • The raphe magnus and locus coeruleus then descend via the dorsolateral funiculus.
  • They release serotonin/noradrenaline to inhibit dorsal-horn cells.
  • β-endorphin, met-enkephalin and dynorphin are released — this is naloxone-reversible.
  • It has a slower onset but hours of carry-over, best for chronic pain.
  • Other mechanisms — counter-irritation / hyperstimulation analgesia: intense input suppresses pain at spinal and supraspinal levels (brief-intense TENS).
  • Vasomotor and anti-oedema effects: muscle pumping and IFT improve circulation and clear pain-causing metabolites; HVPG reduces oedema-dependent pain.
  • Placebo/expectation: a genuine neurobiological component through descending pathways — honestly explaining the modality makes it work better.
  • Modality settings — conventional TENS: 80-100 Hz, 50-100 μs, 20-30 min (gate control).
  • Acupuncture-like TENS: 2-4 Hz, 200-300 μs, muscle twitch (opioid/descending).
  • IFT: beat 20-80 Hz (DeLisa); 90-130 Hz analgesia common in practice (2-10 Hz also); vector and quadripolar (gate + circulation).
  • HVPG: high voltage, twin-peaked pulses (deep comfort + oedema).
  • Ultrasound: 3 MHz superficial, 1 MHz deep (thermal + non-thermal tissue repair).

TENS pair: conventional 40-80 Hz (DeLisa; 80-100 Hz in Indian texts) vs 2-4 Hz (up to 8 Hz) acupuncture-like (with contraction, naloxone-reversible).

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 2b; Paper II Unit 10.
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. — pain-suppression systems.
  • Melzack R, Wall PD. Science. 1965 (primary).
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).
310 marks

Methods used to improve balance after an ankle sprain.

Full answer →

Give the causal chain (torn mechanoreceptors to poor balance to re-sprain) FIRST, then the training methods.

  • What earns marks: state the rationale first — torn mechanoreceptors lead to poor balance and re-sprain risk · give the progression (floor to foam to wobble board to BOSU to perturbation) and a discharge criterion · quote the recurrence-reduction figure only if you attribute it correctly (Verhagen et al.); otherwise say "substantially reduces".
  • Why balance training at all: ligament injury damages the mechanoreceptors of the ATFL/CFL.
  • This causes an arthrogenic proprioceptive deficit — delayed peroneal reaction time and impaired single-leg stance.
  • This is the strongest predictor of chronic ankle instability and re-sprain.
  • Balance retraining cuts recurrence roughly by half in trials — this is the rationale the examiner wants in line one.
  • Static balance progression: single-leg stance on the floor — eyes open, then eyes closed, then head turns.
  • Progress to foam/air-disc surfaces and a stork stance with reach tasks.
  • Bilateral to unilateral stance on a tilt board fixed to one plane.
  • Target 30-45 s of stable single-leg stance as a milestone before using dynamic tools.
  • Dynamic balance training: wobble/rocker boards and BOSU — two-leg, then single-leg, then with ball-catch; 3-5 min sets daily.
  • Star Excursion / Y-Balance Test as both training and retest (target: within about 90%+ of the uninjured limb and no pain).
  • Multi-directional stepping/lunges onto discs and resisted band walks with single-leg control.
  • Reactive and sport-specific: perturbation training — the therapist nudges the tilt board while the patient stabilises; sudden ball drops for reaction training.
  • Hopping/jumping progressions — sagittal, frontal, rotational; single-leg hop-and-stick landings.
  • Agility: shuttle runs, ladder drills, cutting and turning on the previously injured ankle; taping/bracing as an adjunct during early return.
  • Progression and discharge: progress by surface (stable to unstable), stance (bilateral to unilateral), sensory (eyes open to closed to distracted) and task (static to dynamic to reactive).
  • Discharge: symmetric SEBT reach, at least 95% hop-test limb symmetry, and confident single-leg balance — before return to sport.

Balance progression ladder: floor, foam, disc, wobble board, BOSU, perturbation.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 3c.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — balance training chapter.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).
  • Verhagen E et al. Balance-board training & ankle-sprain recurrence. Am J Sports Med. (primary evidence)

Functional training in individuals who have undergone TKR.

Full answer →

Follow the post-op timeline, give criteria for each stage, and add Indian daily-life tasks with the flexion-limit caveat.

  • What earns marks: follow the post-op timeline (day 0-3 to 6-12 weeks) and make it criteria-based, not calendar-based · quote the stair rule "up with the good, down with the bad" · add Indian-context tasks (low toilet, cross-legged sitting, temple kneeling) with the flexion-limit caveat.
  • Principles: functional training practises the task itself — transferring, walking, climbing — in the real environments the patient returns to (home, fields, factory floors).
  • It is built on a foundation of range of motion (ROM), strength and endurance.
  • After TKR the sequence follows post-op days and is criteria-based, not calendar-based.
  • Day 0-3: ankle pumps, quad sets, SLR (if active extension allows), CPM as per protocol, cryotherapy.
  • Sit on the bed edge and stand within the frame — think hallux-to-hip activation, not just the knee.
  • Day 1-5: transfer training — log-roll to sit, sit-to-stand from a raised chair pushing the armrests.
  • Gait in a walker/rollator (frame, then crutches, then stick, as quad control returns).
  • Short ward-walk distances building up to 100 m.
  • Stair training in late week 1-2: "up with the good, down with the bad."
  • Week 2-6: functional strengthening — mini-squats (0-45°), step-ups on a 10-15 cm block, sit-to-stand from lowering chair heights, leg press in safe ROM.
  • Stationary cycle starting with a high seat, gradually lowered; outdoor uneven-terrain walking.
  • Week 6-12: advanced function — reciprocal stairs, single-leg balance, tai-chi-style weight-shifts, cycling outdoors, swimming (avoid breast-stroke whip-kick with prosthetic stress).
  • Return to light work and driving usually at 6 weeks or more, once quad control and reflexes are sound.
  • ADL integration: practise the actual tasks — squatting to a low Indian toilet (start with a commode chair).
  • Floor-level activities with caution for high-flexion prostheses; carrying weights while walking.
  • Temple kneeling/lotus positions graded per implant flexion limits (most standard implants 110-125° flexion — deep squat/sitting cross-legged needs caution and prosthetic design advice).
  • Progress criteria: independent painless gait, stair-descent control and TUG.

TKR timeline skeleton: day 0-2 bed exercises + first ambulation; about 2 wk ~90° flexion, wounds healed; about 6 wk normal gait pattern; about 3 months full function.

Sources

Describe the neurodynamic management of the peripheral nervous system.

Full answer →

Define slider vs tensioner in one crisp line each, and name a technique with its nerve bias.

  • What earns marks: define slider vs tensioner in ONE crisp sentence each · name a technique with its nerve bias (e.g. ULNT1 = median nerve) · state the dosage and precautions — vague talk of "nerve stretching" loses the whole technique section.
  • Concept: neurodynamics (Butler, Shacklock) examines and treats the mechanical interface of the nervous system.
  • Nerves must glide, slide (a few mm) and elongate (about 2-15% strain tolerance) within their containers.
  • These containers include the intervertebral foramina, muscle tunnels (carpal tunnel, pronator) and fascial beds.
  • When interfaces narrow (disc bulge, oedema, fibrosis) or the nerve becomes mechanically sensitive, movement reproduces symptoms — this is "adverse neural tension".
  • Neurodynamic tests — ULNT1 (median nerve): shoulder abduction-external rotation, forearm supination, wrist-finger extension, elbow extension; neck side-flexion sensitises.
  • ULNT2 (median, anterior): shoulder girdle depression + elbow extension + wrist supination/extension.
  • ULNT3 radial bias; ULNT4 ulnar bias.
  • Lower limb: straight-leg-raise + ankle dorsiflexion/eversion; slump long-sit — to tell neural from hamstring.
  • Interpret by the symptom response across the sensitising additions, side-to-side differences, and whether structural differentiation changes the symptoms.
  • Treatment — sliders (gliding): move the joint proximal to the nerve one way while the distal joint moves the opposite way.
  • This gives maximal nerve glide with minimal tension; painless, used in irritable conditions (e.g. during ULNT1, abduct the shoulder while flexing the neck).
  • Tensioners: lengthen both ends of the nervous system at the same time (e.g. knee extension with cervical flexion).
  • Tensioners give a stronger stretch — used only when irritability is low, always short of symptom reproduction.
  • Progression and precautions: dosage is low amplitude, low velocity, frequent (10-15 oscillations, several sets daily), progressed by range and load.
  • Contraindicated/cautioned over acute inflammation, spinal cord signs, unresolved central sensitisation and recent nerve repair.
  • Evidence: neural mobilisation adds small-to-moderate benefit over exercise alone for carpal tunnel syndrome and cervicobrachial pain — combine it with interface treatment, never as an isolated ritual.

Neurodynamics rule: tensioners lengthen both ends (strong); sliders move one end while the other releases (gentle) — slide for irritable, tension for stable.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 4b.
  • Butler DS, Jones MA. Mobilisation of the Nervous System. (reference 26).
  • Shacklock M. Clinical Neurodynamics. (reference 27).

What are the therapeutic effects of orthotics? What are the various orthotics used in the upper limb?

Full answer →

Match each orthosis to ONE indication and ONE joint position, starting from the three-point pressure system.

  • What earns marks: start from the three-point pressure system — one corrective force, two counter-forces · match each orthosis to ONE indication and ONE joint position · add joint-position specifics (e.g. MCPs at 60-70° flexion in the resting splint).
  • Therapeutic effects: an orthosis (an externally applied device) supports and stabilises — it rests painful joints.
  • It immobilises/protects (fracture, tendon repair).
  • It corrects or prevents deformity (serial casting principles; prevents contracture).
  • It assists or substitutes for weak muscles (dynamic splints).
  • It gives controlled motion (hinged joints permitting a safe arc).
  • It controls oedema and scar, and reduces pain through rest and alignment.
  • It enhances function (positioning the hand for use).
  • Classification: static (no moving parts) vs dynamic (with springs/rubber-band outriggers).
  • Also prophylactic vs corrective vs functional; serial vs wearable.
  • Materials: low-temperature thermoplastics, plaster, prefabricated vs custom.
  • Hand and wrist-hand orthoses: cock-up/resting wrist splint (median nerve palsy, wrist tendonitis, carpal tunnel).
  • Static resting hand splint (spastic hand, burns).
  • Thumb spica (de Quervain's, CMC OA, scaphoid).
  • Gutter/MCP-ulnar drift splint (RA); opponents splint; finger gutter and mallet-finger splints.
  • Knuckle-bender and dorsal block (after flexor-tendon repair); swan-neck/zig-zag correction rings.
  • Dynamic splints: spring-wire outriggers for radial nerve palsy (wrist drop); low-profile dynamic MCP flexion assist; reverse knuckle benders.
  • Elbow: static posterior splint / hinged-locked brace (ligament injury, post-op limits); turnbuckle splint for elbow flexion contracture.
  • Shoulder: sling/abduction pillow (post-op repair, humeral fracture — 30-45° for rotator cuff repair); airplane splint (burn axilla); clavicle strap, figure-of-eight; hemi-sling for subluxation after neurological injury.
  • Prescription principles: match the orthosis to the pathology phase and the goal.
  • Check the fit (no pressure over bony prominences — ulnar head, radial styloid); check skin at each removal and daily.
  • Use the 3-point pressure system for correction; review at every visit.
  • Combine with therapeutic exercise — the splint positions, but the muscle still has to be retrained.

Every orthosis answer starts at the three-point pressure system: one corrective force, two counter-forces.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 5b & Paper IV Unit 6c.
  • Chui KC et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation. (reference 18).
  • Saunders R et al. Hand and Upper Extremity Rehabilitation. (reference 20).
  • Cooper C. Fundamentals of Hand Therapy. (reference 21).
710 marks

Describe the evidence-based electrotherapy management in soft tissue injury.

Full answer →

Match the modality and dose to the healing phase, and quote one negative trial to prove you are evidence-based.

  • What earns marks: match the modality and dose to the healing phase — dose logic first · quote at least ONE negative trial finding (e.g. Cochrane: ultrasound vs sham — no significant difference) · end with the message that exercise is the driver and modalities only buy the pain-free window.
  • Phase logic first: soft-tissue healing passes through haemostasis/inflammation (days 0-5), proliferation (day 5 to 3 wk) and remodelling (3 wk to 12+ mo).
  • "Evidence-based" means the modality and dose must match the phase's cell population.
  • Exercise — not machines — remains the primary driver of repair.
  • Acute/inflammatory phase: give analgesia without adding swelling — conventional TENS (80-100 Hz) or IFT (beat 20-80 Hz per DeLisa; 90-130 Hz for pain in Indian practice) for the pain gate.
  • Cryotherapy in the first 48 h for vasoconstriction and analgesia.
  • Pulsed shortwave (non-thermal, low intensity) and low-dose therapeutic ultrasound (pulsed 1:4, 0.1-0.3 W/cm²) to support membrane repair and oedema resolution — evidence modest; use where pain/effusion blocks active movement.
  • HVPG for oedema control (muscle pumping).
  • Microcurrent (µAT) claims to boost ATP for epithelial repair — weak clinical evidence.
  • Proliferative and remodelling phase: continuous therapeutic ultrasound (3 MHz, 0.5-1.0 W/cm² for superficial structures like the lateral epicondyle; 1 MHz for deep).
  • Its thermal effect increases collagen extensibility (before stretch) and perfusion.
  • Low-level laser (820-904 nm) for tendon injuries — evidence debated: DeLisa finds no benefit in lateral epicondylitis, while newer trials report short-term pain relief.
  • Extracorporeal shockwave therapy for insertional tendinopathies (plantar fasciitis, calcific supraspinatus) — the strongest modern evidence in this family.
  • Progressive loading exercise is the proven remodelling driver — modalities buy the pain-free window that allows it (e.g. eccentric Alfredson protocol for Achilles tendinopathy).
  • Evidence caveats: Cochrane reviews find ultrasound no better than placebo for most soft-tissue injuries.
  • Shockwave and eccentric loading carry the strongest support; TENS has short-term analgesic benefit.
  • So justify every modality with a goal (pain window, tissue extensibility, oedema), set measurable reassessment endpoints, and stop what isn't working.
  • That — not brand loyalty to machines — is the evidence-based behaviour.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 5 (b-e).
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).
  • Robertson VJ, Baker KG et al. Electrotherapy evidence reviews. Phys Ther / Aust J Physiother.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — tissue-healing & loading chapters.
810 marks

Plan an ergonomic table for a software professional who has a condition of Trapezitis.

Full answer →

Give a real table (element/specification/reason) and link every element to trapezius overload.

  • What earns marks: give a real table with element / specification / reason columns · the "reason" column linking each element to trapezius overload is where the higher marks live · include the break and micro-pause schedule and a follow-up/outcome plan.
  • The problem: trapezitis in a software professional is a classic work-related upper-limb disorder.
  • Static upper-trapezius elevation + forward head posture during 8-10 h of screen work causes ischaemic overload and trigger points.
  • The ergonomic plan removes the sustained postural demand.
  • A RULA/rapid exposure assessment documents the risk before redesign.
  • Monitor: top at/slightly below eye level, 50-70 cm away, perpendicular to windows — kills forward-head and sustained flexion.
  • Chair: lumbar support, seat height letting feet rest flat, hips 90-110° — unloads the cervico-scapular chain.
  • Armrests: height so elbows rest at 90-100° with shoulders relaxed — prevents chronic trap elevation, the direct culprit.
  • Keyboard/mouse: close to the body, elbows at sides, wrists neutral; document holder beside the screen — avoids reaching and trap activation.
  • Desk: at elbow height; keyboard tray/standing-desk option — position variation and neutral limbs.
  • Laptop: never on the lap for long work — use a riser + separate keyboard/mouse; otherwise neck flexion is forced.
  • Lighting: ambient + task light, anti-glare, contrast set — prevents leaning-in postures.
  • Phone: use a headset — never shoulder-crunching; that is classic acute trap overload.
  • Breaks and movement: rest breaks of 2-5 min every 30-60 min.
  • True micro-pauses of 20-30 s every 20-30 min of typing; the 20-20-20 rule for the eyes.
  • Trap-specific routine every hour: shoulder shrug-rolls x10, chin tucks x10, doorway pectoral stretch 30 s, scapular retractions x10; plus hydration.
  • Follow-up: reassess the RULA score at 2 and 6 weeks; track pain (VAS/NPS) and NDI.
  • Combine with physiotherapy (postural re-education, trigger-point release, scapular strengthening — lower/middle trap and serratus).
  • Educate about early-warning symptoms so the patient self-corrects.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 6 (a, c).
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — posture & work-related disorder chapters.
  • OSHA Computer Workstations eTool / McAtamney & Corlett RULA (ergonomic standards).
910 marks

Physiotherapeutic strategies for Osteosarcoma.

Full answer →

Show that therapy is phased around the CHEMOTHERAPY cycle, not just the surgery, and name an outcome measure.

  • What earns marks: state that physiotherapy is phased around the CHEMOTHERAPY cycle, not just the surgery · say that high-impact sport is contraindicated after a megaprosthesis · name an outcome measure (TESS or MSTS) in the conclusion.
  • Overview that matters: osteosarcoma is the commonest primary malignant bone tumour of adolescents/young adults.
  • It arises typically at the distal femur/proximal tibia metaphysis (about 60% of cases are near the knee).
  • Management: neoadjuvant chemotherapy, then wide resection by limb-salvage surgery with a megaprosthesis/endoprosthesis (or rotationplasty/amputation), then adjuvant chemo.
  • Physiotherapy is needed across ALL phases, always inside the oncology team.
  • Pre-operative and peri-operative: baseline assessment (ROM, strength, function — MSTS score, TESS) and patient education.
  • Pre-hab: maintain knee/hip ROM and quadriceps strength between chemo cycles.
  • Aerobic conditioning to counter chemo deconditioning; respiratory preparation; gait training on the planned assistive device; psychological preparation.
  • Post-operative (limb salvage), Phase 1 (0-2 wk): pain management (TENS as adjunct, cryotherapy), oedema control, isometrics within the surgeon's protocol.
  • Protected weight-bearing (touch-down to partial, per prosthesis fixation); chest physiotherapy during chemo-induced immunosuppression.
  • Phase 2 (2-6 wk): progressive active knee ROM, patellar mobilisation, scar/soft-tissue mobilisation.
  • Gradual weight-bearing progression, gait re-education, isotonic quadriceps/hamstring work.
  • Phase 3 (6 wk to months): strengthening in functional patterns, proprioceptive and balance training, endurance walk programme.
  • Return to low-impact function — usually NOT high-impact sport with a megaprosthesis; home-programme compliance training.
  • Precautions and complications: protect against pathological/periprosthetic fracture (fall prevention, controlled loading).
  • Guard against infection (pin/wound), extensor-mechanism insufficiency after distal-femoral resection, and prosthetic loosening.
  • Adjust for chemo side effects (fatigue, neuropathy, cardiotoxicity); avoid forceful passive stretching; monitor for recurrence symptoms in follow-up.
  • Holistic care: energy-conservation pacing during chemo, nutritional counselling referral, psychosocial support (body image, school/work re-entry for adolescents).
  • Palliative and end-of-life physiotherapy when disease progresses — comfort, positioning, chest care.
  • Outcome tracking with TESS/MSTS and quality-of-life scales; in amputees, prosthetic rehabilitation.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Units 1-5 (integrative clinical application).
