  • Wilk KE et al. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation. (reference 14).
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10) — oncology rehabilitation chapter.
1010 marks

Types of meniscal tear. What are the causes and mechanism of injury to the meniscus? Plan PT intervention.

Full answer →

Cover the tear types with a sketch, the mechanism sentence, and the conservative-vs-surgery evidence reversal.

  • What earns marks: give the mechanism sentence — flexed, loaded knee + rotation · link a locked knee to a bucket-handle tear · state the conservative-vs-surgery evidence reversal for degenerative tears (FIDELITY/METEOR).
  • Types of tears: bucket-handle — a longitudinal vertical tear with the central fragment displaced into the intercondylar notch; the classic "locked knee".
  • Longitudinal (vertical) — runs along the circumference; common in young athletes.
  • Radial — from the free edge toward the periphery (parrot-beak when oblique).
  • Oblique/flap — diagonal, with symptomatic catching.
  • Horizontal cleavage — splits the meniscus into upper/lower laminae; common in older, degenerative menisci (often with cysts).
  • Complex/degenerative — multi-pattern tears in the aged meniscus.
  • Causes and mechanism: traumatic (young athletes) — the foot is planted, the knee is flexed and loaded while the femur rotates on the fixed tibia.
  • The meniscus is crushed and sheared between the condyle and plateau, tearing like a washer twisting under a bolt.
  • Seen in squatting-and-twisting in cricket, football cutting and kabaddi.
  • The medial meniscus tears more often — it is firmly attached to the medial capsule and less mobile.
  • Degenerative (40+): age-related chondrocalcinosis and mucoid degeneration tear from trivial activities (rising from a cross-legged squat) — horizontal/complex patterns.
  • Risk factors: discoid meniscus, ACL insufficiency (an unstable knee shears the menisci), repetitive deep-squatting occupations.
  • Vascular zones: the red-red peripheral third is vascular (heals).
  • The red-white middle has partial healing potential; the inner white-white two-thirds is avascular.
  • This decides repair vs partial meniscectomy vs conservative care.
  • PT intervention — conservative (small, stable, degenerative tears; now the evidence default): phase-wise — control effusion/pain (cryotherapy, TENS), restore ROM.
  • Then quadriceps/hamstring strengthening (isometrics to closed-chain), proprioception, gait normalisation, return-to-sport criteria.
  • Evidence (FIDELITY and METEOR trials) shows structured exercise matches arthroscopic partial meniscectomy for degenerative tears.
  • Post partial meniscectomy: rapid progression — day 1-3 quadriceps activation, full weight bearing as tolerated, ROM, closed-chain strengthening from week 1, running at about 4-6 wk, sport at about 6-8 wk.
  • Post meniscal repair: protected — brace limiting flexion (0-90° for about 4-6 wk), toe-touch to partial weight bearing 4-6 wk, no deep squats/deep flexion for 12-16 wk.
  • Progressive strength and proprioception — healing is the priority, speed comes later.
  • Outcome tracking: Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), Tegner activity scale, effusion and thigh-circumference measures.

Meniscus: outer third = red-red zone (vascular, heals best), inner two-thirds avascular; bucket-handle tears lock the knee.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Units 1-3.
  • Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. (reference 1) — knee menisci.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4) — McMurray/Apley tests.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — post-meniscal surgery protocols.
110 marks

What is the importance of functional training in individuals with total hip replacement?

Full answer →

Explain WHY functional training matters after a total hip replacement and then show how it is done — mechanism first, then assessment, task progression, precautions and joint protection.

  • Marks first for the reason: explain WHY functional training matters (muscle weakness from disuse, fear, and dislocation risk) before listing any exercises.
  • Then give the early milestones and the hip precautions — the safe and danger positions.
  • Then show the task progression (bed → transfer → walking → stairs) and the joint-protection and ADL advice.
  • Why it matters: the surgery fixes the joint, but the patient's real problem is function — getting out of bed, walking to the bus, squatting to an Indian toilet, sitting cross-legged.
  • Functional training turns a good operation into good daily life.
  • Mechanism: the new hip is a stable, pain-free lever, but the muscles around it — gluteus medius, gluteus maximus, hip flexors — are weak and switched off after months of limping and disuse.
  • Weak hip abductors leave the patient with a positive Trendelenburg pattern until the hip muscles are re-educated.
  • Functional training works on these weak muscles while rehearsing the exact tasks the patient must do at home.
  • Assess on day zero or day one: active straight-leg raise, hip abduction and extension strength, quadriceps control, and the ability to shift in bed.
  • Early milestones: sitting over the edge of the bed by day zero or one, standing transfers, and walking with a frame by day one or two.
  • Record pain (VAS), range of movement, and a baseline functional score such as the Harris Hip Score or Oxford Hip Score so progress can be shown.
  • Teach each task as a rehearsed sequence, not a single exercise.
  • Bed mobility: use log-rolling; turn to the sound side, not the operated side.
  • Sit-to-stand: keep the operated leg forward.
  • Walking aids in order: walker, then crutches, then a single stick held in the opposite hand.
  • Move from frame to stick only when hip abduction control keeps the pelvis level.
  • Stairs come last, with the taught rhyme — good leg to heaven, bad leg to hell (up with the sound leg, down with the operated leg).
  • Hip precautions (posterior approach) — safe zone: keep flexion less than 90 degrees, no adduction past midline, no internal rotation in flexion.
  • Danger zone: deep squat or low chair, crossing the legs or an adducted twist, and bending to pick up from the floor.
  • Dislocation risk is highest in the first 6 weeks — train the rules in early.
  • ADL retraining and joint protection: raised chair and commode, long-handled reacher for dressing, sock aid, slip-on footwear, and a pillow between the knees for sleeping.
  • For Indian floor-level living: a raised Western-style seat for the first weeks, graded squat training only after surgeon clearance, and a side-lying method to get down to and up from the floor.
  • Strengthening: progress from isometrics to open-chain abduction in side-lying, then closed-chain work — mini-squats within the safe range, step-ups, stationary cycling with a high saddle.
  • Add balance boards and treadmill walking for endurance.
  • By week 6 to 12 the goal is independent walking in the community, with long-term activity at the WHO recommendation of 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity per week.
  • Evidence: enhanced-recovery protocols with structured early mobilisation reduce hospital stay and complications without increasing dislocation; functional scores improve most when exercise is task-specific and progressive.
  • Conclusion: the implant restores the joint; functional training restores the person.

Stair rhyme — good leg to heaven, bad leg to hell (up with the sound leg, down with the operated leg).

Sources
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. Hip chapter.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Total hip replacement section.
  • WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour, 2020.
210 marks

What are the recent advances in electrotherapy management of above-knee amputation?

Full answer →

Cover the goals of electrotherapy after an above-knee amputation, then the recent, brain-focused advances — mirror therapy, graded motor imagery and phantom motor execution with session doses.

  • The word 'recent' holds the marks — after TENS, write graded motor imagery and phantom motor execution with session doses.
  • Do NOT claim TENS is proven for phantom pain; say the Cochrane evidence is absent but the risk is nil — that maturity earns marks.
  • Name the stump assessment and the four electrotherapy goals first.
  • Electrotherapy after an above-knee amputation has four goals: control residual-limb and phantom pain, shrink and condition the stump, prevent hip flexion contracture by keeping residual muscles working, and prepare the patient for prosthetic control.
  • Assess before choosing any modality: stump healing (semicircular grading of wound maturity), sensation, volume, hip range and strength.
  • Pain control: conventional high-frequency TENS (40–80 Hz per DeLisa; 80–100 Hz in common practice, strong but comfortable) over the stump or proximal dermatomes for residual-limb pain.
  • TENS works through segmental gating of pain.
  • For phantom limb pain, electrodes on the contralateral intact limb or over the stump can be tried.
  • Evidence caution: the Cochrane review found no randomised trials of adequate quality to prove or refute TENS for phantom and stump pain — so it stays a safe, cheap option rather than a proven cure.
  • Interferential current gives deeper comfortable stimulation for stump-oedema ache and can be combined with active muscle pumping.
  • Oedema, shaping and conditioning: high-voltage pulsed current (HVPC) and interferential therapy help early postoperative oedema, along with compression bandaging and stump shaping.
  • NMES over the residual quadriceps, hamstrings and adductors keeps muscle bulk and the muscle-tendon bed for later prosthetic suspension.
  • NMES also gives the pumping action that reduces oedema.
  • Functional patterns matter more than raw intensity — stimulate the patient into attempting the contraction at the same time.
  • EMG biofeedback over the hip abductors and residual thigh muscles re-educates recruitment, reduces co-contraction, and gives the patient a visible target.
  • If a myoelectric or microprocessor-controlled prosthesis is planned, the same surface electrodes train graded, well-separated contraction of residual muscle groups.
  • The important recent shift is from stimulation to re-training the brain's map of the missing limb.
  • Mirror therapy and graded motor imagery (laterality recognition, imagined movements, then mirror work) now carry the strongest evidence for phantom pain prevention and relief.
  • Phantom motor execution: myoelectric pattern recognition decodes the intended phantom movements from residual-limb EMG and drives a virtual limb on screen — typically 15 sessions at 2 to 3 per week, with good reported reductions in phantom pain.
  • Surgical advance: targeted muscle reinnervation gives the prosthesis user intuitive control sites.
  • Home training is now feasible through textile-electrode bands.
  • Other additions: sensory desensitisation programmes, transcutaneous vagus or auricular stimulation (investigational), and shockwave therapy for stump neuroma pain in selected cases.
  • Evidence: mirror therapy with graded motor imagery has the best non-drug evidence, though Cochrane rates it low certainty; TENS for phantom pain lacks trial evidence but is safe and cheap; phantom motor execution shows promising phase-two data.
  • Conclusion: modern electrotherapy after an above-knee amputation is less about the machine and more about neuromodulation — restoring the cortical representation of the limb.
Sources
  • Johnson MI et al. TENS for phantom pain and stump pain. Cochrane Database Syst Rev.
  • Chui L et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation. Amputation chapters.
  • Guideline on prevention and management of phantom limb pain, J Orthop Surg Res 2026.
  • Pilot studies of phantom motor execution with textile-electrode systems, J Neuroeng Rehabil 2026.
310 marks

Describe the physiotherapy interventions in correction of posture in scoliosis.

Full answer →

Describe scoliosis-specific postural correction — the Schroth three-dimensional self-correction and rotational breathing — with the Cobb-angle thresholds and the brace and screening roles.

  • Quote the Cobb-angle thresholds — 10, 20 and 45 degrees.
  • Never write 'strengthen the convex side and stretch the concave side' alone — that earns half marks; pair it with the three-dimensional self-correction and rotational breathing of PSSE.
  • Scoliosis is a lateral curvature of the spine with vertebral rotation.
  • In adolescent idiopathic scoliosis the deformity feeds itself: by the Hueter-Volkmann principle, unequal loading slows growth on the concave side and speeds it on the convex side — so early postural correction matters more than late.
  • Assess with the Adam's forward-bend test (a rib hump on the convex side), a scoliometer reading, and the radiographic Cobb angle.
  • Cobb angle guide: under 10 degrees is spinal asymmetry only; 10 to 20 degrees need exercise and observation; 20 to 40 to 45 degrees get bracing plus exercises; beyond that, surgery is discussed.
  • Record curve flexibility on side-bending films.
  • Correction uses physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises (PSSE), of which the Schroth school is the best known.
  • The Schroth correction block has three self-correction parts in front of a mirror: elongation (de-rotation by making the spine longer, which unlocks the rotation), then sagittal correction, then frontal-plane correction — the therapist's hands guide the concavity open.
  • Then rotational angular breathing: breathe into the collapsed concave zones to de-rotate the ribs from inside while holding the corrected posture.
  • Finally, muscle activation in the corrected position — the patient is trained to hold the corrected spine, not just repeat generic exercises.
  • Adjunct exercises: stretch the shortened concave-side muscles (quadratus lumborum, latissimus, hip abductors on the concavity).
  • Strengthen the convex side and the deep core, with emphasis on the multifidus and transversus abdominis.
  • Add symmetrical postural endurance work and breathing exercises to restore thoracic expansion.
  • Unstable-surface and body-weight training keep the programme home-friendly.
  • Postural re-education: mirror-aided self-correction, sitting and bag-carrying advice for schoolchildren, and review every 4 to 6 months during the growth spurt.
  • When a brace is prescribed, physiotherapy continues inside it — exercises keep trunk strength, prevent stiffness, and help brace-wear adherence; the SOSORT consensus recommends exercise as an adjunct, especially for mild and moderate curves and during brace weaning.
  • Evidence: SOSORT-endorsed PSSE programmes have RCT support for reducing curve progression risk and improving cosmetic trunk appearance in mild curves; generic exercises alone do not.
  • Conclusion: the curve is corrected in three dimensions — sagittal, frontal and transverse — by elongation, de-rotation and breathing, then stabilised by muscle.

Schroth correction block — Elongate → De-rotate → Rotational breathing → Hold with muscle work.

Sources
  • SOSORT consensus guidelines on conservative scoliosis management.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Scoliosis and spinal deformity section.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Spinal posture chapter.
410 marks

Write the principles and concept of the McKenzie technique.

Full answer →

Explain the McKenzie concept — assessment by repeated movements, centralisation and directional preference, the three syndromes, and self-management.

  • Hit the four syllabus words: centralisation, directional preference, classification and self-management.
  • Show assessment by repeated end-range movements and the three mechanical syndromes.
  • Robin McKenzie's concept: most spinal and limb pain of mechanical origin behaves in a predictable, directional way — some movements make it worse and the opposite movements ease it.
  • Assessment uses repeated end-range test movements in one direction — flexion in lying, extension in lying — and watches the effect on the site of pain.
  • The directional response found in the first session drives the entire treatment.
  • Centralisation: when repeated movement removes distal or peripheral pain and draws it back toward the midline — this is therapeutic and the prognosis improves.
  • Peripheralisation: pain travelling further down the limb — this is a stop signal.
  • Directional preference is the movement direction that centralises or abolishes pain; it is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
  • Three mechanical syndromes (D-P-D): Derangement, Postural and Dysfunction — plus an OTHER group.
  • Derangement syndrome: internal displacement of nuclear material; pain changes within a single session, flexion makes it worse, and changes are rapid.
  • Dysfunction syndrome: structurally shortened tissue stretched painfully; pain only at end range, does not centralise, and improves over weeks.
  • Postural syndrome: pain only from prolonged static loading of normal tissue, eased by a change of position.
  • OTHER (non-mechanical or chronic presentations such as CRPS or neural compromise) needs a different route — red flags and central sensitisation states, where McKenzie principles alone do not apply.
  • Treatment uses patient-generated force first, therapist force only if needed.
  • Force progression: static (sustained) positions → dynamic movements → patient overpressure → clinician overpressure → mobilisation and traction.
  • Education is central: the patient learns which postures to adopt (lumbar lordosis) and which to avoid (slumped sitting, flexion in derangement), so self-management reduces recurrences.
  • In dysfunction syndrome the principle flips — stretch the short tissue repeatedly at end range; in postural syndrome the cure is postural correction and endurance.
  • Maintenance: once pain centralises and settles, the patient keeps the directional-preference exercise and the postural habit — lumbar support in sitting, regular breaks from flexion, and a home programme in the lost direction.
  • Evidence: centralisation is a validated prognostic sign; McKenzie care is better than generic advice short-term for acute low back pain and equals other active therapies long-term.
  • Conclusion: assess by repeated movement, classify by behaviour, treat with the patient's own force in the preferred direction, and make the patient their own therapist.

McKenzie law — centralise = continue, peripheralise = stop. Three syndromes D-P-D: Derangement (directional preference), Postural (correction), Dysfunction (end-range stretch).

Sources
  • McKenzie R, May S. The Lumbar Spine: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Spine chapter.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Intervention sections.
510 marks

Write down the role of physiotherapy in management of glenohumeral dysfunction in swimmers.

Full answer →

Explain swimmer's shoulder — its mechanism, acute and definitive-phase management, technique and load correction, and return-to-pool criteria.

  • Name all three mechanisms: internal impingement, micro-instability and scapular dyskinesis.
  • Half the answer is NOT in the shoulder — GIRD, scapular dyskinesis and the thoracic-core link fetch the full marks.
  • Name the stroke phase (hand entry, pull-through) when you describe the mechanism; vague 'overhead activity' is a half-mark sentence.
  • Swimmer's shoulder is an overuse problem of the shoulder girdle during the pull-through and recovery phases of freestyle.
  • During recovery and hand entry the shoulder rotates under load; combined external rotation and abduction squeezes the posterior-superior labrum and rotator cuff — internal impingement.
  • Micro-instability from capsular laxity and fatigue lets the humeral head migrate.
  • Fatigued periscapular muscles cause scapular dyskinesis — a dropped, protracted scapula that narrows the subacromial space.
  • Assess with the swimming history (stroke, weekly distance, hand-entry pattern), painful arc, Neer or Hawkins tests, labral provocation tests, scapular observation in repeated elevation, and a measured glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD) using the side-lying comparison against total arc rotation.
  • Acute phase: relative rest from the aggravating volume, not total rest — swimmers decondition fast and can kick-train with a pull-buoy between the ankles.
  • Modalities are optional adjuncts; the real work is pain-free range, isometric cuff loading, and posture correction.
  • Address posterior capsule tightness early with sleeper and cross-body stretches.
  • Definitive phase — rebuild the power chain from inside out: rotator cuff strength with external rotation at 0 and 90 degrees abduction using elastic resistance.
  • Then scapular control — retraction, low-row, prone Y-T-W and serratus wall slides.
  • Then closed-chain work and plyometric catching.
  • Then dry-land swim-specific strength — pull-ups and cable internal rotation mimicking the pull-through.
  • Correct GIRD to bring the total rotation arc back to symmetry (sleeper stretch, cross-body adduction stretch and joint mobilisations in external rotation).
  • Restore thoracic extension-rotation for the breathing pattern and core strength to anchor the kinetic chain.
  • Technique and load: correct thumb-entry to fingertip-first entry, avoid midline crossover, balance bilateral breathing, and increase body roll.
  • Coordinate with the coach on training-load change — cut only the painful sets and keep the aerobic base.
  • Return to full training when the shoulder is pain-free through the full arc, external-rotation strength is within 10 percent of the sound side, and the scapula stays controlled after a fatigue set.
  • Prevention: a season-long programme of cuff and scapular strengthening, GIRD surveillance, and a gradual (not sudden) rise in weekly distance.

GIRD rule — internal rotation deficit more than 20 degrees with total-arc asymmetry = stretch programme.

Sources
  • Wilk KE, Brotzman SB. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation. Shoulder chapters.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Shoulder chapter.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Shoulder section.
610 marks

Explain the role of assistive devices in the workplace.

Full answer →

Define and classify assistive devices, show the ergonomic assessment and matching, and give named low-tech and high-tech examples with benefits and barriers.

  • Structure the answer as classify → assess → match → train → follow up.
  • Give at least six named devices, each with one condition it helps.
  • Generic phrases like 'helps the worker' carry no marks.
  • An assistive device is any tool, product or technology that lets a person with an impairment do a task they otherwise could not do, or do it more safely.
  • They run along a spectrum: low-tech ergonomic aids, mid-tech, and high-tech assistive technology.
  • Low-tech examples: reachers, splints, adapted cutlery.
  • Mid-tech examples: ergonomic keyboards, voice-amplifiers, sit-stand desks, powered wheelchairs.
  • High-tech examples: screen readers, voice-recognition software, environmental control units.
  • Orthoses, prostheses and mobility aids used on the job belong to the same family.
  • Prescribe only after an ergonomic job analysis: the physical demands of the post (lift, reach, keyboard hours, standing time), the environment, the impairment profile, and the worker's own goals.
  • Match the device to the task, not to the diagnosis.
  • Involve the worker in selection — a device the worker rejects is a device that will sit in a cupboard.
  • Check safety, training time, maintenance and cost before finalising the recommendation.
  • Low-tech devices (cheap and immediate): reachers and long-handled tools for limited mobility after back injury.
  • Adjustable chair with lumbar support and footrest for the desk worker with chronic low back pain.
  • Angled or split keyboards and vertical mice for carpal-tunnel and work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSD).
  • Standing desks and anti-fatigue mats.
  • Lifting aids such as hoists and transfer boards in hospitals.
  • Jar openers, one-handed boards and splints in food or assembly work.
  • Amplified phones and visual alarms for hearing impairment.
  • High-tech: voice-recognition software for severe hand WRMSD or high spinal involvement; screen readers, magnification and Braille displays for visual impairment.
  • Eye-gaze systems and environmental controls for severe motor loss; powered mobility with work-specific modifications; myoelectric hands for amputees returning to office or technical work.
  • Indian context: the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 obliges employers to provide reasonable accommodation.
  • Benefits: earlier and safer return to work, retention of employment and income, reduced re-injury and compensation cost, improved productivity and morale.
  • Barriers: cost, employer attitudes, lack of trial and training, poor follow-up.
  • Evidence: providing ergonomic devices with workplace assessment reduces WRMSD symptom progression and lost workdays versus advice alone; work-hardening programmes that use the actual devices and tasks return more workers to sustained employment.
  • Conclusion: the device is the visible half — the assessment, training and follow-up are what make it work.

Sequence — Classify → Assess → Match → Train → Follow up.

Sources
  • Maxey L, Magnusson P. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. Work and ADL chapters.
  • Chui L et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Work conditioning section.
710 marks

What are the tendon transfer techniques for median nerve injury? Add a note on physiotherapy management.

Full answer →

Give the principles of tendon transfer, the specific transfers for low and high median nerve lesions, and the pre- and post-operative physiotherapy including re-education.

  • Name the donor AND the insertion for each transfer (FDS of ring finger TO abductor pollicis brevis) — a transfer without its insertion is half a mark.
  • Do not forget the physiotherapy half of the question: splint, donor-contraction re-education, then strengthening.
  • A tendon transfer re-routes the muscle-tendon unit of a working muscle to the insertion of a paralysed one.
  • Donor requirements: the muscle must be expendable, of adequate strength (grade 4 plus) and similar amplitude.
  • Joints must be mobile and supple, the transfer should run straight in a single direction, and it should be synergistic with the movement it replaces.
  • Fix correctable contractures and get adequate soft-tissue cover first — no transfer survives a stiff, scarred bed.
  • Low median lesion paralyses the thenar intrinsic muscles, so thumb opposition and abduction are lost, and sensation over the radial three and a half digits is absent.
  • Low-lesion transfer: the FDS of the ring finger (Royle-Thompson) routed subcutaneously to the abductor pollicis brevis insertion.
  • Camitz transfer: palmaris longus with a strip of palmar aponeurosis passed to the APB — quick, single-incision, and best in carpal-tunnel thenar wasting.
  • Extensor indicis proprius split and transferred to the first dorsal interosseous and APB for opposition plus pinch.
  • A slip of abductor digiti minimi (Huber) for thenar bulk in visible thumb-position deficit.
  • The goal is a thumb that can abduct, rotate and reach the fingers — the opponensplasty.
  • High median lesion (above the elbow) also loses FPL and FDP to the index, so thumb interphalangeal and index distal joint flexion go as well as opposition and sensation.
  • High-lesion reconstruction: brachioradialis or extensor carpi radialis longus to FPL for thumb flexion.
  • Side-to-side tenodesis of the index FDP to the middle-finger FDP for index flexion.
  • The same opposition transfers as above, plus an FCR or ECRL addition when a strong donor is needed.
  • Sensation can be improved by neurovascular island flaps in selected cases.
  • Pre-operatively: keep full passive joint range, mobilise scar and oedema, strengthen the donor muscles consciously (the patient must fire FDS or palmaris longus on command), and desensitise and protect the anaesthetic zones.
  • Post-operatively: the transferred tendon is protected in a thumb-spica splint for 3 to 4 weeks, then controlled mobilisation begins.
  • Re-education is the heart of physiotherapy: the transferred muscle still fires in its old pattern, so train the new action — the patient flexes the ring finger (donor action) while watching and feeling the thumb abduct.
  • Use biofeedback, mirror work and repeated attempted opposition until it becomes a single unconscious synergy.
  • Then progress through graded resistance to functional pinch, precision grip and ADLs, with sensory re-education for the median territory in parallel.
  • Outcomes: well-selected opposition transfers achieve functional pinch in most hands, though power and fine sensory discrimination never equal the original.
  • Conclusion: surgery re-routes the tendon; physiotherapy rewires the movement.

Re-education rule — think donor action, get thumb opposition; thumb-spica 3–4 weeks.

Sources
  • Saunders RJ. Hand and Upper Extremity Rehabilitation. Nerve injury chapters.
  • Cooper C. Fundamentals of Hand Therapy. Tendon transfer sections.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Peripheral nerve injuries.
810 marks

Describe the role of myofascial release in trapezitis.

Full answer →

Explain the mechanism of trapezitis and trigger points, how to assess them, the MFR techniques for the upper trapezius, and the release-lengthen-strengthen progression.

  • The sequence 'release — lengthen — strengthen' is the spine of this answer.
  • Write the referral pattern of the upper trapezius (temple, angle of jaw, ipsilateral neck) — examiners ask it in vivas more often than the techniques themselves.
  • Trapezitis is overload of the upper trapezius: sustained low-grade contraction from desk posture, phone-on-shoulder habits, emotional stress and poor workstation ergonomics keeps the muscle continuously active and exhausts its local circulation.
  • The resulting myofascial trigger point is a hyperirritable spot in a taut band.
  • Integrated hypothesis: an energy crisis — ischaemia releases sensitising substances that lower the local pain threshold and sustain abnormal acetylcholine release, producing the taut band, which further compresses the local vessels.
  • The patient feels aching at the point plus the classic referral to the temple, angle of jaw or between the scapulae.
  • Diagnose on palpation: a taut band in the upper trapezius, an exquisite spot, reproduction of the patient's recognised pain, a local twitch response to snapping palpation, and restricted painful cervical rotation or side-flexion.
  • Screen for perpetuating factors — sleep, workstation, spectacles, stress — because a trigger point with perpetuating factors never stays released.
  • MFR works on the fascia-muscle complex with sustained, low-load, gentle pressure and elongation rather than forceful kneading.
  • Direct release: gentle thumb or knuckle pressure at 90 degrees to the taut band, held until the tissue softens (typically 60 to 90 seconds).
  • Skin rolling over the cervicothoracic fascia to restore fascial mobility.
  • Positional release: find the tender point, move the neck into the position of ease and hold, letting the point quieten.
  • Sustained stretch with the head side-flexed away and gently rotated toward, held for the full release time.
  • Follow every release with active use of the range gained — the muscle must learn its new length.
  • Progression order: release the trigger point, lengthen the muscle, then retrain.
  • Dosage: 2 to 3 sessions per week over 3 to 4 weeks, with a home programme of heat, self-pressure with a ball, and stretching.
  • Adjuncts: spray-and-stretch with ethyl chloride or ice, post-isometric relaxation, dry needling for stubborn points, ergonomic correction of the workstation, breathing retraining for stress-related elevation, and strengthening of the mid and lower trapezius.
  • Evidence: MFR and sustained-pressure techniques give short-term reductions in pain and improved neck range and disability versus placebo in neck-pain trials, strongest when combined with exercise; dry needling adds short-term benefit.
  • Conclusion: MFR releases the taut band, but only posture correction and lower-trapezius retraining keep it released — treat the fire, then remove the fuel.

Release — Lengthen — Strengthen.

Sources
  • Butler DS, Jones MA. Mobilisation of the Nervous System / myofascial approaches.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Soft-tissue intervention chapter.
  • Shacklock M. Clinical Neurodynamics. Mechanosensitivity chapters.
910 marks

How do you manage pain in fracture cases based on educational and behavioral strategies?

Full answer →

Show how education and behaviour change control fracture pain — gate control, pain neuroscience education, pacing, operant methods and graded exposure by healing phase.

  • The question is set under educational and behavioural strategies — do NOT spend half the answer on TENS and cryotherapy; one sentence on adjuncts is enough.
  • Build the marks on gate control, pain education, pacing, operant reinforcement and graded exposure.
  • Fracture pain is acute nociceptive pain with an inflammatory phase, then movement-related pain during healing, and — if mishandled — a shift to chronic pain with fear of movement, guarded patterns and disuse.
  • Gate control theory explains it: descending anxiety and attention open the gate; confidence and understanding close it.
  • Educational and behavioural strategies change what the patient does and expects, which changes what the nervous system transmits.
  • Education first — pain neuroscience: explain in the patient's language that pain is an alarm produced by the brain on the basis of danger, not a meter of tissue damage; a healing fracture protected by a cast is safe to move.
  • Show the healing timeline (inflammation days 1 to 5, soft callus to about 3 weeks, hard callus to about 3 months) so the patient reads twinges correctly.
  • Give clear rules: weight-bearing status, dos and don'ts, red flags.
  • Set expectations for mobilisation pain and control pathways, and teach relaxation breathing to use before and during painful procedures such as cast removal and pin-site care.
  • Give a written home plan — knowledge that is not written down does not travel home.
  • Behavioural techniques: relaxation and breathing retraining, progressive muscle relaxation of uninvolved segments, guided imagery and distraction for procedural pain.
  • Cognitive restructuring to catch catastrophising thoughts (for example, 'the bone is breaking again').
  • Pacing to break the boom-bust cycle of overdoing on good days.
  • Operant strategies: teach the family to reinforce function ('well done for walking to the gate') and not to reinforce pain behaviour.
  • Goal-setting and self-monitoring with a simple diary, and positive reinforcement tied to achievement, not to suffering.
  • After immobilisation, many patients show fear-avoidance: they equate pain with damage and stop moving.
  • Assess with the Tampa Scale and map their fear hierarchy, then expose them in graded steps — pain-free isometrics, assisted range, weight-bearing, stairs and return to work — each step mastered before the next.
  • Use time-contingent rather than pain-contingent scheduling ('walk ten minutes at 8 am daily') so the patient is not ruled by the pain meter.
  • Combine with goal-setting for functional milestones and progress visible to the patient.
  • Evidence: pain neuroscience education reduces pain, disability and fear in musculoskeletal cohorts; behavioural graded activity matches or beats standard physiotherapy for return-to-function after injury.
  • Conclusion: the physiotherapist controls the psychology and behaviour of pain — education that the patient can repeat back is the cheapest analgesic on the ward.

Melzack and Wall 1965 — fear opens the gate, education and movement close it.

Sources
  • Melzack R, Wall PD. Pain mechanisms: a new theory. Science 1965.
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Pain chapters.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Pain management chapter.
1010 marks

Explain the physiotherapy intervention for improving endurance in individuals with a sedentary lifestyle.

Full answer →

Explain why endurance fails in the sedentary, how to screen and test, and how to design and progress an aerobic programme using the FITT principle.

  • Quote two number-sets: 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity per week plus strengthening on two days (WHO 2020), and the 10-percent-per-week progression rule.
  • Write FITT as four separate labelled boxes, not one paragraph.
  • A sedentary lifestyle produces deconditioning through central and peripheral mechanisms.
  • Central: a lower stroke volume and cardiac output reserve.
  • Peripheral: reduced capillary and mitochondrial density in muscle, and a shift toward glycolytic fatigability.
  • Insulin sensitivity falls, visceral fat accumulates, and the patient gets breathless on one flight of stairs.
  • The good news is the trainability — even modest volumes of activity reverse much of this, and the WHO position is that some activity is always better than none.
  • Screen with a physical-activity readiness questionnaire (PAR-Q+) and risk-factor profile; flag the sedentary middle-aged desk worker with hypertension or diabetes for medical clearance before vigorous training.
  • Baseline tests that need no lab: resting and exercise heart rate, the six-minute walk test, a submaximal step or cycle test (Astrand or Chester), a sit-to-stand test for strength endurance, and simple anthropometry.
  • Always record the baseline — the whole motivational architecture of the programme depends on being able to show change.
  • Prescribe by the FITT framework — Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type.
  • Frequency: five days per week of moderate, or three of vigorous, aerobic activity.
  • Intensity: begin at 40 to 50 percent of heart-rate reserve or a Borg RPE of 10 to 12, progressing to 60 to 70 percent; use the talk test as the field check.
  • Time: start at 20 to 30 minutes of accumulated moderate activity — three 10-minute walks count — progressing to 150 to 300 minutes per week (WHO 2020), plus muscle-strengthening on two or more days.
  • Type: walking is the Indian default — cheap, safe and sociable — with cycling, swimming, or home-based step-ups and dance as alternatives.
  • Add circuit training with body-weight resistance (sit-to-stand, step-ups, wall push-ups, resistance band rows) at 12 to 20 repetitions, two days per week.
  • Progress by roughly 10 percent per week in duration first, then intensity.
  • Monitor with RPE, morning resting heart rate, session adherence and symptom review, plus step counters or phone apps.
  • Include warm-up, cool-down and safety education.
  • Adherence decides the outcome: match the intervention to the patient's stage of change, use motivational interviewing, goal-setting and self-monitoring, embed activity into daily routine (stairs, walking to the market, cycle commutes), and use social supports and follow-up.
  • Conclusion: the WHO 2020 message — some activity is better than none, more is better still.

FITT — Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type.

Sources
  • WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour, 2020.
  • ACSM's Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Aerobic endurance chapters.
110 marks

Describe the impaired mobility seen in ankle injuries.

Full answer →

A two-sided answer: show BOTH stiffness (hypomobility) and ligamentous instability (hypermobility) in the ankle, with the mechanism, assessment and treatment.

  • What earns marks: give a two-sided answer — name BOTH stiffness (hypomobility) and instability (ligamentous hypermobility). Most students write only about stiffness · name the ankle capsular pattern — more restriction of dorsiflexion than plantarflexion · give the one-line mechanism — no posterior talar glide means no dorsiflexion.
  • What it means: ankle injuries (usually inversion sprains of the anterior talofibular ligament, but also fractures, syndesmotic injuries and chronic instability) disturb mobility in two opposite directions.
  • Acute stage: fluid (effusion) in the tight talocrural joint plus pain inhibition of the anterior tibial muscles splints the joint in a comfortable plantarflexed-inverted position, so active movement is lost all over.
  • Subacute stage: scar adhesion and shortening of the anterior capsule and the anterior talofibular ligament give a true capsular pattern.
  • Arthrokinematic problem: dorsiflexion needs the wide front of the talus to roll and glide backwards between the malleoli; if posterior talar glide is lost, movement is blocked even when the capsule looks normal.
  • Opposite direction: a torn ligament leaves the joint too roomy, giving instability rather than stiffness.
  • Talocrural joint: loss of dorsiflexion dominates — often 10–20 degrees short of the normal 20 degrees; at least 10 degrees of dorsiflexion is needed for normal terminal stance.
  • Because of that loss the patient walks with a compensated abducted gait, early heel lift or a functional equinus.
  • Subtalar joint: restriction of inversion and eversion follows sinus tarsi involvement or cast immobilisation, disturbing shock absorption on uneven ground.
  • Syndesmosis injury: end-range dorsiflexion is painful because the widened mortise jams the wider anterior talus; the squeeze test and loss of external rotation mark it.
  • Accessory movements lost: posterior glide of the talus on the tibia, and glide of the fibula on the tibia at the distal tibiofibular joint.
  • Hypermobile side: a torn anterior talofibular ligament gives a positive anterior drawer; a torn calcaneofibular ligament gives a positive talar tilt — this laxity drives recurrent sprains when proprioception is not retrained.
  • Assessment: measure active then passive range with a goniometer (align along the fibula and fifth metatarsal) and compare sides — the uninjured ankle is the best control.
  • Weight-bearing dorsiflexion by the knee-to-wall (lunge) test is more functional than table goniometry; assess accessory glides and end-feel (talus gliding posteriorly, fibula gliding anteriorly).
  • Grade ligament laxity with the anterior drawer and talar tilt tests; confirm functional instability with single-leg stance, the star excursion balance test or a wobble-board balance timer; palpate the joint line for effusion and the sinus tarsi for tenderness.
  • Treatment: protect and settle first (relative rest, ice, compression, elevation), then restore arthrokinematics.
  • Mobilisation: grade I–II oscillatory posterior talar glides for pain, progressing to grade III–IV sustained glides with the joint at the end of available dorsiflexion.
  • Convert to self-treatment quickly: knee-to-wall lunges, self-mobilisation with a strap, towel stretches, and eccentric calf work in the functional range.
  • Rebuild proprioception progressively: double-leg to single-leg, stable to unstable surfaces, eyes open to closed, adding hopping and cutting when control returns; tape or brace during the risky late phase.
  • Progression order: settle, glide, stretch, load, retrain balance.
  • Evidence: Verhagen and colleagues showed a proprioceptive and balance training programme roughly halves the recurrence of ankle sprains.
  • Conclusion: ankle injuries cause stiffness (effusion, capsular shortening, lost accessory glide) and instability (ligament laxity plus proprioceptive deficit) in the same joint; treatment of one without the other fails.

No posterior talar glide, no dorsiflexion — draw the talocrural joint with one arrow.

Sources
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — ankle hypomobility and ligamentous instability sections.
  • Verhagen et al., ankle-sprain recurrence, American Journal of Sports Medicine.
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation (10) — ankle and foot interventions.
210 marks

Write in detail about the role of various educational strategies in managing low back pain.

Full answer →

Show education as active treatment — list at least five delivery modes, link content to behaviour change, and end with the evidence that advice alone is weak but education plus graded exercise works.

  • What earns marks: the marks sit in the MENU — list and classify at least five modes, with one content line each · close with the evidence line — advice alone is weak; education plus graded exercise is strong.
  • Most low back pain is non-specific: no fracture, no nerve root compression, no sinister pathology.
  • What decides the outcome is not the imaging but the patient's beliefs and behaviour — whether they fear the pain, rest too much, or keep moving.
  • Education is a real treatment tool in the biopsychosocial model: it targets the psychosocial flags (fear-avoidance beliefs, catastrophising, low self-efficacy) that turn an ordinary sprain into chronic disability.
  • In the Indian clinic, 'complete bed rest for 15 days' is still commonly advised — correcting beliefs early is high-yield treatment.
  • Individual advice in the consultation: stay active, avoid prolonged bed rest, keep working, and understand that 'hurt does not equal harm'.
  • Back schools: structured group programmes of anatomy, posture, lifting technique and exercise, first formalised in Sweden; effective mainly in occupational settings when combined with exercise.
  • Printed and audio-visual media: pamphlets, videos, mobile-phone messages; cheap and scalable but passive.
  • Pain neurosciences education: explaining pain processing so the patient understands pain reflects sensitivity of the nervous system, not ongoing damage; best delivered before or alongside exercise.
  • Group exercise classes with embedded education, and cognitive-behavioural informed classes (the UK Back Pain Exercise And Manipulation trial model), have the best evidence for reducing disability.
  • Yoga-based programmes suit our context — movement, breathing and relaxation in a culturally familiar package.
  • Content must change behaviour: reduce fear-avoidance, teach graded activity and pacing rather than boom-and-bust cycling, and set self-management goals.
  • Correct faulty beliefs about imaging ('disc degeneration is normal ageing, like grey hair') and give clear flare-up plans so a bad day does not become a catastrophe.
  • Education should always be paired with an active component — advice alone changes little; advice plus exercise changes function.
  • Evidence: systematic reviews find education alone (especially pamphlets) gives small short-term effects; structured programmes combining education with exercise reduce pain and disability more meaningfully.
  • Back schools show modest benefit in occupational cohorts; bed-rest advice is actively harmful.
  • Conclusion: education is the frame on which every other low back pain intervention hangs; delivered early, matched to the patient's beliefs and paired with graded activity, it is among the most cost-effective treatments.

Education alone = small effect; education + exercise = real effect.

Sources
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation (10) — education and back school content.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — functional activity education sections.
  • McKenzie & May, The Lumbar Spine (24) — patient self-management and education principle.
310 marks

Describe the role of anti-gravity muscles in maintaining postural stability.

Full answer →

Name the anti-gravity muscles and give the mechanism first (postural tone and the gamma system), then the balance strategies, then assessment and training.

  • What earns marks: the three names that lift this answer are the gamma motor system, the anticipatory postural adjustment, and the ankle strategy · give the mechanism (spindle bias) first, then the strategies, then assessment and training.
  • Anti-gravity muscles are the tonic extensors that hold the skeleton upright against gravity: soleus (the workhorse of standing), quadriceps, gluteus maximus, the lumbar erector spinae, and the neck extensors for the head.
  • They are the slow, fatigue-resistant, type-I fibre-rich muscles of the extensor thrust system.
  • In decerebrate rigidity their tone is exaggerated — classical proof that the nervous system is biased to keep the extensor chain ready.
  • In quadrupeds the anti-gravity muscles are the limb extensors; in upright humans the same system must fight gravity at every joint above the ground.
  • Standing is not a statue's pose: the body continuously sways over the base of support, and the anti-gravity muscles turn that sway into controlled sway.
  • Low-level tonic activity in soleus and erector spinae holds resting posture, driven by the gamma motor system, which keeps muscle spindles sensitive so the tonic stretch reflex can respond within milliseconds.
  • Postural tone is a reflex background, continuously recalibrated by the cerebellum and vestibular nuclei against visual, vestibular and proprioceptive input.
  • The result is a stable but adjustable column — like a stick balanced on a moving hand, where the 'hand' is the ankle strategy.
  • When balance is threatened, the muscles act in coordinated muscle synergy patterns, not one by one.
  • Small sway on a firm surface: the ankle strategy — gastrocnemius-soleus and hamstrings on posterior sway, tibialis anterior and quadriceps on anterior sway.
  • Faster or compliant-surface perturbation: the hip strategy — rapid trunk and thigh motion using the same extensor chain; large displacements: the stepping strategy.
  • These muscles also fire BEFORE movement: anticipatory postural adjustments — transversus abdominis and multifidus with the diaphragm pre-tension the trunk, and the soleus stiffens the ankle before the arm lifts.
  • Fatigue of the anti-gravity muscles shifts control to the hip strategy, increases sway velocity, and is a documented risk factor for falls in the elderly.
  • Assessment — static: Romberg test, sharpened Romberg, single-leg stance time (less than 10 seconds with eyes open flags falling risk in older adults), functional reach test, and limits-of-stability platform measures.
  • Assessment — dynamic: timed up-and-go, Berg Balance Scale, or computerised posturography which quantifies sway path and strategy use.
  • Test eyes open versus closed to separate the sensory contributions, and fatigue the muscles (repeated heel raises) to expose the reserve.
  • Training: progressive balance work (stable to unstable, double to single leg, eyes open to closed), perturbation training, eccentric and endurance work for soleus and quadriceps, and core stability training that restores the anticipatory postural adjustments.
  • Conclusion: postural stability is a reflex-managed equilibrium where the tonic extensor chain supplies the force against gravity, the spindle-gamma system supplies the sensitivity, and the CNS supplies the strategy; treat instability by training all three layers.

Soleus, erector spinae, gluteus maximus, quadriceps, neck extensors — the tonic extensor chain vs gravity.

Sources
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — postural reflexes and muscle spindle-gamma system.
  • Hislop, Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing (7) — anti-gravity muscle testing positions.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — balance and postural stability training progression.

Describe McKenzie's principles of mobilization.

Full answer →

Avoid 'McKenzie means extension exercises' — show response-guided loading, where centralisation decides the direction and the syndrome decides the technique; name all three syndromes.

  • What earns marks: do not write 'McKenzie means extension exercises' — the principle is RESPONSE-GUIDED loading · name all three syndromes with one treatment line each.
  • MDT (Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy), the McKenzie method, rests on one idea: the patient's symptomatic response to repeated end-range loading is the most reliable guide to classification and treatment.
  • Assessment begins with a full history and baseline symptom mapping (where the pain is now, how far it spreads, what makes it better and worse).
  • The examiner performs repeated movement testing — sagittal first (flexion, extension in lying and standing), then frontal plane if needed — five to ten repetitions at end range, watching the DISTAL extent of symptoms.
  • McKenzie deliberately says little about pathology; the behaviour of the pain under load is the diagnosis.
  • Centralisation: referred or radicular pain retreats proximally towards the midline spine in response to a specific repeated movement — the single best prognostic sign in MDT.
  • Peripheralisation is the opposite: the pain marches distally, and that movement is immediately withdrawn and avoided.
  • Directional preference is the movement direction that produces centralisation or lasting relief — most commonly extension in the lumbar spine; a patient with a directional preference is treated in that direction.
  • Derangement syndrome (most common): internal displacement of nuclear material causing mechanically changeable, intermittent pain that centralises or peripheralises.
  • Derangement treatment: repeated end-range movements in the directional preference (classically prone press-ups or standing extension); force is progressed only as far as needed to achieve centralisation.
  • Postural syndrome: pain only on sustained end-range static loading (slumped sitting in a young, normal spine), relieved instantly by position change; treatment is postural correction plus education, with no hands-on needed.
  • Dysfunction syndrome: shortening or scarring of tissue producing consistent end-range pain in a fixed direction that does not change with repetition (for example, flexion dysfunction after a healed disc episode).
  • Dysfunction treatment: static end-range stretching in the restricted — and painful — direction, remodelling the adapted tissue over weeks.
  • Always mention the 'other' category (non-mechanical presentations, red flags, chronic pain states) for red-flag safety.
  • Force progression ladder (only if the response is incomplete): patient-generated movement, then clinician overpressure, then sagittal mobilisation, then (rarely) manipulation — always re-testing centralisation after each step.
  • Second pillar: the patient treats the patient — exercises are home exercises performed ten times a day; the clinician finds, teaches and progresses them.
  • Maintenance: posture correction (lumbar roll, standing extension after prolonged sitting), regular self-mobilisation, and recurrence management.
  • Evidence: systematic reviews support directional preference as a real, clinically useful phenomenon, centralisation as a strong prognostic marker, and MDT as at least as effective as other conservative care for acute and subacute low back pain.
  • Conclusion: MDT is a classification-driven, assessment-led system where repeated end-range loading identifies a directional preference, defines one of three syndromes, and hands the treatment to the patient.

Repeated movements → centralisation / peripheralisation / no change → three syndromes.

Sources
  • McKenzie R & May S, The Lumbar Spine: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy (24).
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — spine mobilisation progression context.
  • Butler & Jones, Mobilisation of the Nervous System (26) — contrast with neurodynamic schools.

Describe the role of various external appliances used for rehabilitation in patients following L2-L3 disc prolapse.

Full answer →

Say that L2-L3 is upper lumbar, so a plain belt will not do — the orthosis must extend thoracically; and state the weaning principle (orthosis plus exercise, never instead).

  • What earns marks: avoid a generic 'lumbar belt' essay — L2-L3 is upper lumbar, so the orthosis must extend thoracically (TLSO logic) · state weaning — orthosis plus exercise, never orthosis instead of exercise.
  • An L2-L3 prolapse is an UPPER lumbar lesion: the segment moves mainly in the sagittal plane, and the extension-biased loading taught for L4-S1 must be applied with more caution this high.
  • The appliance has four jobs: limit painful flexion, raise intra-abdominal pressure so the abdominal cylinder shares spinal load, give proprioceptive feedback ('posture reminder'), and in the acute phase allow movement while protecting the healing annulus.
  • A well-fitted corset can reduce the load on the lumbar column by roughly a third during lifting.
  • An lumbosacral orthosis is a prescribed spinal support whose rigid panels and closure system control segmental motion — the umbrella term for most of what follows.
  • Soft canvas corset with abdominal binder: commonest in Indian practice — inexpensive, off the shelf, gives abdominal compression and posture cueing with little true motion control; suits the comfort phase.
  • Semi-rigid lumbosacral orthosis: corset with posterior moulded plastic or metal stays and paraspinal steels; controls flexion-extension partially — the workhorse for the four-to-six-week protected phase.
  • Rigid three-point lumbosacral orthosis (chairback or Williams-type): anterior and posterior panels with a three-point system (sternal/sacral and abdominal pads) that genuinely blocks lumbar flexion.
  • Rigid thoraco-lumbo-sacral orthosis: for an L2-L3 lesion, control must extend above the lesion, so the orthosis must include a thoracic band (Boston-type overlap or custom-moulded TLSO) — the key level-specific point.
  • Hyperextension orthosis (Jewett type): blocks flexion while allowing some extension, mainly post-fracture but worth naming.
  • Each of these works WITH the physiotherapy programme, never instead of it.
  • Ancillary appliances in the acute phase: an adjustable walking aid (rollator or cane on the opposite side) to reduce axial load and improve confidence; a firm mattress or bed board under a lumbar roll for sleeping; and log-rolling technique taught.
  • For daily activities: raised toilet seat and commode chair, long-handled reacher and shoe horn (dressing without trunk flexion), elevated chair with armrests, and a lumbar cushion for unavoidable sitting.
  • Prescription principles: fit at the level of the lesion with the pelvic band anchored on the sacrum, worn during activity and weaned at rest, and checked for pressure areas in our hot climate.
  • Pair from day one with an isometric abdominal and back programme — because every orthosis unloads the very muscles that must eventually take over.
  • Wearing schedule typically tapers over four to six weeks; prolonged bracing produces trunk muscle atrophy and dependence — the classic complication to warn about.
  • Evidence: randomised evidence suggests orthoses add only modest benefit over exercise-plus-advice alone for uncomplicated disc prolapse, so the modern role is a short, well-defined protective and confidence-building phase.
  • Conclusion: at L2-L3 the appliance must reach higher (TLSO logic), buy time for the annulus, use the abdominal cylinder to unload the segment, cue posture, and be withdrawn before dependency develops.

Three-point system blocks flexion; control must extend ABOVE L2.

Sources
  • Chui et al., Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation (18) — spinal orthosis designs and control levels.
  • Maxey & Magnusson (13) — orthotic prescription and wearing schedules.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — spinal intervention progression.
  • McKenzie & May, The Lumbar Spine (24) — loading considerations at upper lumbar levels.
610 marks

Describe the evidence-based electrotherapy management of fibromyalgia.

Full answer →

Frame electrotherapy as an adjunct to exercise and education, never a substitute, and grade each modality honestly as strong, moderate or weak evidence.

  • What earns marks: the scoring phrase is 'adjunct to exercise and education — never a substitute' · grade each modality as strong / moderate / weak evidence instead of listing every machine.
  • Fibromyalgia, by the Wolfe et al. American College of Rheumatology criteria, is chronic widespread pain lasting at least three months with somatic and cognitive symptoms — classified by the widespread pain index and symptom severity scale (the older 1990 criteria counted tender points out of 18).
  • It is a disorder of central pain processing: diffuse hyperexcitability with reduced descending inhibition, fatigue and non-restorative sleep.
  • Electrotherapy never treats the disease; it treats pain and sleep symptoms as an ADJUNCT to the cornerstones — graded aerobic exercise, education and cognitive-behavioural therapy.
  • Mechanism: by the gate control theory of Melzack and Wall, stimulating large-diameter A-beta afferents in the dorsal horn closes the gate on nociceptive transmission — high-frequency, sensory-intensity TENS exploits this.
  • Low-frequency, acupuncture-like TENS at motor intensity recruits endogenous opioid release.
  • Any modality must be judged by whether it increases activity and sleep, not by immediate pain relief alone, because the problem is central sensitisation.
  • TENS: the most studied; best used high-frequency (40–80 Hz per DeLisa; 70–100 Hz in practice), strong but comfortable, over the most symptomatic regions for 30 minutes, several times daily, self-applied for flares; trials show modest short-term pain reduction.
  • Interferential therapy (four-pole; beat 20–80 Hz per DeLisa, commonly 90–100 Hz for pain in Indian clinics): widely used with a similar gate-control rationale; comfort-oriented evidence, less trial support than TENS.
  • Microcurrent therapy (microamperage currents): small trials suggest pain and sleep benefit; evidence remains weak.
  • Electroacupuncture: systematic reviews find it better than sham for pain and stiffness in the short term — one of the better-supported electrical options.
  • Frequency-specific magnetic stimulation and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation target the central component directly; promising but not yet routine physiotherapy practice — mention them as emerging evidence.
  • Superficial heat (hot packs, warm showers before exercise) and warm-water balneotherapy or hydrotherapy are the strongest physical-agent options: randomised trials show durable improvements in pain, function and quality of life; cryotherapy has a role for local flares.
  • Evidence grading: strongest — warm-water exercise and graded land-based aerobic exercise (core, not adjunct); moderate — electroacupuncture, some TENS benefit for short-term pain; weak — interferential, microcurrent, static magnets.
  • Conclusion: an evidence-based electrotherapy plan uses TENS or electroacupuncture for symptomatic relief and heat or hydrotherapy to enable activity, always subordinate to graded exercise, sleep and education — and is reviewed against function, not pain scores alone.

Large fibres in, gate closes, pain falls (Melzack & Wall).

Sources
  • Wolfe F et al., American College of Rheumatology fibromyalgia criteria.
  • Melzack R & Wall PD, Pain mechanisms: a new theory, Science 1965.
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — pain physiology and descending inhibition.
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation (10) — chronic pain rehabilitation.
710 marks

Describe adjuvant therapies in managing pain.

Full answer →

Give the definition first, then classify adjuvants into four shelves (physical, hands-on, psychosocial, pharmacological), and close with the evidence that they multiply the engine.

  • What earns marks: definition marks are free — 'administered alongside primary treatment to enhance effect or reduce drug burden' — write it in the first line · classify into four shelves instead of a random list; structure turns a list into a 10-mark answer.
  • Definition: an adjuvant therapy is one administered ALONGSIDE the primary treatment to enhance its effect, address a component the primary therapy does not reach, or reduce overall drug burden.
  • In pain management the primary tools are exercise, manual therapy, education and analgesics; adjuvants are the supporting cast.
  • Mechanism: most adjuvants work through segmental gate control, descending inhibitory pathways, altered tissue fluid dynamics, or psychological (attention and expectancy) mechanisms — which is why they relieve pain without changing the disease.
  • Classify them as physical, hands-on and movement-based, psychosocial, and pharmacological — a four-shelf answer.
  • Physical — superficial heat (hot packs, paraffin wax baths for hand pain) reduces muscle spindle excitability and stiffness before exercise.
  • Physical — deep heat (ultrasound, 1 MHz) targets deeper fascia and tendon; cryotherapy reduces conduction velocity and acute inflammation after trauma.
  • Physical — topical counterirritation (menthol, methyl salicylate, capsaicin balms) stimulates superficial receptors to compete with nociceptive input; capsaicin also depletes substance P over days of use.
  • Physical — TENS and interferential therapy act as electrical adjuvants through the gate mechanism; time them around the active programme (heat before stretching, cold after loading).
  • Hands-on — massage (effleurage and petrissage) reduces perceived pain and muscle guarding via mechanoreceptor stimulation and improved local circulation; myofascial release and soft-tissue mobilisation address trigger points.
  • Hands-on — dry needling and acupuncture de-nociceptise trigger points and stir endogenous opioid release — moderate evidence in myofascial pain.
  • Hands-on — kinesio taping provides continuous cutaneous afferent input and tactile cueing of posture.
  • Movement and mind-body — relaxation techniques (progressive muscle relaxation, diaphragmatic breathing), yoga and meditation modulate sympathetic arousal and improve pain coping.
  • Pharmacological (know what the physician adds): adjuvant analgesics — tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline at low dose for neuropathic and fibromyalgia pain), serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, anticonvulsants (pregabalin, gabapentin), and topical lidocaine and capsaicin patches.
  • Psychosocial — cognitive-behavioural therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy, and guided imagery target catastrophising and fear-avoidance, the strongest drivers of chronicity.
  • Evidence: adjuvants reliably deliver short-term symptomatic relief and rarely change long-term outcomes alone; their value appears when combined with exercise, education and graded exposure.
  • Conclusion: adjuvant therapies are the multiplier, not the engine, of pain management — selected to remove the barriers (pain, stiffness, fear, arousal) that block the primary active treatment, timed around it, and reviewed by whether the patient can do more.

Adjuvants feed the engine (exercise + education), never replace it.

Sources
  • Melzack R & Wall PD, Science 1965 — gate control mechanism of most adjuvants.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — soft-tissue and physical agent adjuncts.
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — pain modulation pathways.
  • Wolfe F et al., ACR fibromyalgia criteria — context for adjuvant use in widespread pain.

Describe wrist ergonomics for a computer operator.

Full answer →

Give the neutral-wrist principle with the key numbers (extension beyond about 15 degrees, elbow near 90 degrees, RULA above 5), the workstation layout, and the breaks/education.

  • What earns marks: numbers buy marks — wrist extension beyond about 15 degrees is the danger zone; elbows near 90 degrees; RULA grand score above 5 needs prompt change · mention that palm rests are for pauses, not typing — a favourite examiner discriminating detail.
  • Mechanism: carpal tunnel pressure rises steeply when the wrist leaves neutral — wrist extension beyond about 15 degrees, plus sustained ulnar deviation and forearm pronation, increase pressure inside the tunnel.
  • Repetition matters: fast keyboard work can reach 8,000 to 12,000 keystrokes per hour — the exposure the NUDATA study linked to arm and elbow pain.
  • Add static loading, contact stress at the wrist rest, and cold or vibration, and you have the recipe for carpal tunnel syndrome, De Quervain's tenosynovitis and non-specific forearm pain.
  • Goal: keep the hand working on a neutral wrist posture — forearm supported, wrist straight, no lean — while the bigger joints (elbow at about 90 degrees, shoulders relaxed) absorb the posture.
  • Keyboard: flat or negatively tilted (back feet folded DOWN, not up), directly in front, at elbow height, and close to the body so the wrists need not extend to reach.
  • Mouse: beside the keyboard at the same height, size matched to the hand, operated with the whole arm; a keyboard tray with a mouse platform prevents reaching.
  • Wrist or palm rests: used during PAUSES, not while typing — leaning on them while typing creates contact stress.
  • Chair: height so the forearms are parallel to the floor, feet flat, lumbar support; forearms lightly supported on the chair arms or desk edge.
  • Monitor: top at or just below eye level, an arm's length away, so a flexed neck does not drag the whole kinetic chain down.
  • Desk: adequate depth so the monitor is not pushed back into extension-heavy reaching; document holder inline with the screen.
  • Indian setting: the commonest faults are laptop use at a low table (forced wrist and neck flexion) and shared workstations never adjusted for the individual.
  • Assessment: screen with the OSHA Computer Workstations eTool checklist, and quantify posture with RULA (the Rapid Upper Limb Assessment of McAtamney and Corlett) — a grand score above 5 demands prompt change.
  • Symptom survey (discomfort charts), keystroke rates and overtime patterns complete the picture; risk factors to hunt are deviation, extension, repetition, static hold, contact stress, cold and psychosocial pressure.
  • Work organisation: micropauses of 30-60 seconds every 20-30 minutes; stretch the wrist flexors and extensors; alternate tasks; keep typing load realistic with software break reminders.
  • Encourage early symptom reporting with a no-blame culture; educate the operator in self-checking neutral posture — the 'handshake' position is the memory hook.
  • Evidence: ergonomic interventions (adjusted workstation plus education plus breaks) reduce discomfort and symptoms in office workers more consistently than exercise alone, and combined ergonomic-plus-exercise programmes are most effective.
  • Conclusion: wrist ergonomics is the marriage of a neutral-wrist workstation (keyboard and mouse at elbow height, flat keyboard, palm rests for pauses only) with regular breaks and posture education — engineering first, behaviour second, both audited by RULA.

Neutral = the 'handshake' position for the wrist.

Sources

  • Cooper C, Fundamentals of Hand Therapy (21) — wrist pathology and activity modification.
  • Saunders, Hand and Upper Extremity Rehabilitation (20) — tendinopathy management context.
910 marks

Describe the role of assistive devices in industrial setups which work with heavy loads.

Full answer →

Open with the hierarchy of controls, give the NIOSH numbers (23 kg constant; lifting index above 1 = risk), list the device categories, and dismiss the back belt.

  • What earns marks: open with the hierarchy of controls — eliminate, engineer, redesign, administrate, protect · give the NIOSH numbers (23 kg constant for an ideal lift; lifting index above 1 flags risk) and dismiss the back belt explicitly.
  • Mechanism: during a freestyle stoop lift the lumbar disc compression can exceed the 3.4 kN action limit for repeated loading — approaching the NIOSH maximum permissible limit of about 6.4 kN — because the spine acts as a long lever with a short, poor-efficiency erector spinae moment arm.
  • The disc, not the muscle, is the weak link.
  • Manual handling is the single largest source of occupational injury in Indian industry — construction sites, godowns, warehouses and small-scale assembly units.
  • The professional answer does not begin with 'teach safe lifting'; it begins with the hierarchy of controls: eliminate the lift, engineer it away, redesign the task, change the work organisation, and only lastly rely on training and personal protective equipment.
  • Assistive devices are the engineering tier — the most effective one.
  • Category 1 — load movement instead of load lifting: trolleys, hand trucks, pallet trucks, conveyor belts, roller tracks and chutes (the cheapest, highest-yield tier).
  • Category 2 — position the load at waist height: lift tables, scissor lifts, tilt tables, turntables and self-levelling dispensers, so the worker never bends below knuckle height or reaches above shoulder height.
  • Category 3 — vertical handling: hoists, jib cranes, gantry cranes, vacuum tube lifters for sacks and sheet material, and powered stackers — removing the spine from the chain altogether.
  • Category 4 — tool-integrated supports: balancers and torque arms that absorb the weight and reaction of heavy power tools.
  • Emerging — passive industrial exoskeletons that support the shoulders or trunk during sustained overhead or stooped work; promising for fatigue, still accumulating safety evidence.
  • The back belt is NOT a reliable assistive device: evidence shows it does not prevent injury in untrained workers and may promote over-reliance — mention it to dismiss it correctly.
  • Assessment: the NIOSH lifting equation computes a recommended weight limit from horizontal distance, vertical height, travel distance, asymmetry, frequency and coupling quality (a constant of 23 kg for an ideal lift under it), giving a lifting index — a value above 1 means the task exceeds the recommended limit.
  • Supplement with postural screens (RULA or REBA) for the upper limb and whole body, and a walkthrough of the actual task in the actual shift pattern; the assessment drives the purchase, not the catalogue.
  • Human tier: manual-handling training (load close to the body, neutral spine with hip hinge, pivot not twist, team lifts above about 25 kg per person) and job rotation across loading tiers.
  • For the injured worker returning to heavy industry, a structured work hardening and work conditioning programme — simulated job tasks at real loads with cardiovascular conditioning and ergonomic education — has good evidence for return-to-work outcomes.
  • Evidence: engineering controls (mechanical aids, adjustable workstations) show consistent reductions in manual-handling injury rates, whereas lifting-training-only interventions have small and short-lived effects; back belts do not prevent low back injury.
  • Conclusion: assess with the NIOSH equation and RULA, then push the fix up the hierarchy — eliminate, then mechanise (trolleys, conveyors, hoists, lift tables), then position (waist-height zones), then prepare the worker with training and work hardening.

Zones make the risk visible; devices move every lift into green.

  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — work conditioning and functional progression.
  • OSHA Computer Workstations eTool — assessment checklist principles (adapted to manual handling walkthrough).
